P0001: Fuel Volume Regulator A Control Circuit/Open

The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure.
Connector at the regulator loose, corroded or unplugged
Solenoid coil of the regulator open
Broken wire in the harness, e.g. chafing or rodent damage
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
Engine cranks but does not start, or stalls (normally closed valve)
Loss of power or limp mode (normally open valve)

P0005: Fuel Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open

The fuel shutoff valve is a solenoid valve that opens or blocks the fuel supply. On diesel engines it is usually closed without current, so that the engine stops reliably when switched off. The engine control module energises it to let fuel flow and monitors its control circuit continuously. P0005 is set when this control circuit is open.
Wire or connector interrupted or corroded
Fuse or relay in the valve supply faulty
Output driver in the engine control module faulty
Engine cranks but does not start

P000A: A Camshaft Position Slow Response Bank 1

This monitor does not judge the end position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. The adjustment speed depends directly on oil flow, so worn or wrong oil and a partly clogged screen are the usual causes.
Oil too thick or too thin, sludged, or oil level low
Screen at the oil control valve partly clogged
Cam phaser leaking internally or worn
Generally weak oil pressure, e.g. worn oil pump or bearings

P000F: Fuel System Over Pressure Relief Valve Activated

On common-rail diesel and some gasoline direct-injection systems a spring-loaded pressure relief valve protects the rail and injectors: if pressure rises too far, it opens and returns fuel to the tank, often holding a reduced pressure for limp-home operation. The control module recognises the opening from the rail pressure signal and stores P000F.
Fuel volume regulator stuck open or without current, pump over-delivers
Rail pressure sensor reading wrong, control runs into overpressure
Pressure control valve faulty, where fitted
Fuel return line blocked or kinked
Relief valve itself leaking or fatigued
Sudden loss of power or limp mode

A solenoid valve routes engine oil to a valve control element on the intake side of bank 1. Depending on the manufacturer this is a valve lift changeover or a camshaft phaser. P0026 is a plausibility fault: the electrical control is in order, but the expected effect does not occur or comes too late.
Oil level too low, wrong viscosity or sludged oil
Feedback oil pressure switch faulty or leaking (systems with switch)
Screen in front of the solenoid clogged, or solenoid sticking
Mechanical fault in the valve train, e.g. locking pin or phaser sticking
Contact resistance in wiring or connector
Loss of power, no extra pull at higher engine speed
Rough idle possible if a phaser is affected

P0033: Turbocharger/Supercharger Bypass Valve A Control Circuit

The turbocharger bypass valve A is the compressor recirculation (diverter) valve: it connects the pressure side of the compressor with the intake side upstream of the turbocharger. It opens when the throttle closes quickly at high boost, so the compressor does not surge and the compressor wheel keeps its speed for the next acceleration.

On Ford's 6.7 diesel it means the injector's high side is shorted to its low side, reported within 0.3 s.

Injector coil shorted internally (too low resistance, overcurrent)
Short between supply and control wire in harness or connector
Driver stage in the engine module faulty
Misfire and rough running, misfire code P0306
Injector shut off, limp mode possible on diesels

P027A: Fuel Pump Module B Control Circuit/Open

On demand-controlled fuel systems the engine module does not drive the pump itself but sends a pump control module the desired pump output on a separate control line, usually as a duty cycle; the module reports back on a monitor line or via CAN. Module B is a second pump module, for example on dual-tank commercial vehicles.
Control line to the pump module open or shorted, often along the frame
Connector at the pump module corroded or wet (module often mounted on the frame)
Fuel shortage when running from the second tank

P027E: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity A Lower Than Expected

P027E is the cold-start counterpart of P026C: during cold start the engine gets less fuel than commanded, for example because a catalyst-heating injection does not arrive. The check probably works as in warm running, from airflow and lambda against the commanded quantity.
Rail pressure builds too slowly at cold start (filter, wax, pump)
Poor cold start, rough running when cold
P027F: Cold Start Fuel Injection Quantity A Higher Than Expected

P027F is the cold-start counterpart of P026D: during cold start the engine gets more fuel than commanded, for example from a leaking injector or an EGR valve or throttle in the wrong position that reduces fresh air. The check probably works as in warm running, from airflow and lambda against the commanded quantity.
EGR valve or intake/exhaust throttle in the wrong position (less fresh air)
Lambda/NOx sensor or airflow sensor reading wrong
White or black smoke after a cold start

Speed signal disturbed (loose contact, interference, tone wheel)
Usually no warning light, code only stored
Vehicle limits speed at its maximum
With a disturbed signal: jumping speedometer, odd shifting

High load in heat (trailer, mountain pass, stop-and-go)
Cooling or fan problem (clogged radiator, fan, thermostat, low coolant)
Oil cooler clogged or oil thermostat stuck
Oil temperature or level sensor reading too high
Low oil level or wrong oil

P037A: Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit Low

Diesel engines show the driver a wait-to-start lamp while the glow plugs preheat; the engine module switches it with a high-side driver. P037A means the lamp control circuit is too low – in practice a short to ground on the line to the instrument cluster.
Lamp control wire chafed through to ground between engine module and cluster
Lamp or LED driver in the instrument cluster shorted internally
Moisture or corrosion in the module or cluster connector
Driver in the engine module faulty
Glow plug light does not come on or stays dim
Check engine light on (GM after two trips)
Driver starts too early, possibly poor cold start
P037B: Glow Plug/Heater Indicator Control Circuit High

P037B is the counterpart of P037A: the control circuit of the wait-to-start lamp is too high, i.e. the line carries voltage although the engine module's driver is off, or the driver sees a short to battery voltage.

Fault in the instrument cluster feeding voltage back
Water damage in a connector bridging to a neighbouring pin
Driver in the engine module faulty
Glow plug light stays on or flickers
Check engine light on (after two trips)
P037C: Cold Start Camshaft Profile System Performance

To heat the catalyst quickly after a cold start, some engines select a particular camshaft profile; CARB counts altered valve timing among these cold-start measures and requires components of the cold-start strategy to have their own diagnostics. P037C checks whether the requested profile is actually engaged during this phase.
Profile actuator (sliding cam pin) sticking or not switching
Wrong oil viscosity or low oil level, mechanism stiff when cold
Rough running or stalling when cold (for example on remote start)

P0390: Camshaft Position Sensor B Circuit Bank 2

Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor; bank 2 is the side without cylinder 1, so the code only occurs on V and boxer engines with one exhaust cam sensor per bank. P0390 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive from bank 2 while the crankshaft turns.

Loss of power (bank 2 exhaust cam timing in its base position)

Chafing or water in harness or connector

P0B64: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense I Circuit Range/Performance

P0B64 is a rationality fault: channel I is connected and reads a believable number, yet it does not move with the other cells. GM's 2016 Chevrolet Volt compares the movement of each cell with the average; if channel I does not follow when the average moves by more than 0.022 V, 7 out of 8 seconds fail the check, Type A.
Channel I measuring input frozen at a constant value
Battery controller software misjudging the channel
High-resistance cell tap damping the signal
Reduced hybrid assist or electric range
P0B65: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense I Circuit Low

The 2012 GM two-mode hybrids show a detail worth knowing for P0B65: their battery pack control module only declares channel I, nickel-metal hydride block 9, too low when block 9 and its neighbour block 10 both read under 2 V, and only after 15 of 20 samples at 100 ms; the fault is Type B and needs two trips.
Channel I sense lead shorted to ground or a lower tap
Connector fault affecting adjacent blocks 9 and 10 (two-mode)
Failed measuring input in the battery controller
Engine runs more often, electric assist reduced
P0B66: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense I Circuit High
When channel I claims a voltage above what its cell or block can physically reach, the controller stores P0B66.
Channel I lead touching a higher-potential tap
Open reference or ground of the measuring chip
Genuinely overcharged cell after a charging control fault
P0B67: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense I Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

SAE J2012 reserves P0B67 for an unsteady signal on channel I, meaning readings that spike, drop and recover. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and none of the GM tables that define the other four channel I codes includes an erratic test.
Sense contact on channel I opening under vibration or heat
Corroded terminal in the module connector
Sporadic warning without a reproducible pattern
P0B68: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense J Circuit

For owners of a 2019 or 2020 Ford Fusion plug-in hybrid, P0B68 is best known from bulletin 23-2039: the car will not start, the battery energy control module stores one or more open sense line codes from P0B3B to P0B7C, and the prescribed repair is a complete high-voltage traction battery.
Internal traction battery failure, pack replacement (Ford Fusion PHEV 2019-2020)
Open sense wire or cell tap on channel J
Bad bus bar or splice connection near channel J
No start, vehicle does not become ready
Hybrid system warning on the cluster
P0B69: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense J Circuit Range/Performance

P0B69 is set when channel J is electrically present but its readings do not behave plausibly. GM's BAS Plus mild hybrid explains the logic most clearly: once the average cell voltage moves by more than 0.045 V, the cell under test must move in the same direction and by at least half as much; 20 failures in 40 samples set the code as Type B, two trips.
Channel J input reacting too little to real voltage changes
Calibration error in the battery controller
P0B6A: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense J Circuit Low

A reading of almost zero on channel J points to the measurement, not to the cell, and that is what P0B6A records. In GM's lithium-ion systems (2016 and 2019 tables) the battery energy control module sets it at 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A.
Channel J lead chafed through and shorted to ground
Damaged measuring input on the monitoring board
Cell on channel J internally shorted
P0B6B: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense J Circuit High

On GM's 2012 two-mode hybrid trucks the battery is divided into 20 nickel-metal hydride blocks, and channel J is block 10. The battery pack control module samples it every 100 ms while the 12 V supply is between 9 and 18 V; if block 10 reports more than 23 V in 15 of 20 samples, P0B6B is stored as Type B, so the MIL comes on after the second trip.
Channel J lead shorted to a higher block or cell tap
Faulty measuring input in the battery pack control module
MIL after the second drive (Type B systems)
P0B6C: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense J Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
No manufacturer documents P0B6C publicly. The code stands for a channel J signal that is unstable, with brief jumps or dropouts, as opposed to the steady faults covered by P0B68 to P0B6B.
Marginal contact in the channel J harness or connector
Cracked solder joint on the monitoring electronics
P0B6D: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense K Circuit

P0B6D marks an open circuit on voltage sense K, the eleventh cell measuring channel. GM has used the code since its first published hybrid tables: in 2011 the open-line test already checked bus bar voltages, flagging more than 0.7 V.
Loose or corroded bus bar connection at the channel K tap
Internal traction battery fault, pack replacement (Ford Fusion PHEV)
Broken sense wire between cells and monitoring board
Hybrid or EV system warning with MIL
P0B6E: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense K Circuit Range/Performance
In a nickel-metal hydride pack with 20 equal blocks, twenty times one block voltage should roughly equal the whole pack voltage.
Block or cell voltage measurement of channel K out of calibration
Pack voltage sensor reading off, distorting the comparison
Measuring input stuck at one value
Less electric assist, more engine running
P0B6F: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense K Circuit Low

GM's BAS Plus mild hybrid, the eAssist system in table 13OBDG05C, gives P0B6F a simple rule: if the cell sense line for channel K measures below 1.4 V in 7 of 10 samples at 200 ms while the 12 V supply is above 8.8 V, the code is stored as Type B, two trips.
Channel K sense line shorted to ground or a lower tap
Failed measuring input in the battery interface module
Blown protective element in the sense line
Hybrid warning and MIL after the second trip
Auto stop and electric assist disabled
P0B70: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense K Circuit High

P0B70 says that cell voltage K reads too high to be genuine. GM's 2019 battery energy control module sets it at 4.8 V or more, held for 1.4 s within 2 s, as a Type A fault with immediate MIL, and only when no communication loss, open sense line or internal module fault takes precedence.
Channel K lead in contact with a higher tap
Floating measuring input after loss of its lower reference
P0B71: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense K Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B71 belongs to the unsteady fault type: the channel K reading flickers or drops out momentarily without staying beyond a fixed limit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Fretting corrosion on channel K connector terminals
Sense harness under strain losing contact with movement
Occasional short loss of electric power
P0B72: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense L Circuit

P0B72 reports an open circuit on voltage sense L, the twelfth channel. One detail sets it apart from its neighbours: GM's 2011 hybrid tables list every open sense line code from P0B3B upward except P0B72 (and P0B90), so the early system did not use it, while L's range, low and high codes were present. Later GM tables include it.
Open sense lead, crimp or cell tap on channel L
Internal traction battery failure, pack replacement (Ford Fusion PHEV)
High-resistance splice or bus bar joint
No start or no ready mode
P0B73: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense L Circuit Range/Performance

Channel L delivers a value, but P0B73 tells you that the value is not credible. GM checks this in three ways. The 2016 Chevrolet Volt and the 2019 lithium-ion systems test whether cell L moves in the same direction as the average once that average changes by more than 0.022 V, failing 7 of 8 seconds or 35 of 40 samples respectively, Type A.
Channel L input not following real cell voltage changes
Battery controller software or calibration issue
Corroded cell tap slowing the signal
P0B74: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense L Circuit Low

P0B74 is set when channel L reads implausibly low. On the 2012 GM two-mode hybrids, where L is nickel-metal hydride block 12 of 20, the battery pack control module needs both block 12 and block 13 under 2 V in 15 of 20 samples before it stores the code as Type B; no battery control module fault P0A1F may be active.
Channel L sense lead shorted to a lower potential
Defective measuring input in the battery controller
Cell or block on channel L actually failed
P0B75: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense L Circuit High

With P0B75 the battery controller rejects channel L because it reads above any value a real cell or block can reach. GM's lithium-ion systems in the 2016 Volt and the 2019 tables set it at 4.8 V or more over 1.4 s in a 2 s window, Type A, one trip; GM's BAS Plus mild hybrid at above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B.
Channel L lead touching a higher tap
Floating measuring input after an open reference line
Real overvoltage of the cell after a charging fault
MIL and hybrid or EV warning
P0B76: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense L Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B76 closes the channel L group and covers an erratic signal: values that jump or vanish briefly while the circuit otherwise works.
Intermittent contact at the channel L cell tap
Cracked solder joint on the monitoring board
Warning clears after restart and comes back
P0B77: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense M Circuit

P0B77 flags an open or high-resistance tap on voltage sense M, the thirteenth cell channel. GM's 2019 battery energy control module checks seven cases: adjacent cells differing by 1.3 V or more, a balancing gate reading below 36 mV, or splice voltages above 0.1 V (0.5 V at a busbar splice). M is the last channel there with the short 0.6 s window, Type A.
Open or corroded tap of sense lead M at the cell connector
Fault inside the traction battery (Ford Fusion PHEV TSB 23-2039)
High resistance at a splice or busbar joint in the sense path
MIL with hybrid or EV system warning
Vehicle may not start or go into ready mode
P0B78: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense M Circuit Range/Performance

With P0B78 the controller doubts the reading of channel M rather than its wiring. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain processor watches for a frozen value: whenever the average of all cells moves by more than 0.022 V, cell M must follow by at least 0.005 V in the same direction, and 35 failures in 40 samples at 100 ms set a Type A fault.
Measuring channel M stuck at a fixed value
Battery controller software needing an update
Block 13 voltage drifting from the pack on two-mode NiMH packs
MIL on, often without noticeable driving change
P0B79: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense M Circuit Low

P0B79 means that the voltage reported for sense M is too low to be real. GM's lithium-ion battery controllers of 2016 and 2019 set it at 0.2 V or less, held for 1.4 s inside a 2 s window, Type A, and only while no open sense line fault is active, so a broken lead is reported by P0B77 first.
Sense lead M shorted to ground or a lower cell potential
Failed measuring input on the monitoring board
Cell or NiMH block on channel M actually collapsed
MIL and service hybrid or EV system message
P0B7A: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense M Circuit High

A reading on channel M above what any healthy cell can deliver produces P0B7A. For lithium-ion packs GM sets the line at 4.8 V or more for 1.4 s in a 2 s window and treats it as Type A, illuminating the MIL on the first trip. The BAS Plus mild hybrid already reacts above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples, Type B.
Sense lead M in contact with a higher cell potential
Measuring input of channel M reading high
Real overvoltage of the cell after a balancing fault
MIL on from the first trip (GM lithium-ion, Type A)
P0B7B: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense M Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0B7B is reserved for a sense M signal that flickers: short dropouts or jumps while the circuit is otherwise intact. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's tables for channel M contain open, plausibility, low and high tests but no erratic test, and Ford's Fusion bulletin lists only the open-circuit code P0B77.
Loose crimp or connector at the channel M tap
Chafed wire in the cell sense harness
Cracked solder joint on the monitoring board
Hybrid warning appearing and clearing again
P0B7C: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense N Circuit

Voltage sense N, the fourteenth channel, reports a broken or high-resistance sense lead with P0B7C. It is the last code in Ford's TSB 23-2039: 2019-2020 Fusion plug-in hybrids that fail to start with any open-circuit code from P0B3B up to P0B7C get a replacement traction battery; the bulletin names no channel beyond N.
Internal traction battery fault (Ford Fusion PHEV 2019-2020)
Sense lead N broken or with excessive resistance
Fault on the cell monitoring board
No start or vehicle does not become ready
MIL and stop-safely or service message
P0B7D: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense N Circuit Range/Performance
P0B7D concerns a channel N value that stays inside its limits yet does not behave like a real cell.
Channel N value not tracking the other cells
Block 14 or 15 voltage mismatch on two-mode NiMH packs
Shorter electric range or less assist
P0B7E: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense N Circuit Low

P0B7E sets when channel N reads below the lower plausibility limit. GM's 2016 program with a separate battery sense module uses less than 0.20 V and needs 14 failures in 18 samples, about 1.8 s at 100 ms each, before a Type A fault; the open-circuit test must not be failing at the same time.
Sense lead N shorted to a lower potential
Damaged input stage in the sense module
Deeply discharged or failed cell on channel N
MIL from the first trip on lithium-ion GM systems
Combustion engine does not shut off at standstill
P0B7F: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense N Circuit High

Channel N reporting more voltage than a cell can hold leads to P0B7F. GM uses three thresholds depending on the system: 4.8 V or more for 1.4 s in 2 s on most lithium-ion battery controllers, above 4.90 V in 14 of 18 samples on the 2016 program with a separate sense module, both Type A, and above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples on the BAS Plus mild hybrid, Type B.…
Sense lead N touching a higher potential
Drifted measuring input in the battery controller
Real overvoltage of the cell on channel N
MIL and warning in the instrument cluster
P0B80: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense N Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0B80 describes an unsteady channel N signal: the voltage drops out or jumps for moments, then looks normal again. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Contact at the N tap opening under vibration
Fretting corrosion in the sense harness connector
Solder joint cracking with temperature cycles
P0B81: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense O Circuit

P0B81 stands for an open sense lead on channel O, the fifteenth cell tap. GM has used it from the start: the 2011 Volt battery tables already list P0B81 among the open sense line codes and detect, among other cases, a busbar connection voltage above 0.7 V.
Loose or high-resistance busbar joint at the O tap
Broken sense wire O in the battery harness
Reduced power or no electric drive
P0B82: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense O Circuit Range/Performance

P0B82 is a plausibility verdict on channel O. GM's 2016 program with a battery sense module asks cell O to trend at least 0.002 V in the direction of the average whenever the average moves by more than 0.022 V; 35 failed evaluations out of 40 set a Type A code. The 2019 controllers use the same logic with 0.005 V.
Channel O reading frozen in the monitoring electronics
Rising resistance in the O sense tap distorting the reading
State of charge display jumps or is inaccurate
P0B83: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense O Circuit Low

P0B83 reports that channel O reads implausibly low. It is not the same as an open lead: GM's lithium-ion controllers run this check only while no open sense line fault is present, so a broken wire shows as P0B81 instead. The low limit there is 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A.
Short in the O sense path towards ground or a lower cell
P0B84: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense O Circuit High

P0B84 is stored when channel O sits above the upper limit of a credible cell voltage. For GM lithium-ion packs that limit is 4.8 V, held 1.4 s in a 2 s window, Type A; the 2016 program with a separate sense module tolerates up to 4.90 V and counts 14 failures in 18 samples, also Type A.
Sense lead O shorted to a higher cell tap
Monitoring input of channel O reading too high
P0B85: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense O Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0B85 would mark a channel O signal that is present but unsteady, with spikes or brief gaps. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; even GM, whose public tables cover channel O in detail from 2011 onward, defines only the open, rationality, low and high tests for it.
Loose busbar screw changing contact resistance at tap O
Moisture or corrosion in the sense harness connector
Cracked joint on the monitoring board
P0B86: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense P Circuit
P0B86 belongs to channel P, the sixteenth sense lead, and indicates that this lead has lost its connection to the cell.
Sense lead P open at the cell tap or connector
Excessive resistance in the sense line (corrosion, loose screw)
Defective input of the sense module
MIL and hybrid system fault message
Vehicle runs only on the engine or with reduced power
P0B87: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense P Circuit Range/Performance

P0B87 says channel P is delivering numbers that do not fit the rest of the battery. On GM's BAS Plus mild hybrid the cell under test must move at least 50 percent as far as the average cell voltage; if not, 20 failures in 40 samples set the code as Type B, i.e. MIL after two trips.
Measuring electronics for channel P out of tolerance
Software or calibration of the battery controller
NiMH block 16 or 17 out of balance with the pack
MIL after two trips on Type B systems
Engine start-stop or electric assist less frequent
P0B88: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense P Circuit Low

A too-low value on sense P, the sixteenth channel, is what P0B88 records. GM's BAS Plus mild hybrid sets it at a cell sense line below 1.4 V for 7 of 10 samples, sampled every 200 ms and only with the 12 V battery above 8.8 V; it rates the fault Type B.
Lead P shorted to a lower potential or chassis
Defective input in the battery interface module
P0B89: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense P Circuit High

P0B89 covers the opposite case to P0B88: the voltage reported on channel P is above the plausible range. GM's 2012 two-mode hybrids assign P to NiMH block 16 and set the code when the block exceeds 23 V in 15 of 20 samples at 100 ms, Type B, provided no battery controller fault P0A1F is active.
Lead P in contact with a higher cell tap
Input fault in the cell monitoring electronics
Genuine overvoltage of the cell or block
P0B8A: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense P Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0B8A is the erratic-signal member of the channel P group. There is no public manufacturer documentation for it: GM describes open, rationality, low and high diagnostics for sense P in its 2016 and 2019 tables, but none for an intermittent signal, and the Ford bulletins stop at channel N.
Fatigued wire at a bend of the sense harness
Connector losing contact as the pack warms up
Sporadic fault in the cell monitoring chip
Warning lamp that goes out again
Occasional engine start without demand on hybrids
P0B8B: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Q Circuit

P0B8B marks an open circuit on voltage sense Q, the seventeenth channel. In GM's BAS Plus mild hybrid tables Q is the first channel whose open test is blocked by code P1B37 instead of P1B36, which suggests it sits in the next measuring group of the battery interface module; the criterion stays lines N and N-1 below 1.4 V with a change above 0.5 V in 200 ms,…
Sense lead Q open between cell tap and module
Loose or corroded connector at the second measuring group
Fault in the battery interface module
P0B8C: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Q Circuit Range/Performance

P0B8C is set when channel Q reports a voltage that fails the plausibility test against the other cells or the pack. On GM's 2012 two-mode trucks Q is NiMH block 17; the battery pack control module takes block 17 and block 18, multiplies each by twenty and compares with the measured pack voltage, failing beyond 70 V in 160 of 170 samples, Type B.
Block 17 or 18 voltage deviating on two-mode NiMH packs
MIL with little change in driving
P0B8D: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Q Circuit Low

P0B8D reports a voltage on sense Q below the lowest credible cell value. GM's lithium-ion battery controllers in the 2016 and 2019 tables use 0.2 V or less for 1.4 s within 2 s, Type A, and the 2016 program with a separate sense module 0.20 V with 14 of 18 samples. GM's BAS Plus mild hybrid applies 1.4 V, 7 of 10 samples, Type B.
Short in the Q sense path to a lower potential
Engine runs more often on hybrids
P0B8E: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Q Circuit High

Channel Q reporting an implausibly high voltage sets P0B8E. On the 2012 GM two-mode hybrids, where Q is NiMH block 17, the limit is 23 V for 15 of 20 samples, Type B, checked only while the 12 V system lies between 9 and 18 V.
Damaged harness letting lead Q touch the next tap
Measuring input of channel Q reading high
Real cell overvoltage after a balancing failure
P0B8F: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense Q Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0B8F closes the channel Q group and stands for a sense Q signal that is erratic rather than absent or out of range. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's tables for sense Q, from the 2011 Volt to the 2019 battery controllers, list circuit, range, low and high monitors only, and the Ford Fusion bulletin ends four channels earlier at N.
Cracked crimp at the channel Q tap
Damaged flexible circuit between cells and monitoring board
Cold solder joint at the measuring chip
Power briefly reduced, normal after restart

P0B90 is stored when the battery controller concludes that the tap of sense R, the eighteenth cell channel, is open or too resistive. Loose, corroded or broken tap of sense lead R
Excessive resistance at a splice or busbar joint feeding channel R
Faulty measuring or balancing input on the cell monitoring board
MIL with service hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced propulsion power or no ready mode
P0B91: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit Range/Performance

Here the wiring of sense R is intact, but its value does not behave like a real cell. GM's 2019 hybrid powertrain processor demands that cell R moves at least 0.005 V in the same direction whenever the cell average shifts by more than 0.022 V; 35 failures out of 40 samples at 100 ms give a Type A fault.
Measuring channel R reporting a stuck value

P0B93: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense R Circuit High

P0B95: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit
P0B95 reports that the sense S lead, channel nineteen, no longer connects its cell reliably to the monitoring electronics.

Defective input of the battery sensor module for channel S

P0B96: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Range/Performance

P0B98: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit High

P0B99: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense S Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0B99 is the erratic variant within the sense S group. A public manufacturer description does not exist. GM's tables cover channel S from the 2011 Volt via the 2012 two-mode trucks and eAssist to the 2019 controllers, yet only with circuit, range, low and high codes (P0B95 to P0B98).

P0B9A: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit
P0B9A is the open-circuit code for sense T, the twentieth cell channel. GM uses it only on lithium-ion packs.
Open sense lead T at the cell tab or connector

P0B9B: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Range/Performance

P0B9D: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit High

P0B9E: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense T Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0B9F: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit

P0BA0: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Range/Performance

P0BA0 tells the technician that channel U gives a number, but the number does not move with the pack. GM checks this rationality only on lithium-ion systems, since the two-mode NiMH trucks end at block 20.
Measuring channel U holding a fixed value
Software or calibration issue in the battery controller

P0BA1: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Low

P0BA1 is stored when sense U reads close to zero. GM's lithium-ion controllers of the 2016 Volt and ELR and of 2019 treat 0.2 V or less over 1.4 s in a 2 s window as a Type A fault, provided no open sense line, lost slave communication or balancing fault is already active.

P0BA2 flags an excessive voltage on channel U. GM's eAssist mild hybrid uses the lowest threshold of the documented systems: above 4.65 V in 7 of 10 samples with the 12 V supply above 8.8 V, Type B.

MIL and hybrid or EV warning
P0BA3: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense U Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

Within the sense U group, P0BA3 is the slot for a signal that is present but unsteady. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM, the only maker whose tables cover channel U in detail, uses P0B9F to P0BA2 and nothing more.
Fatigued crimp on sense lead U
Loose fastener at the busbar tap of channel U

P0BA4: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit
P0BA4 reports an open or poorly connected sense V lead, the twenty-second channel and the last before W begins at P0BA9.

High-resistance splice or busbar joint on channel V

MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Vehicle may not become ready to drive
P0BA5: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sense V Circuit Range/Performance

P0BA5 describes a sense V value that stays within limits but fails a rationality check against the other cells. GM's 16OBDG02 programme demands a trend of at least 0.002 V in the same direction as the average whenever that average moves more than 0.022 V, with 35 failures in 40 evaluations giving Type A.

P0C16: Drive Motor B Inverter Phase W Over Temperature

P0C16 is set by the motor B inverter when phase W runs too hot and the temperature sensor itself shows no fault. GM's tables give PIM sensor F above 98 °C for the 2011 Volt, above 88 °C with an 85 °C reset for the 2012 two-mode trucks, and 131 °C for 1.2 s within 2 s for the 2016 Volt, with 1.5 s in the 2019 table; each is Type A, one trip.
Low coolant level or air in the power electronics loop
Electric coolant pump of the inverter failed or blocked
Dirty low-temperature radiator or inoperative fan
Malfunction indicator lamp after one drive
Reduced propulsion, notably at high load or high ambient temperature
P0C17: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Not Learned

P0C17 means the controller has no valid learned offset for the resolver of motor A, which it needs to align rotor position with the stator field. GM runs the learn at key-off and sets the code if it fails without a stored value: motor speed above 50 rpm, DC voltage below 192 V (200 V on the 2016 Volt), phase current below 15 A or a learn time over 1.4 s.
Offset learn not performed after replacing the inverter, motor or resolver
High voltage not reaching the inverter during the learn, e.g. contactor or HV cable fault
Loose three-phase ring terminals after a repair
Engine starts and stalls or will not start after a repair
Malfunction indicator lamp with reduced propulsion message
P0C18: Drive Motor B Position Sensor Not Learned

P0C18 is the motor B version of P0C17: the resolver offset of the second motor has not been learned and no valid earlier value is stored. GM performs the learn at key-off; it fails if motor speed exceeds 50 rpm, DC voltage stays below 192 V, phase current stays below 15 A or the learn takes longer than 1.4 s.
Offset learn not completed after replacing the inverter, motor B or its resolver
No high voltage at the drive motor control module, e.g. contactor fault or disconnected HV cable
Control module needs reprogramming to enable a wide position sensor learn
Malfunction indicator lamp after a repair or module programming
Reduced propulsion or vehicle will not enter ready mode
Motor B unavailable for driving or charging
P0C19: Drive Motor A Torque Delivered Performance

P0C19 is a plausibility check: the torque that motor A actually delivers, calculated by the motor control processor, does not follow the slewed torque command. GM sets it when the difference exceeds 123 Nm for 0.1875 s within 0.2 s on the 2016 and 2018 tables, Type A, one trip; eAssist uses 36 Nm as Type B, two trips.
Implausible rotor position signal from the motor A resolver or its wiring
Faulty phase current sensing distorting the calculated torque
Internal fault of the inverter power stage or motor winding
Electric drive shuts off and the engine takes over
Engine stop-start no longer works or a service hybrid system warning appears
P0C1A: Drive Motor B Torque Delivered Performance

P0C1A compares the torque command for motor B with the torque the motor control processor calculates as actually delivered. GM's 2016, 2018 and 2019 tables set it when the difference exceeds 132 Nm for 0.1875 s in a 0.2 s window, Type A, one trip, and only while listed resolver and motor control faults are inactive.
Short in the internal transmission wiring connector (Chrysler Pacifica Hybrid 21-008-23)
Implausible rotor position signal from the motor B resolver
Hybrid control or inverter module software requiring an update
Faulty phase current sensing for motor B
Vehicle in limp mode with reduced propulsion
Hybrid system warning, engine runs more often
P0C1B: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Too High
P0C1B is a protection code: the electronics that drive the auxiliary transmission fluid pump measure a valid but excessive internal temperature. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
High transmission fluid temperature from heavy load, towing or a weak fluid cooler
Pump running against high resistance (binding, clogged filter) and heating its driver
Poor heat transfer from the module (mounting, contamination) or internal module fault
Transmission or hybrid warning, MIL depending on manufacturer
Harsh engagement when driving off after a stop
P0C1C: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit

P0C1C is the general circuit fault of the temperature sensor inside the auxiliary pump control module, used when the signal is invalid without fitting the low, high or range checks. No manufacturer documents it publicly.
Temperature sensor or its measuring circuit on the module board faulty
Unstable supply or ground of the pump module distorting the sensor reading
Moisture or fluid inside the module housing
P0C1D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P0C1D means the internal temperature sensor of the auxiliary pump module delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit the other temperatures in the vehicle. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Board temperature sensor drifted or measuring circuit out of tolerance
Reference value wrong because the transmission fluid or coolant temperature sensor is faulty
Internal fault of the pump control module
P0C1E: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit Low

P0C1E reports that the signal voltage of the module's internal temperature sensor is below its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor, low voltage corresponds to a very high temperature, so a short to ground looks like an overheated board. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Board temperature sensor or its signal path shorted to ground inside the module
Measuring circuit of the pump control module faulty
Fluid or moisture on the module board
Pump switched off as if overheated, auto-stop unavailable
P0C1F: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor Circuit High

P0C1F means the internal temperature sensor of the auxiliary pump module delivers a voltage above its valid range, which for an NTC thermistor reads as an implausibly cold board and usually indicates an open sensor path. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Board temperature sensor open or its solder joint cracked
Measuring circuit of the pump control module faulty
Ground offset at the pump module shifting the sensor voltage
Start-stop restricted, pump in protective mode
P0C20: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit/Open
P0C20 means at least one of the three motor phases of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump carries no current, typically an open lead, terminal or winding.
Motor connector of the pump not fully seated, or loose phase terminal
Open phase lead between pump inverter and motor
Power switch of one phase in the pump inverter not conducting
Open winding in the pump motor
MIL and Service Vehicle Soon message
Reduced propulsion or no electric drive mode
P0C21: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit Low

P0C21 reports a low condition on the phase U, V or W circuits of the auxiliary pump motor, usually a phase lead shorted to ground or a voltage at a phase terminal that stays below what the inverter commands. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Phase lead chafed through and shorted to ground or the transmission case
Transmission fluid or water in the motor connector creating a leakage path
Low-side switch or phase sensing in the pump inverter faulty
Motor winding shorted to the stator core
MIL and transmission or hybrid warning
Auxiliary pump off, no engine auto-stop
P0C22: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Phase U-V-W Circuit High

P0C22 reports a high condition on the U-V-W phase circuits of the auxiliary pump motor, for example a phase lead shorted to the supply or a phase voltage that stays high while the inverter should pull it down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Phase lead shorted to supply voltage or to another phase
High-side switch of the pump inverter stuck conducting
Phase current sensing in the inverter reads too high
Shorted turns in the pump motor winding
MIL and hybrid or transmission warning
Pump shuts down, harsh engagement after stops
P0C23: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit/Open

P0C23 is set by the controlling module, usually the PCM, TCM or hybrid controller, when the circuit to the auxiliary pump control module is open. J2012 does not name the line further; in practice it is the command or enable wire.
Open command or enable wire between controller and pump module
Pushed-out or corroded terminal at the pump module or controller connector
Input stage of the pump control module faulty
Harsh engagement after an engine stop
P0C24: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit Low

P0C24 means the circuit from the controlling module to the auxiliary pump control module is held low, typically a short to ground on the command line. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Command wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed at the transmission case
Fluid or corrosion in the pump connector pulling the line low
Output stage in the PCM/TCM or input of the pump module faulty
P0C25: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Circuit High

P0C25 reports that the circuit from the controlling module to the auxiliary pump control module sits high, for instance a command wire shorted to battery voltage or an output that cannot pull the line down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Command wire shorted to battery or another supply voltage
Output stage in the PCM/TCM stuck high
Input stage of the pump control module faulty
Pump runs continuously or start-stop is disabled
P0C26: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current

P0C26 is the general motor current fault of auxiliary pump A: the current drawn does not match what the commanded operating point should need, without clearly being too low or too high. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Low or aerated transmission fluid at the pump intake
Pump binding or contaminated, changing the motor load
Current sensing in the pump driver implausible
Outdated control software of the pump or controlling module
P0C27: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current Low

P0C27 means motor A of the auxiliary transmission fluid pump draws less current than expected, a sign that the pump is not loaded, for example because it sucks air or turns without delivering. Ford documents it twice.
Air entering the pump supply tube (Ford 6F35, new tube with check ball)
Calibration of PCM and hybrid module (Ford Fusion/C-Max Energi)
Low transmission fluid level letting the pump draw air
High resistance or open circuit in the pump motor wiring
Harsh transmission engagement after a start-stop event
P0C28: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Current High

P0C28 is the overcurrent protection of auxiliary pump motor A. GM uses it on Volt, ELR and later hybrids: the inverter trips when any of the U, V or W phases exceeds 35 A, in 2016 within about 4 ms of a 62 ms window, or when the d-axis current falls below a stator temperature limit, Type A, MIL on the first trip.
Pump control software faulty (Cadillac CT6 update 18199, Ford Energi TSB 18-2282)
Pump seized, contaminated or running against blocked flow
Short between motor phases or to ground
Current sensing or power stage in the pump inverter faulty
Auxiliary pump shuts down, no auto-stop or electric mode
P0C29: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Driver Circuit Performance
P0C29 means the driver stage of auxiliary pump A does not behave as commanded, for instance the pump does not reach its target or the activation is reported as implausible.
Auxiliary hydraulic pump V475 of early production faulty (VW/Audi 0GC)
Poor contact at the pump electrical connection
Transmission control software not updated per service action
Gearbox Malfunction warning in the instrument cluster
Consequential clutch or gear actuator codes, limp mode
P0C2A: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Stalled
P0C2A means motor A of the auxiliary pump is commanded but does not turn, or turns far slower than required.
Auxiliary pump seized or jammed by debris (Ford F-150 2.7L replaces the pump)
PCM calibration causing false stall detection (Ford TSB 17-2056)
Very cold, thick fluid or wrong fluid type raising drag
Open phase so the motor cannot develop torque
Start-stop inactive, harsh engagement after stops
P0C2B: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal
P0C2B concerns the status signal the auxiliary pump control module sends back to the controlling module.
Wiring or terminal tension fault between hybrid controller and pump control module
Early pump control module (GM date code 089-11 or older)
Key held in crank for a long time during a no-start
Bumps, lulls or surges around auto-stops
P0C2C: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Range/Performance

P0C2C means the feedback signal from the auxiliary pump control module is present and electrically valid but does not make sense, for example a reported speed or status that contradicts the command. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Electronics of the pump module reporting wrong status or speed
Intermittent contact on the feedback line distorting the signal
Pump not following the command mechanically, so feedback and command differ
Reduced propulsion power or no start-stop
P0C2D: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal Low

P0C2D reports that the feedback signal from the electric transmission fluid pump module stays low, below its valid range. GM documents it for the 2021-23 Chevrolet Bolt EV and 2022 Bolt EUV in bulletin 21-NA-148: the driver sees Propulsion Power is Reduced and a Service Vehicle Soon lamp, with P0C2D, P2797 or P2798 stored.
Faulty solder joints in the electric transmission fluid pump (Chevrolet Bolt, GM 21-NA-148)
P0C2E: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump Control Module Feedback Signal High

P0C2E means the feedback line from the auxiliary pump control module sits above its valid range, for example shorted to supply voltage or no longer pulled down by the module. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly.
Feedback line shorted to supply voltage
Output stage of the pump control module no longer switching
Lost ground at the pump module letting the line float high
MIL or Service Vehicle Soon lamp
P0C2F: Internal Control Module Drive Motor/Generator - Engine Speed Sensor Performance
P0C2F is an internal plausibility check of the hybrid control processor: the engine speed it reads through its own sensor path must match other speed information.
Control module software flagging the comparison falsely (Ford Mach-E, fixed by reprogramming)
Speed signals disagree because of a faulty input or a disturbed CAN signal
Internal fault of the hybrid control module
One pedal drive or regenerative functions switched off (Ford Mach-E)
Reduced hybrid assist or limited power
P0C30: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack State of Charge High

P0C30 is the counterpart of P0A7D: the battery controller finds that the state of charge of the high-voltage pack stays above its usable window. CARB requires hybrid OBD to flag a state of charge that can no longer be kept inside the manufacturer's range.
Wrong SOC estimate from a drifting pack current or voltage measurement
Battery or hybrid control software not drawing the charge down as intended
Electric assist blocked by another fault, so the pack cannot discharge
Changed brake pedal feel and higher fuel consumption
P0C31: P0C31 reports that the cooling circuit of a second power inverter does not remove heat as expected; inverter A has its own code, P0A93. Vehicles with two separately cooled power electronics units, for example a front and a rear drive unit, need this second code.
Low coolant level or air trapped in the inverter B circuit
Weak or failed electric coolant pump of the circuit
Clogged radiator or inoperative cooling fan
Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Reduced drive power, especially under load or in heat
Coolant level low in the electronics reservoir
P0C32: Hybrid/EV Battery Cooling System A Performance

P0C32 is the functional check of the battery thermal system that CARB asks for. GM tunes it per vehicle: the 2012 Volt (12OBDG01A) fails it when the average pack temperature stays above 40 °C in active cooling or below −17 °C in active heating, after 4200 s or 9000 s, Type A, one trip.
Battery cooling fan stopping at low 12 V system voltage (GM eAssist)
Low coolant, air or a weak pump in a liquid-cooled pack circuit
Blocked cooling air intake or ducts of an air-cooled pack
Failed pack heater or chiller valve
Charging system or battery warning message (eAssist)
P0C33: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit

Battery temperature sensor F is the sixth thermistor in the high-voltage pack; GM's Volt bulletin 18-NA-342 lists the F codes under temperature sensor 6 of nine. P0C33 is the general circuit code for an electrical fault the controller does not classify as low, high or erratic.
Loose or corroded connector of sensor F at the sensing board
Faulty input on the battery sensing board or module
Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Battery cooling running more than usual
P0C34: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Range/Performance
P0C34 checks whether sensor F, GM's sensor 6, agrees with the rest of the pack. The controller compares its reading with the average of the other battery temperature sensors.
Sensor F drifting or poorly seated on its cell group
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
Real local temperature difference from a weak cell group or uneven cooling
Battery too cold or reduced power message
P0C35: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Low

Sensor F is an NTC thermistor with a pull-up on the sensing board, so its voltage drops as temperature rises; a short to ground looks like an extremely hot cell group. Low refers to the signal, not to the temperature.
Sensor F signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Faulty input on the battery sensing board
Battery cooling running at high speed
Strongly reduced charge and drive power
P0C36: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit High

P0C36 means the voltage from battery temperature sensor F sits above its valid range. With GM's NTC thermistor and pull-up, an open circuit, a broken wire or an unplugged connector pulls the input up and reads as an impossibly cold cell group.
Open circuit or unlatched connector of sensor F
Module software setting the code falsely in the cold (GM Volt)
Battery too cold, plug in to warm message
P0C37: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C37 targets a sensor F signal that jumps instead of following the slow temperature change of a heavy battery.
Loose terminal or connector of sensor F not fully latched after pack work
Cracked sensor wire with intermittent contact
Faulty battery sensing board, often with several sensors affected
Intermittent hybrid warning, often on rough roads
P0C38: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Circuit

The DC/DC converter steps the high-voltage battery down to the 12 V system and replaces the alternator in hybrids and EVs. Its power stage carries temperature sensors so the controller can derate before the semiconductors overheat. P0C38 is the general circuit code for sensor A.
Control unit software misjudging the sensor after long parking (Hyundai Palisade Hybrid)
Fault in the circuit of sensor A inside the converter or power control unit
Internal fault of the DC/DC converter requiring replacement
12 V charging reduced or switched off
Code appearing after the car has stood for a long time
P0C39: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance

P0C39 is the plausibility check of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A: its reading lies within the electrical range but does not fit the converter's operating state or a second sensor. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid, where the code is called temperature sensor 1 performance.
Outdated hybrid control software (Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21)
Sensor A drifting or with poor thermal contact to the power stage
Uneven cooling of the converter making the readings disagree
MIL, after one trip with updated Ram software
Mild hybrid assist or 12 V supply reduced
P0C3A: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Low

P0C3A means the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor A is below its valid range. Low refers to the signal voltage: with an NTC thermistor and pull-up, as GM uses for its hybrid temperature sensors, a short to ground or a failed element reads as extreme heat. No manufacturer documents P0C3A publicly.
Sensor A signal shorted to ground inside the converter or its harness
Shorted temperature element A, usually requiring converter replacement
Converter really overheated due to a cooling fault
12 V battery warning, system voltage dropping
P0C3B: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A High
P0C3B reports a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A above its valid range, typically a short to positive or an open circuit pulled up by the input.
Faulty wake-up behaviour of the converter putting it into an error state (Mercedes 243/465)
Open circuit or short to positive in the sensor A circuit
Internal defect of the DC/DC converter
Red 12 V battery warning in the cluster
White or yellow high-voltage system warning
12 V battery no longer charged while driving
P0C3C: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic

P0C3C covers a signal from DC/DC converter temperature sensor A that drops out or jumps for short moments while staying mostly within range. The heat sink of a converter warms and cools slowly, so fast jumps point to the signal path rather than to real temperature changes. No manufacturer documents P0C3C publicly.
Loose terminal or moisture at the converter connector
Harness damaged by vibration with intermittent contact
P0C3D: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Circuit

P0C3D is the general circuit code for the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter, which turns high-voltage battery power into 12 V supply. Converters with two sensors watch separate parts of the power stage or cross-check one sensor against the other. No manufacturer documents P0C3D publicly.
Connector or wiring fault in the sensor B circuit
Failed temperature element B inside the converter
Converter or hybrid control software misjudging the sensor
P0C3E: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance

P0C3E flags DC/DC converter temperature sensor B as electrically valid but implausible, for instance when it disagrees with sensor A or with what the converter load should produce. FCA uses it on the 2021 Ram 1500 with the 3.6 litre eTorque mild hybrid under the name temperature sensor 2 performance.
Outdated hybrid control software (Ram 1500 eTorque, bulletin 08-037-21)
Sensor B drifting or with poor thermal contact
Uneven converter cooling making sensors A and B disagree
MIL, after one trip with updated Ram software
Mild hybrid assist or 12 V supply reduced
P0C3F: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Low

P0C3F is stored when the voltage from the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter falls below the lowest plausible value. These sensors are normally NTC thermistors fed through a pull-up resistor, so a low voltage corresponds to an extremely hot reading; a short to ground or a shorted element produces exactly that.
Sensor B signal line shorted to ground in the converter or harness
Shorted thermistor B, usually only fixable by replacing the converter
Converter actually overheating because its cooling fails
Hybrid or EV system warning in the cluster
12 V battery warning or falling on-board voltage
Reduced power or switched-off comfort consumers
P0C40: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B High

P0C40 means the second temperature sensor of the DC/DC converter delivers a voltage above its valid window, which on a thermistor circuit points to a short to positive or an open line pulled up to the reference. Mercedes-Benz documents it for the EQB (series 243) and the G-Class including the electric G 580 (series 465).
Converter entering a fault state after incorrect wake-up (Mercedes 243/465)
Open circuit or short to positive in the sensor B wiring
Internal defect of the DC/DC converter
Red 12 V battery message in the instrument cluster
12 V battery no longer charged while driving
P0C41: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic

P0C41 concerns a reading from DC/DC converter temperature sensor B that jumps or briefly drops out while it mostly remains inside the valid range. A converter heat sink changes temperature slowly, so abrupt steps indicate a signal problem rather than real heating. No manufacturer documents P0C41 publicly.
Loose terminal or moisture at the converter connector
Harness chafed or cracked by vibration
Hybrid or EV warning that comes and goes
P0C42: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit

P0C42 is the general circuit code for the first coolant temperature sensor in the liquid loop of a hybrid or EV battery, typically placed at the pack inlet. The battery controller uses it to decide when to pump, heat or chill the coolant.
Battery controller software flagging the circuit wrongly (Volvo XC90 T8)
Corroded or loose connector or damaged wire at the coolant sensor
Check engine lamp, often without other complaints
Battery cooling or heating running on substitute values
Reduced charging or drive power in hot or cold weather
P0C43: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0C43 flags battery coolant temperature sensor A as electrically valid but not believable.
Too tight plausibility limits in the control software (Audi Q5 TFSI e, update 80C9)
Coolant sensor A drifting away from its characteristic
Added resistance in the sensor circuit shifting the reading
MIL after a cold start, often with no other complaint
Battery thermal management working on substitute values
P0C44: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low

P0C44 reports that the voltage of battery coolant temperature sensor A is too low. The sensor is an NTC thermistor, so a low voltage translates into a very hot reading, and a short to ground or a shorted element is the classic cause.
Sensor signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the connector bridging the pins
MIL and hybrid or EV system message
Coolant temperature shown implausibly high in live data
P0C45: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P0C45 indicates that the signal of battery coolant temperature sensor A sits near the reference voltage. On an NTC circuit with pull-up this looks like extreme cold and usually comes from an open circuit, an unplugged connector or a short to voltage.
Open signal or ground wire, or connector not latched
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Coolant temperature shown at about -40 °C in live data
Reduced charging power in extreme temperatures
P0C46: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0C46 points to a battery coolant temperature signal that jumps faster than liquid in the loop can physically change temperature. GM's 2019 hybrid tables explain the check: every 100 ms the hybrid controller takes the difference to the previous inlet coolant value, adds up ten of these absolute steps and counts a failure when the sum exceeds 64 °C.
Loose or spread terminal at the coolant sensor connector
Corrosion at connector or ground point
Harness rubbing or cracked near the battery coolant lines
MIL that may go out again for a while
Jumping coolant temperature in live data
P0C47: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Circuit/Open

P0C47 means the controller sees an electrical fault on the line that commands battery coolant pump A. GM's 2019 tables catch open, short to ground and short to power by current: with the pump on, less than 200 mA or more than 3 A on the control line count as failures, with the pump off less than 120 µA; 4 s within 5 s set a Type B code.
Corroded or painted ground point or corroded pump connector (Porsche Cayenne 92A)
Corroded splice or chafed harness in the pump circuit (Audi Q4 e-tron, Bentley)
Failed electric coolant pump or its relay
Electrical or drive system warning with reduced power
Vehicle refuses to become ready to drive
P0C48: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low

P0C48 narrows a fault on the control line of battery coolant pump A down to a signal that stays too low, as caused by a short to ground or a driver output that cannot pull the line up. Ford lists the code for the 2020 Explorer, Police Interceptor Utility and Lincoln Aviator with the hybrid powertrain.
Battery control module software (Ford/Lincoln 2020 hybrids, TSB 20-2345)
Pump control wire shorted to ground
Internal fault in the pump electronics pulling the line low
Hybrid system message, battery power possibly limited
P0C49: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High

P0C49 is set when the control signal to battery coolant pump A remains too high, for example because the line is shorted to battery voltage or, on a pulled-up input, interrupted. Ford uses it on the 2020 Explorer, Police Interceptor Utility and Lincoln Aviator hybrids.
Battery control module software (Ford/Lincoln 2020 hybrids, TSB 20-2293/20-2345)
Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Control line interrupted at the pump connector
Battery power reduced during long climbs or fast charging
P0C4A: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Control Performance

P0C4A says pump A runs electrically but does not achieve its cooling effect. The 2011 Chevrolet Volt fails the test when the pump has been on for over 60 s and the pack inlet coolant temperature has moved by less than 5 °C, rated Type B.
Air trapped in the battery coolant loop, often after a coolant service
Low coolant level or a leak in the low-temperature loop
MIL shortly after cooling system work
Electric drive warning, reduced power or capped EV speed
Gurgling noise from the coolant loop
P0C4B: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit/Open

P0C4B refers to the power feed of battery coolant pump A rather than its command line: the controller sees no or only an implausible supply voltage at the pump, typically because a fuse, relay, connector or wire in the feed is open. Ford documents the code on its 2020 hybrids.
Battery control module software (Ford Escape HEV, Explorer and Aviator 2020)
Blown fuse or failed relay in the pump supply
Open feed wire or pushed-out pin at the pump connector
Battery coolant pump not running, power limited when warm
P0C4C: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit Low

P0C4C reports that the supply voltage reaching battery coolant pump A is below the expected level while the circuit is not fully open. Typical reasons are high resistance in the feed, a corroded fuse contact, a weak relay, a poor ground or a short to ground that drags the line down. No manufacturer documents P0C4C publicly.
High resistance from corroded fuse, relay contacts or connector
Supply wire chafed and shorted to ground
MIL or hybrid or EV warning
Coolant pump running slowly or intermittently
Battery power reduced when the pack warms up
P0C4D: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump A Supply Voltage Circuit High

P0C4D is the counterpart to P0C4C: the voltage measured on the supply of battery coolant pump A is higher than the controller allows. That can come from a feed wire shorted to another, more highly loaded circuit, from a relay that stays closed when the pump should be off, or from an overall excessive on-board voltage, for example a faulty DC/DC converter.
Supply wire shorted to another voltage-carrying circuit
Excessive 12 V system voltage from a faulty DC/DC converter
MIL or hybrid or EV warning
Coolant pump running although the system is switched off
P0C4E: Drive Motor A Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P0C4E says the resolver offset of drive motor A was learned, yet the learned value is unacceptable. That offset lines up the zero point of the resolver with the rotor magnets.
Resolver or rotor position shifted after replacing the motor, resolver stator or transaxle
Internal transaxle fault on affected Kia Sorento PHEV models (TSB TRA112)
Hybrid or motor control software that needs an update
Damaged resolver that delivers a shifted angle
Malfunction indicator lamp, often first noticed after a repair
Jerk or rough feel when switching between electric and hybrid drive
P0C4F: Drive Motor B Position Exceeded Learning Limit
P0C4F covers the second traction motor: its resolver offset learn finished, but the angle it produced lies outside what the controller will accept.
Motor B resolver stator fitted in a different position after a repair
Learn disturbed by a moving rotor or unstable high voltage at key-off
Damaged motor B resolver giving a shifted angle
Malfunction indicator lamp after shutdown cycles
Reduced propulsion or motor B unavailable
Unusual noise or shudder under electric drive
P0C50: Drive Motor A Position Sensor Circuit A

P0C84 is set when the sensor H line sits too high in voltage, which the controller converts into an impossible cold reading. The pull-up drives an interrupted circuit upward, so an open wire, a pushed-out pin or a broken thermistor are the classic triggers.
