False set by battery module software (GM Volt, 18-NA-342)
P0C85: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor H Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C85 points to a sensor H reading that flickers. A battery pack warms and cools slowly, so fast swings in one channel suggest an electrical contact problem rather than real heat.
Intermittent contact at the sensor H terminal
Partly broken sensor H wire inside the pack harness
Noisy measuring channel on the sensing board
Sensor H value jumping in live data
P0C86: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor F/G Correlation

P0C86 compares the neighbouring battery temperature sensors F and G with each other. After the pack has rested, both should settle to nearly the same value; a persistent gap means at least one reads wrong although neither circuit is open or shorted. No manufacturer documents P0C86 publicly.
Thermistor F or G drifted without an electrical fault
Sensor F or G no longer in contact with its module
Real temperature difference between the two module groups
Battery management calibration with an overly narrow window
Sensors F and G far apart in live data after a cold soak
P0C87: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor G/H Correlation

P0C87 checks that battery temperature sensors G and H tell a consistent story. The controller would set it when, after enough rest for the pack to equalise, the two values remain apart by more than a calibrated margin. No manufacturer documents this pair code publicly.
Thermistor G or H drifted while staying in range
Sensor G or H detached from its cell group
Real temperature gap from a weak cell group or blocked cooling
Battery module software needing an update
P0C88: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor I Circuit
P0C88 is the general circuit code for battery temperature sensor I, chosen when the fault is electrical but not classified as low, high or erratic. No manufacturer documents P0C88 publicly.
Connector fault on the sensor I circuit
Defective input channel in the battery sensing electronics
Generic scan tools may show the code without a description
P0C89: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor I Circuit Range/Performance

P0C89 says sensor I delivers an electrically valid but implausible temperature. GM checks it against the average of the remaining sensors: the 2019 table 19OBDG02 fails it beyond 25 °C in 50 of 67 samples, Type B, two trips, and suspends the test while a low, high or communication fault is present; the 2016 Cadillac ELR table (16OBDG01) uses 20 °C.
Module software setting the code falsely, fixed by reprogramming (GM Volt)
Thermistor I drifted within its electrical range
Sensor I displaced from its measuring point
Real local heating at the cell group of sensor I
Check-engine or hybrid lamp, often after a long rest
P0C8A: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor I Circuit Low

P0C8A records a sensor I voltage below the valid band. As the element is an NTC thermistor fed through a pull-up, a low voltage translates into a cell group that seems dangerously hot, typically caused by a short to ground.
Sensor I signal shorted to ground
Thermistor I shorted, for example after coolant or moisture entry
Cell monitoring unit input for sensor I faulty
Sensor I shown extremely hot in live data
P0C8B: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor I Circuit High

P0C8B covers a sensor I signal stuck above its valid voltage, which the controller interprets as extreme cold. An interrupted circuit lets the pull-up lift the line, so the root cause is usually an open connection or a failed thermistor rather than the weather.
Open wire or loose connector in the sensor I circuit
Battery module software causing false cold readings (GM Volt, 18-NA-342)
Battery-too-cold message although outside temperature is mild
P0C8C: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor I Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C8C reports that sensor I changes faster and more often than any real battery temperature could.
Fretting or loose terminal on the sensor I connector
Sensor I wire broken inside its insulation
Sensing board with unstable supply or ground
Warning lamp appearing now and then
Sensor I value jumping in live data
P0C8D: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit

P0C8D covers electrical trouble in the circuit of battery temperature sensor J that the controller cannot pin down to a low, high or jumping signal. There is no public manufacturer documentation for P0C8D.
Corroded or loose plug between sensor J and the monitoring board
Faulty input channel on the cell monitoring board
Hybrid system warning, on many models also the check-engine lamp
Less electric power and slower charging
P0C8E: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit Range/Performance
P0C8E sets when sensor J delivers an electrically valid temperature that disagrees with the other modules.
Thermistor J drifted but still within its electrical range
Sensor J no longer pressed against its cell group
Actual temperature difference from a weak cell or blocked cooling path
Warning lamp appearing after the car has been parked for many hours
Battery power reduced while the pack is cold or warm
P0C8F: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit Low

P0C8F means the voltage on sensor J has dropped below its valid window. The NTC thermistor is powered via a pull-up resistor, so a grounded signal line reads as an absurdly hot cell group; low refers to the signal.
Sensor J signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Thermistor J shorted internally, for example after moisture
Monitoring board input pulling the line low
Warning lamp with clearly reduced electric power
Battery fan or chiller running constantly
Engine starts more often on plug-in hybrids
P0C90: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit High

P0C90 reports the opposite case: sensor J reads above its voltage window, which with a pull-up circuit points to an open thermistor, a broken lead or a disconnected plug, and the controller sees an impossibly cold module.
Open lead or unplugged connector at sensor J
Terminal pushed back in the monitoring board plug
Battery-too-cold message although the weather is mild
Little or no electric drive power
Battery heater switching on without need
P0C91: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor J Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0C91 watches for a sensor J reading that changes too fast and too often for a heavy battery. GM's tables 16OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 add up how far the value moves between samples over a 10-sample window taken every 100 ms; a sum above 10 fails the window, and 4 failing windows out of 5, about half a second, store the code, Type B over two trips.
Fretting or loose terminal in the sensor J plug
Conductor broken inside the insulation, opening under vibration
Unstable reference or ground on the monitoring board
Warning lamp that comes and goes between drives
Sensor J value jumping in live data
P0C92: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit

P0C92 is stored when the input from battery temperature sensor K has an electrical fault that the controller leaves unclassified. Public manufacturer documentation for exactly this code does not exist.
Poor contact at the sensor K plug
Defective input channel on the cell monitoring board
Reduced electric power until the fault is repaired
P0C93: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit Range/Performance
P0C93 compares sensor K with its neighbours: the reading is electrically fine but too far from the pack average.
Thermistor K reading off while still electrically valid
Sensor K lifted off its cell group
Real temperature spread from uneven coolant flow or a weak cell
Warning lamp, often first noticed after a cold start
P0C94: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit Low

With P0C94 the controller sees the sensor K signal pulled below its lower limit, a pattern produced by a chafed wire touching ground or an internally shorted thermistor, which the conversion turns into an extreme temperature.
Sensor K signal line shorted to ground
Moisture or coolant reaching the sensor K connection
Warning lamp and reduced electric power
Battery cooling running although the pack is not hot
P0C95: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit High

P0C95 is set when sensor K delivers a voltage above its valid range. In the usual NTC layout a broken circuit allows the bias resistor to drive the input high, so the controller sees an impossibly cold module.
Open circuit or disconnected plug at sensor K
Sensor lead damaged during earlier work on the pack
Battery-too-cold or plug-in-to-warm message in mild weather
P0C96: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor K Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0C96 flags an unsteady sensor K signal, the kind of noise a loose contact produces while the value still sits inside its valid band.
Loose contact in the sensor K connector
Partly chafed sensor lead touching intermittently
Monitoring board with unstable supply or ground
P0C97: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit

P0C97 is the catch-all for battery temperature sensor L, used when the input misbehaves electrically but fits none of the low, high or erratic categories. No manufacturer publishes this exact code. GM's 2011 hybrid table counts L as temperature sensor 12 of sixteen, and its 2012 and later tables cover L only with P0C98 to P0C9B.
Connector fault between sensor L and the monitoring board
Faulty measuring channel on the monitoring board
Hybrid or EV warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
P0C98: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit Range/Performance
P0C98 is the plausibility code for sensor L: its reading is electrically valid but strays too far from the other sensors.
Thermistor L drifted within its electrical range
Sensor L no longer in thermal contact with its cells
Genuine local temperature difference in that pack section
Warning lamp after a long standstill
P0C99: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit Low

P0C99 reports a sensor L voltage below the valid range. Because the thermistor works against a bias resistor on its monitoring board, any ground fault or an internally shorted sensor drags the voltage down, which reads as a very hot module.
Sensor L signal shorted to ground
Monitoring board channel pulling the input low
Warning lamp and reduced battery power
Battery cooling running for no apparent reason
P0C9A: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit High
P0C9A is the high-voltage fault of sensor L: an open thermistor, a broken lead or a disconnected plug lets the bias resistor raise the input, and the reading looks like deep frost.
Open circuit or unplugged connector at sensor L
Corroded terminal with very high contact resistance
Electric power reduced, engine running more on plug-ins
P0C9B: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor L Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0C9B covers a sensor L signal that jitters. GM's tables 18OBDG02 and 19OBDG02 integrate the absolute sample-to-sample changes over ten readings spaced 100 ms apart; when the integral exceeds 10, that window fails, and 4 failures within 5 windows store the code, classed Type B.
Fretting pin in the sensor L connector
Cracked conductor in the sensor L lead
Loose ground on the cell monitoring board
Warning lamp that may switch off again by itself
Erratic sensor L value in live data
P0C9C: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit

P0C9C flags an electrical problem, not further classified, with current sensor B of the 14 volt power module, the DC/DC converter that supplies the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery; GM calls it the accessory power module (APM).
Current sensor B inside the power module failed
Poor contact at the power module signal connector
Control software of the power module or hybrid controller
Warning lamp, sometimes a charging-system message
12 V battery running low over time
P0C9D: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0C9D means the output current reported by sensor B of the 14 V power module is electrically valid but implausible for the operating state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Offset or gain drift of current sensor B
Converter output really differing from the commanded power
High resistance at the 12 V output cable or ground
Warning lamp without obvious driveability change
12 V battery charge state remaining low
P0C9E: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit Low

P0C9E is set when current sensor B of the 14 V power module reads too little. GM documents it for the eAssist accessory power module in its 2013 table 13OBDG05C: the APM output current measured by the sensor must stay below 2 A for 1.5 s, counted as 60 of 80 samples at 25 ms, with the vehicle in run/crank; the code is Type B, so the MIL comes on after the se…
Output current sensor B failed inside the module
Sensor signal open or shorted to ground
Converter not delivering output although enabled
Low 12 V voltage, flickering lights or warning messages
P0C9F: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit High
P0C9F reports an output current from sensor B of the 14 V power module that exceeds what the converter can plausibly supply.
Internal defect of output current sensor B
Sensor signal shorted to a voltage source
Poor ground of the power module shifting the reading
Converter output reduced, 12 V battery discharging
P0CA0: 14 Volt Power Module Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent

P0CA0 covers short dropouts or spikes in the signal of current sensor B, the output-side sensor of the 14 V power module (DC/DC converter) in GM's numbering. Between the events the reading looks normal, which separates it from the hard low and high faults P0C9E and P0C9F.
Loose or fretting connector at the power module
Corroded ground or 12 V output connection
Current sensor B failing intermittently inside the module
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Occasional dim lights or voltage messages
P0CA1: Drive Motor Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

P0CA1 is a request code, not a component fault: the drive motor control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks the engine control module to light the MIL, which stores P0CA1.
Emissions-relevant fault stored in the drive motor control module
Module software reacting to a low 12 V battery (Subaru 07-82-14R)
Weak or discharged 12 V auxiliary battery
Check-engine lamp, often with further warning lamps such as stability control
Hybrid drive behaving normally or with reduced electric assistance
P0CA2: DC/DC Converter Step Down Voltage Performance
P0CA2 means the step-down function of the DC/DC converter, which brings high-voltage battery power down to the 12 V network, is not working correctly.
Failed power semiconductor in the converter's step-down stage
Internal fault of the power module or power pack assembly
Spurious detection without a hardware fault, for example after supply dips
Check-engine lamp on the first trip, often with a charging warning
Falling 12 V voltage, low-voltage codes such as P0562
P0CA3: DC/DC Converter Step Up Voltage Performance

P0CA3 says the boost stage of a DC/DC converter fails to lift its output to the voltage the controller has requested. In full hybrids this stage, often called a boost or variable voltage converter, raises the traction battery voltage to a higher bus level that feeds the inverters. No manufacturer documents P0CA3 on a publicly reachable official server.
Failed power transistor or driver in the boost stage
Internal fault of the inverter/converter assembly, e.g. reactor or capacitor
Wrong reading from the voltage sensor before or after the boost stage
Stored as a consequence of another hybrid system fault
Hybrid system warning with check-engine lamp
Noticeably reduced electric drive power or limp mode
Engine running more often than usual
P0CA4: P0CA4 is stored when the traction battery voltage climbs above its permitted limit while energy flows into the pack, for instance because a charger or the drive keeps pushing current although the cells are already full.
Charger or battery control software storing a false entry (Audi 2062631/5)
Charging current not reduced in time as the pack approaches full charge
Faulty pack or cell voltage measurement in the battery management
Charging stops early or does not start
Code found during a check without any noticeable symptom
P0CA5: P0CA5 concerns a battery voltage judged too high while the pack is discharging, that is while it supplies the drive motor or other high-voltage consumers. Under load the terminal voltage normally sags, so an excessive value in this state points more to a measurement or plausibility fault than to genuine overcharge. No manufacturer documents P0CA5 publicly.
Faulty pack voltage sensing in the battery management
Battery or hybrid control software evaluating the voltage wrongly
Loose or corroded high-voltage or sense connection
Hybrid or EV warning, often with check-engine lamp
P0CA6: P0CA6 flags a current into the traction battery that exceeds what the control system expects.
Onboard charger or DC-DC converter delivering more current than requested
Pack current sensor or battery management unit reading wrongly
Fault in the hybrid/PHEV control unit
Check-engine lamp, often found after charging
Vehicle not entering ready mode on some EVs
P0CA7: P0CA7 is set when more current flows out of the hybrid or EV battery than the controller allows.
Starter/generator or battery module software (Audi 2058831, Stellantis 08-054-22)
Belt starter generator drawing excessive current
Battery current sensor or battery management misreading
Electrical system or battery warning in the cluster
Start-stop or electric assistance temporarily unavailable
P0CA8: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit

P0CA8 is the general circuit code for battery temperature sensor M, meant for electrical faults that the controller does not sort into low, high or erratic. No manufacturer publishes this exact code. In GM's 2011 Volt table the rationality list gives M the thirteenth of sixteen positions, yet GM only defines P0CA9 to P0CAC for it.
Poor contact at the plug of sensor M on the monitoring board
Faulty input channel of the cell monitoring board
Hybrid or EV warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
P0CA9: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit Range/Performance

P0CA9 reports that sensor M stays within its electrical limits yet disagrees with what the remaining pack sensors measure. GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A only runs the comparison once drive system, plug-in charging and battery conditioning have rested for over 21,600 s; a spread above 25.3 °C from the mean in 50 of 67 samples is a Type B failure.
Thermistor M drifting while staying in its electrical range
Sensor M lost thermal contact with its module
Module section genuinely warmer or colder, e.g. cooling fault or weak cell
Warning lamp appearing after a long parking period
P0CAA: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit Low

P0CAA means the voltage at sensor M has dropped below its valid band. Sensor M is an NTC element supplied via a bias resistor on the board, so a grounded lead or a shorted element drags the voltage down and reads as an extremely hot spot.
Sensor M signal shorted to ground inside the pack
Measuring input of the cell monitoring unit defective
Warning lamp with strongly reduced battery power
P0CAB: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit High

P0CAB is logged when the input of sensor M rises beyond its upper voltage limit. If the thermistor, one of its wires or the plug opens up, the pull-up resistor lifts the input, and the controller reads a temperature far below anything plausible.
Open circuit or unplugged connector of sensor M
Corroded or spread terminal at the monitoring board
Battery shown as very cold in mild weather
Reduced electric power, engine running more on plug-ins
P0CAC: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor M Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0CAC catches a sensor M signal that jumps around without necessarily leaving its permitted band. GM's HPC2 tables (16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02) add up the absolute changes between successive samples over a ten-sample window at 100 ms; whenever that total passes 10 the window is marked bad, and four bad windows in five lead to a Type B code after two trips.
Fretting or loose contact in the sensor M circuit
Cracked conductor or solder joint on the monitoring board
Unstable ground of the monitoring board
Warning lamp that may go out again on its own
Jumping sensor M value in live data
P0CAD: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit

P0CAD stands for an electrical problem with battery temperature sensor N that the controller cannot assign to a specific failure type. Public manufacturer documentation for this exact code does not exist.
Connector or wire fault between sensor N and the monitoring board
Faulty input channel of the cell monitoring board
P0CAE: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit Range/Performance

P0CAE is the plausibility check for sensor N: the value is electrically acceptable, yet out of line with its neighbours. GM's 2012 Volt table 12OBDG01A demands a rest of more than 21,600 s without propulsion, external charging or thermal conditioning and then fails the test at a deviation above 25.3 °C in 50 of 67 samples, Type B.
Thermistor N reading off while electrically valid
Sensor N detached from its cell or module surface
Real temperature difference in that pack section
Warning lamp after the car has stood for hours
P0CAF: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit Low

P0CAF sets when the signal of sensor N is pulled under its lower voltage limit. A ground fault in the lead or a shorted thermistor causes this, and because the NTC sensor works against a pull-up resistor the controller interprets it as an implausibly hot module.
Sensor N lead shorted to ground
Measuring input of the cell monitoring unit defective
Warning lamp and markedly reduced battery power
Battery cooling running at full effort
P0CB0: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit High

P0CB0 reports a sensor N input above its upper voltage limit, which a pack controller reads as an unrealistically cold module. The NTC sensor is biased by a pull-up resistor, so any interruption in the element, its leads or its plug makes the input rise.
Open lead or disconnected plug of sensor N
Corroded terminal at the monitoring board
Battery reported as far too cold in mild conditions
Less electric range or power, engine starting more often
P0CB1: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor N Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0CB1 points to an unsteady sensor N signal rather than a lasting short or open. GM's 2019 table 19OBDG02 evaluates windows of ten samples, one every 100 ms, by integrating the absolute value of each change; above 10 the window counts as failed, and 4 failed windows within 5 set the code, Type B, two trips.
Loose or fretting pin in the sensor N circuit
Chafed or partly broken sensor N lead
Cracked track on the monitoring board
Sensor N value jumping in live data
P0CB2: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit

P0CB2 is the catch-all electrical code for battery temperature sensor O, reserved for circuit faults that are not classified as low, high or erratic. Poor contact at the sensor O connector on the monitoring board
Damaged lead between thermistor O and the board
Faulty measuring channel in the cell monitoring unit
Hybrid or EV system warning, possibly with check-engine lamp
Reduced electric power or charging rate
P0CB3: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit Range/Performance
P0CB3 is a plausibility code: sensor O delivers an electrically valid reading, yet it strays too far from the rest of the pack.
Thermistor O drifting while its voltage stays in range
Sensor O no longer seated firmly against its module
Module section really warmer or colder, e.g. weak cell or uneven cooling
Warning lamp typically appearing after the car has stood for hours
P0CB4: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit Low

P0CB4 reports a signal voltage of sensor O below its lower limit. The sensor is an NTC thermistor biased by a resistor on the measuring board, so a short to ground or a shorted element looks like extreme heat.
Signal lead of sensor O shorted to ground in the pack
Input stage of the cell monitoring unit defective
Live data showing an implausibly hot module

P0CB5: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit High

P0CB5 is stored when the input of sensor O sits above its upper voltage limit. An open thermistor, a broken wire or a loose plug lets the pull-up resistor raise the input, so the controller sees a temperature colder than any real pack could be.
Open lead or unplugged connector of sensor O
Corroded or loose terminal at the sensing board
Pack shown as extremely cold regardless of weather
Less electric power, engine running more on plug-in hybrids
P0CB6: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor O Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0CB6 targets a sensor O signal that jitters or jumps instead of changing smoothly. Only GM's later HPC2 tables (16OBDG02 to 19OBDG02) define it: every 100 ms a sample is taken, the absolute steps between ten consecutive samples are summed, and a sum above 10 marks that window as failed.
Fretting or loose terminal in the sensor O circuit
Cracked solder joint or trace on the sensing board

Warning lamp that comes and goes
Sensor O value jumping in live data
P0CB7: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit
P0CB7 covers an electrical fault of battery temperature sensor P that the controller cannot pin down as low, high or intermittent. No manufacturer lists this code on a public official server.
Loose or corroded plug of sensor P

P0CB8: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit Range/Performance
P0CB8 flags sensor P as implausible: its value is electrically fine, but after a long rest it disagrees with the temperature of the other modules.
Thermistor P drifted out of calibration
Sensor P detached from its module surface
Real temperature difference of that module, e.g. faulty cell

P0CB9: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit Low

P0CB9 means the voltage of sensor P has fallen under the valid range. As with the other NTC sensors, low voltage corresponds to high temperature, so a short to ground or a collapsed thermistor makes the module appear to be glowing hot.

P0CBA: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit High

P0CBB: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor P Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0CC0: Drive Motor A Coolant Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent

P0CC2: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit Range/Performance
P0CC2 judges whether the pump for drive motor A actually moves coolant, not only whether its wiring is intact.

P0CC3: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit Low

P0CC4: Drive Motor A Coolant Pump Control Circuit High

P0CC7: Charge Port Door A Open Request Switch Circuit
P0CC7 is the general circuit fault of the button that requests opening of charge flap A.

P0D04: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Intermittent/Erratic

P0D04 covers short, irregular disturbances in the ventilation switch circuit: the signal drops out or flickers, while lasting faults would be stored as P0D00, P0D02 or P0D03. Worn or corroded contacts in the charge inlet or module connector, and wires that lose contact under vibration, are the obvious suspects.
Loose or spread terminal in the ventilation switch circuit
Corrosion or moisture in the charge inlet or module connector
Chafed wire with contact loss under vibration
Charging sessions stop without obvious reason
P0D05: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Stuck Off

Stuck Off for the ventilation switch means the module commands the switch closed, yet the pilot does not drop to the level around 3 V that marks a request for charging with ventilation. Possible causes are a switch that no longer closes, an open resistor in the roughly 270 Ω branch, or a measuring fault in the module.
Ventilation switch in the module no longer closing
Open resistor or solder joint in the ventilation branch
Pilot measuring fault in the charging module
Stored code, charging normally still possible
Charging system warning in the cluster on some vehicles
P0D06: Control Pilot Charging Ventilation Switch Stuck On

Stuck On means the ventilation switch remains closed when it should be open, so the pilot is held near 3 V and the station reads a permanent demand for charging with ventilation. Stations that cannot provide ventilation do not supply power in that state, which in practice stops charging altogether.
Ventilation switch contacts welded or sticking closed
Short across the ventilation resistor branch
Module output or software holding the switch on
Charging station does not supply power
Charging error message after plugging in
P0D07: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Circuit

P0D07 is the general circuit code for positive contactor A of the charging system, the switch that joins the plus side of a charging path to the traction battery. Depending on the design this path comes from the DC fast-charge inlet or from the on-board charger; the Chevrolet Volt, for instance, places charging contactors between charger and pack.
Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the contactor branch
Fault in the module that drives and monitors the contactor
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
P0D08: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Stuck Closed

P0D08 means positive charging contactor A has stayed closed although the control module commanded it open, typically because the contacts have welded. The module notices this when voltage remains on the charging side, for instance at the charge port once a session has ended, as a Toyota patent on charge-relay sticking explains.
Contactor contacts welded, for example after switching under load
Battery module software misjudging the contactor state (GM Lyriq, Ram ProMaster EV bulletins)
Driver stage or coil supply that does not switch off
Malfunction indicator lamp and high-voltage service message
Vehicle may not switch to ready mode
P0D09: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Stuck Open
P0D09 is set when positive charging contactor A fails to close: after the command the expected voltage never shows up on the charger side.
Contactor mechanically failing to close or burnt contacts
Fault in the on-board charger or integrated charging unit (Kia ICCU bulletin)
Control software needing an update (Stellantis, GM Lyriq)
Missing coil supply because of a wiring or fuse fault
Charging does not start or ends shortly after plugging in
Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
Charging or high-voltage warning in the cluster
P0D0A: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit/Open
P0D0A covers the drive circuit of positive charging contactor A: the module compares the commanded state of its driver with the voltage and current it actually sees on the coil line.
Open or high-resistance coil control wire or connector
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty high-side driver in the control module
Malfunction indicator lamp (GM Type A or B)
P0D0B: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance

P0D0B reports that the control circuit of positive charging contactor A works electrically but does not behave plausibly – coil current or line voltage outside the window expected for the commanded state, or a response that comes too slowly. No manufacturer documents P0D0B publicly.
Contact resistance or corrosion in the control circuit connectors
Weakening driver stage in the control module
Stored code, possibly with a charging system warning
P0D0C: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit Low

P0D0C stands for a control line of positive charging contactor A that reads too low, usually a short to ground or a driver output pulled down. When the coil is fed through a high-side driver, a grounded line leaves the contactor without power or overloads the driver. No manufacturer documents P0D0C publicly.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector creating a path to ground
P0D0D: Battery Charging System Positive Contactor A Control Circuit High

P0D0D means the control line of positive charging contactor A sits too high, typically from a short to a supply voltage or a driver that no longer switches off. The coil may then stay energised, so the contactor could close without a command, which the module has to prevent.
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open ground return of the coil letting the line float high
P0D0E: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Circuit

P0D0E is the general circuit code for negative contactor A of the charging system, which connects the minus side of the charging path – from DC inlet or on-board charger – to the traction battery. It is used when the module sees an electrical fault on that contactor that it does not classify more precisely. No manufacturer documents P0D0E publicly.
Damaged wiring or corroded connector in the contactor branch
Fault in the module that drives and monitors the contactor
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
P0D0F: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Stuck Closed
P0D0F flags negative charging contactor A as stuck closed: it still conducts after the open command, usually through welded contacts or a misjudged state.
Faulty high-voltage battery junction box with the charging contactors (Ford Mach-E)
Battery module software misjudging the contactor (Stellantis 4xe, GM Lyriq)
Malfunction indicator lamp or wrench lamp
Stop Safely Now message or no ready mode (Ford)
P0D10: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Stuck Open

P0D10 means negative charging contactor A does not close when told to, so the charging path never gets its return line and the session fails. Ford names it in the BECM of the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E next to main-contactor codes; the bulletins (23-2020, 23-2257) replace the high-voltage battery junction box and update the BECM.
Faulty high-voltage battery junction box with the charging contactors (Ford Mach-E)
Battery module software needing an update (GM Lyriq, Stellantis)
Contactor failing to close or burnt contacts
Charging does not start or stops
Malfunction indicator lamp and high-voltage service message
P0D11: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit/Open

P0D11 is the open-circuit and driver check for negative charging contactor A. GM uses it on the Chevrolet Volt (2011, 2014) and the Cadillac ELR: the module compares the commanded driver state with what the line shows; with the driver off, an output above 4 V (2011: 2 V) means open and one close to supply voltage a short to power, and with the driver on a co…
Open or high-resistance coil control wire or connector
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Faulty driver stage in the control module
Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
P0D12: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit Range/Performance

P0D12 points to a control circuit of negative charging contactor A that is electrically intact yet implausible: current, voltage or switching response do not fit the command. No manufacturer documents P0D12 publicly.
Contact resistance or corrosion in the control circuit connectors
Poor ground of the control module or coil return
Stored code, possibly with a charging system warning
P0D13: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit Low

P0D13 means the control line of negative charging contactor A reads too low, which points to a short to ground or a driver output held down. The coil then receives no current, or too little, and the contactor stays open.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Moisture in a connector creating a path to ground
P0D14: Battery Charging System Negative Contactor A Control Circuit High

P0D14 is set when the control line of negative charging contactor A reads too high, for example through a short to the 12 V supply or a driver stage that will not switch off. That can keep the coil energised and the contactor closed without a command, so the module blocks charging.
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open ground return of the coil letting the line float high
P0D15: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit/Open

P0D15 reports an open high-voltage interlock loop in charging system A. This low-voltage loop runs through the connectors and covers of the charging path – inlet, charger and their HV leads – and breaks as soon as one of them is unplugged, so the module can keep that path de-energised.
HV connector in the charging path not fully seated or latched (Volvo XC40)
Broken interlock wire or pushed-back terminal
Missing or loose cover on a charging component
Charge inlet light indicates a fault
P0D16: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit Performance

P0D16 flags a charging interlock loop that delivers a signal, just not the one expected – for example a reading that fails to follow when the module switches its test source on and off. No manufacturer documents P0D16 publicly.
Contact resistance or corrosion in an interlock connector
HV connector in the charging path inserted only partway
Fault in the module's interlock source or measuring stage
P0D17: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit Low

P0D17 means the sensed voltage of the charging HVIL loop is too low. GM documents the check for the Chevrolet Volt (2011, 2014) and the Cadillac ELR: while the module sources 5 V into the loop, a sensed value under 30 % of the reference in two samples out of two at 12.5 ms sets the code as Type A, with the MIL on after one trip.
Interlock wire chafed and touching ground
Moisture or dirt in an interlock connector causing leakage
Fault in the interlock source or measuring circuit of the control module
Malfunction indicator lamp after one trip (GM Type A)
P0D18: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit High

P0D18 flags a charging HVIL signal that sits too high. On the Chevrolet Volt and Cadillac ELR GM tests the loop in two states: with the 5 V source off, a sensed level above 24 % of reference (5 of 6 samples in 2011, 5 of 8 for 2014 and ELR), and with it on, a level above 44 % (4 of 6), set the code as Type A, MIL after one trip.
High resistance or partial break in the interlock loop
Battery module software needing an update (Polestar 2)
Faulty integrated charging unit (Kia Niro EV ICCU)
Interlock wire shorted to a voltage source
Propulsion or high-voltage warning in the cluster
P0D19: Battery Charging System A High Voltage Interlock Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D19 covers a charging interlock loop that drops out and comes back, so the signal flips between valid and invalid within a short time. Loose terminals, a connector that is not fully latched, a chafing wire that only touches over bumps and vibration-sensitive solder joints are typical causes. No manufacturer documents P0D19 publicly.
Loose or spread terminal in an interlock connector
HV connector in the charging path not fully latched
Chafed interlock wire making contact only under vibration
P0D1A: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Control Circuit/Open

P0D1A flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of coolant control valve B, a second actuator in the coolant loop of the hybrid or EV battery. Which physical valve gets the letter B, and what it switches, is up to the vehicle maker. No manufacturer documents P0D1A in a public bulletin or OBD table.
Broken wire or corroded connector in the valve B drive circuit
Open coil or motor winding inside valve B
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
Hybrid or EV system warning and MIL
Reduced charging or drive power because battery temperature cannot be managed
P0D1B: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Performance/Stuck Off
P0D1B is stored when coolant control valve B of the battery loop is electrically intact but fails to reach or hold the position the controller asks for, or stays in its off state.
Valve B mechanically stiff or blocked by debris
Worn valve actuator that no longer reaches its target
Diagnostic limits in the module software set too tightly
Low coolant or trapped air distorting the temperature-based check
MIL or battery thermal system warning
Battery temperature rises during fast charging or hard driving
P0D1C: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Stuck On
P0D1C means coolant control valve B of the battery circuit remains in its active position although the controller has commanded a change.
Valve B jammed in its active position
Output stage or supply that keeps the valve energised
Module software misjudging the temperature response of the loop
MIL or battery thermal system warning
Battery warms slowly in cold weather or charging is slower than usual
P0D1D: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Control Circuit Low
P0D1D reports that the drive line of coolant control valve B reads too low, which normally means a short to ground. No manufacturer publishes P0D1D itself.
Valve B driver wire chafed and shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve motor
MIL after two trips (where the maker uses a two-trip code)
Battery cooling or heating restricted, charging or power limited
P0D1E: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve B Control Circuit High

P0D1E is the short-to-voltage counterpart for coolant control valve B: the controller sees its drive line high at a moment when it should be low. P0D1E is not described in any public manufacturer document.
Valve B driver wire pinched against a supply line
Output stage in the controlling module stuck high
Damaged or contaminated connector bridging two pins
MIL after two trips (where the maker uses a two-trip code)
Battery thermal management in fallback mode, charging or power limited
P0D1F: P0D1F says a control module could not align its internal date and time with the reference the rest of the vehicle uses.
Module software misdetecting the time comparison (Volvo BECM software 2.11)
Timers not yet resynchronised after programming because the car has not slept
Missing or wrong time information from the module providing the reference clock
Check engine light without a noticeable driving fault
Code returns as a variant after a software update until the car has slept
P0D20: Battery Charger A Output Voltage Performance

P0D20 concerns the on-board charger in its constant-voltage phase, typically near the end of a charge, when it should hold its high-voltage output at a set value. The code means the measured output voltage strays too far from that target.
Fault in the charger's power stage or voltage control
Charge control software in the hybrid control module
Charging stops early or the battery does not reach its target level
P0D21: Battery Charger A Output Voltage Too Low
P0D21 is set when the high-voltage output of the on-board charger stays below what the controller expects.
Failing power stage inside the charger
High resistance or fault in the charger's high-voltage output path or heater load
MIL, often after two charging trips
Battery not preheated while plugged in during cold weather
P0D22: Battery Charger A Output Current Performance
P0D22 means the on-board charger does not deliver the high-voltage current it was asked for.
Charge control software in the hybrid or battery control module (GM PIP bulletins)
Internal fault in the on-board charger
Vehicle does not charge or charging stops
MIL on after a charge session ends
Problem shows mainly on AC level 2 stations
P0D23: P0D23 points to a short on the high-voltage output side of the on-board charger. GM runs this check while the charger contactor is only in its precharge state and the multi-purpose contactor is open, a moment when almost no current should flow on the charger bus.
Internal short in the charger's high-voltage output stage
Damaged high-voltage cable between charger and battery
Charging contactor path conducting when it should not
Charging refused immediately after plugging in
P0D24: Battery Charger A Temperature Too High

P0D24 is stored when the on-board charger reports an internal temperature above its permitted limit. Chargers protect themselves by reducing power or stopping, so the driver typically notices slow or interrupted AC charging.
Internal defect in the charger or charging control unit (Kia ICCU replacement)
Low coolant, failed pump or blocked air flow on the charger cooling path
Charger temperature sensor reading too high
AC charging slow, interrupted or impossible while DC fast charging works
Warning message for the electric system, sometimes MIL
P0D25: Battery Charger System Precharge Time Too Short

P0D25 is about the precharge of the charger's high-voltage bus, the short phase before the charging contactors close in which the bus capacitance is brought up to battery voltage through a limiting path. The code means this voltage arrived sooner than physically plausible. No manufacturer documents P0D25 publicly.
Charging contactor welded or closing too early
Bus or pack voltage sensor reporting wrong values
Bus capacitance much lower than expected
Charging refused at the start of a session
P0D26: Battery Charger System Precharge Time Too Long

P0D26 means the charger's high-voltage bus did not come up to battery voltage within the allowed precharge time. GM's Volt 2011 to 2015 and ELR 2014 to 2016 require the bus to sit within 5 % of pack voltage for 0.25 s before 10 s have passed; the 2016 and 2017 Volt allow only 0.700 s to reach 95 % (later 95 to 105 %); all are One Trip Type A.
Open precharge resistor, fuse or contactor in the precharge path
Blown fuse in the manual service disconnect (Bolt EV bulletin)
Erratic proximity signal from a wet or corroded charge port
Vehicle does not charge on 120 V or 240 V
With a blown disconnect fuse, loss of propulsion
P0D27: Battery Charger Input Voltage Too Low
P0D27 says the AC voltage reaching the on-board charger sits lower than the charger accepts while charging is permitted. Unlike most charger codes, the cause often lies outside the car.
Weak or overloaded AC supply at the charging location
Damaged wiring or loose contact between charge inlet and charger
AC charging does not start or stops
House circuit breaker trips when plugging in
P0D28: Battery Charger Input Voltage Too High
P0D28 is the mirror case of P0D27: the AC voltage at the charger input lies above the range the charger can accept.
Input voltage sensing inside the charger reading too high

Actual overvoltage or unstable supply at the charging location

P0D29: Battery Charger Input Current Too Low

P0D29 is set when the on-board charger draws less AC current than expected for the power it was asked to deliver, while voltage and charging permission are present. No manufacturer documents P0D29 publicly.
Charger power stage not ramping up
High resistance at the charge inlet, cable or plug contacts
Input current sensor reading too low
Charging station or cable limiting current more than signalled
AC charging much slower than usual
Charging stops or charging system warning
P0D2A: Battery Charger Input Current Too High

P0D2A reports that the on-board charger draws more AC input current than allowed. GM's Volt and ELR use two limits: more than 17 A at 185 V or above, more than 13 A below 185 V; 240 failures in 300 samples set it as One Trip Type A.

Input current sensor reading too high
AC charging stops shortly after starting
On-board charging inoperative while DC charging may still work
P0D2B: P0D2B concerns the driver circuit of the control pilot indicator, a lamp or LED with which the vehicle signals the state of the pilot connection to the charging station. The code covers the lamp's own wiring, not the pilot signal itself.
Damaged wiring or loose connector to the indicator
Faulty LED driver in the controlling module
Indicator stays dark or lit regardless of charging state
MIL, depending on model after one or two trips
P0D2C: Charge Status Indicator A Control Circuit/Open

P0D2C is set for a fault in the driver circuit of charge status indicator A, the light that tells the driver whether the car is charging. On the Chevrolet Volt that light is part of the diagnosis itself: bulletin PIP4905E has technicians watch whether the charge indicator on the instrument panel stays steady green.
Broken wire or corroded connector to the indicator

MIL, depending on model after one or two trips
P0D2D: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit

Drive motor A's inverter measures the DC link voltage it switches, and voltage sensor A is the channel that passes this value to the motor controller. P0D2D is the general circuit fault for that channel: the signal is missing or electrically unusable, without a more specific low or high verdict. Ford lists P0D2D among its MIL codes.
Inverter or powertrain module software fault (Ford 21B02)
Loose connector or damaged signal wiring of the voltage sensor

No start after charging and remote start (Mach-E)
P0D2E: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0D2E means the inverter voltage reading of drive motor A is electrically valid but disagrees with other measurements of the same high-voltage bus.
Voltage sensing in the power drive unit drifts or reads wrong
Fault in another HV component, e.g. belt starter-alternator (Mercedes)
High resistance or loose high-voltage connection between modules
Engine will not start, only electric driving possible (Mercedes)
P0D2F: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D2F reports that the signal of inverter voltage sensor A for drive motor A sits at the bottom of its range, typical of an open circuit, a short to ground or no high voltage at all.
Blown high-voltage fuse or disconnected HV cable
Voltage sensing in the power drive unit failed (open or short to ground)
Vehicle not ready to drive or electric drive unavailable
P0D30: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit High

P0D30 is the high-side partner of P0D2F: the inverter voltage signal of drive motor A stays near its upper limit. Mitsubishi checks it on the 2018 Outlander PHEV with the front motor unit supplied at 8 to 16 V; a sensor output above 4.7 V, which stands for roughly 440 V, for 0.3 s sets the code.

P0D31: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D31 covers a voltage signal from the drive motor A inverter that drops out or jumps for brief moments without staying out of range long enough for P0D2F or P0D30. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the inverter
Chafed signal wiring with intermittent contact
Sensing circuit in the power electronics fails with heat or vibration
Hybrid system warning that comes and goes
Brief power loss or jerky electric drive
P0D32: P0D32 means DC/DC converter A, which supplies the 12 V network from the high-voltage battery, has become too hot. Unlike the sensor codes P0C38-P0C3C, the reading itself is trusted; the temperature is the problem.

Weak electronics coolant pump or air in the cooling circuit
Internal converter fault with excess heat
P0D33: P0D33 says the DC/DC converter carries more current than its limit. Short in a 12 V cable or consumer on the converter output
Damaged high-voltage or 48 V supply cable
12 V battery not charged, later no start
P0D34: P0D34 is the general code for the current flowing through the high-voltage battery system as a whole. The pack current sensor codes P0ABF-P0AC3 judge the sensor signal; this group judges whether the current itself fits the operating state. No manufacturer documents P0D34 publicly, and its set conditions are not published.
Battery current sensor reads wrong but within range
Unexpected current path in the HV system (contactor, consumer)
Reduced electric power or charging restrictions
P0D35: P0D35 flags a battery system current that swings more than the operating state explains, for example rapid changes while the requested power is steady. No manufacturer publishes set conditions for this code.
Loose high-voltage connection or chattering contactor
Current sensor or its wiring with intermittent signal
Power reduction or jerky electric drive
P0D36: P0D36 means the battery system delivers or accepts less current than the controller expects for the power it commanded. No manufacturer documents a threshold publicly.
High resistance in the HV path or contactor not closing properly
Current sensor stuck at a plausible but too low value
Aged battery pack with high internal resistance

Short or fault in an HV component (charger, DC/DC, A/C, inverter)

EV or hybrid system warning, with MIL on some makes

P0D38: Battery Charger A Input Current Sensor Circuit

P0D38 is the general circuit code for the sensor that measures the AC current entering battery charger A, the on-board charger. Charging fault indication on the dashboard or charge port

P0D39 flags an implausible reading from the sensor that measures alternating current at the input of charger A, the on-board charger. Both documented users test its zero point.

P0D3D: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit

P0D3D is the basic circuit code for voltage sensor A at the input of charger A, which measures the AC supply voltage arriving from the charge inlet. P0D3E: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P0D41: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D41 is reserved for an input voltage sensor A signal at charger A that is intermittent or erratic, i.e. it jumps or drops out briefly. No manufacturer documents this code with set conditions; GM and Mitsubishi only use P0D3E-P0D40 for this sensor.
Electrical noise or poor grounding on the AC supply
Loose contact between charge inlet and charger
Voltage measurement in the charger degrading
Fault appears only at one charging location
P0D42: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit

P0D42 is the circuit code for the sensor that measures voltage at the 14 V output of the battery charger, a low-voltage DC stage built into the on-board charger and distinct from the vehicle's main DC/DC converter.
Open or shorted voltage sense circuit of the charger's low-voltage stage
Poor 12 V or ground connection at the charger
12 V battery discharges while the car is plugged in
P0D43: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0D43 says the voltage reported for the charger's 14 V output does not fit other measurements of the low-voltage system.
Low-voltage sense circuit inside the charger reads wrong
Poor ground or 12 V feed at the charger skews the comparison
P0D44: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Low

P0D44 is logged once the voltage sensor of the charger's 14 V output delivers an implausibly low raw value. In GM's charger module for the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR the limit is a sensor signal of 1.87 V or less, held for 400 of 500 ms while the low-voltage section is awake; it is a Type A fault and lights the MIL.
Voltage sense signal shorted to ground inside the charger
Failed low-voltage stage of the on-board charger
14 V output collapsed by an external short or overload
Charging may stop or not complete
P0D45: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit High

P0D45 is stored when the charger's 14 V output voltage sensor reads too high. GM's battery charger control module in the Volt and ELR fails it at a reading of 16.88 V or above for 400 of 500 ms; the 2011 table rates it Type A, the 2014 table Type B, meaning the MIL comes on only after two consecutive trips.
Voltage sense signal shorted to a higher potential inside the charger
Charger low-voltage stage regulating too high
MIL on (GM, after two trips in later model years)
P0D46: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D46 stands for a sporadic or unstable signal from the voltage sensor at the 14 V output of the on-board charger. No manufacturer documents it publicly. GM monitors this output in the Volt and ELR charger only for plausibility, low and high readings (P0D43-P0D45) and lists no intermittent variant.
Loose 12 V, ground or signal connection at the charger
Voltage sense circuit inside the charger failing intermittently
Electrical interference on the low-voltage network
12 V battery not kept charged while plugged in
P0D47: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Current Sensor Circuit

P0D47 is the general circuit code for the current sensor in the charger's 14 V output, the measurement of how much current the charger's internal low-voltage stage delivers. No manufacturer publishes this code; GM's Volt and ELR charger module measures the same current but reports only low and high readings (P0D49, P0D4A), with 54 A as its upper limit.
Open or shorted current sense circuit of the low-voltage stage
Damaged 12 V output connector at the charger
12 V battery discharges during long charging sessions
P0D48: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0D48 marks a current reading at the charger's 14 V output that lies within its electrical range but makes no sense in context. No manufacturer documents P0D48.
Current sense circuit inside the charger has drifted
Failed low-voltage stage of the charger
12 V support during charging reduced or switched off
P0D49: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Current Sensor Circuit Low

P0D49 reports that the current sensor in the charger's 14 V output reads too low. GM's battery charger control module in the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR sets it when the raw current value is 0.293 A or less for 400 of 500 ms while the low-voltage section is awake, as a Type A fault with MIL; the 2016 ELR charger table also lists it as a precondition for its o…
Open or grounded current sense path inside the charger
Failed low-voltage stage of the on-board charger
12 V supply or fuse of the charger interrupted
P0D4A: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Current Sensor Circuit High

P0D4A sets when the current sensor in the charger's 14 V output reports 54 A or more. GM's battery charger control module in the 2011-2014 Volt and the ELR applies that threshold for 400 of 500 ms with the low-voltage section awake and treats the result as a Type A fault with MIL.
Current sense signal stuck high inside the charger
Overload or short on the charger's low-voltage output
P0D4B: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Current Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D4B covers an erratic or intermittent signal from the current sensor in the battery charger's 14 V output. No manufacturer documents it publicly; GM's Volt and ELR charger module uses only the low and high codes P0D49 and P0D4A for this measurement.
Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the charger
Intermittent contact in the charger's current sense circuit
Electrical interference on the low-voltage network
12 V battery voltage fluctuates while plugged in
P0D4C: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Voltage Sensor Circuit
P0D4C is the general circuit code for the sensor that reports the DC voltage the on-board charger delivers to the high-voltage traction battery.
Voltage sensing electronics inside the on-board charger failed
Interrupted signal path or poor internal connection in the charger
Charger software fault, fixed by reprogramming
Plug-in charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
Vehicle can still be driven on stored energy or fuel
P0D4D: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0D4D means the charger's output voltage reading is electrically valid but fails to match the rest of the system.
Output voltage measurement inside the charger drifted or inaccurate
Integrated charging unit failed (Kia ICCU, GM charger module)
Reference value from the battery voltage measurement wrong
Slow AC charging or no AC charging
P0D4E: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Low

P0D4E reports a signal below the valid range for the sensor measuring the charger's DC output toward the traction battery. In GM's charger module for the 2011-2014 Volt and ELR the raw value must stay at or below 2.62 V for 400 of 500 ms; the fault is Type A and lights the MIL at once.
Voltage sensor signal shorted to ground inside the charger
Internal reference supply of the measuring circuit missing
Charging stops or does not start
P0D4F: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Voltage Sensor Circuit High

P0D4F is the high-side fault of the charger's output voltage sensor: the reading climbs beyond anything the battery could actually present. GM's 2011-2014 charger module for the Volt and ELR flags a decoded value of 482 V or more for 400 of 500 ms as a Type A fault with immediate MIL.
Voltage sensor signal shorted to a supply voltage inside the charger
Measuring stage of the on-board charger failed
P0D50: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Voltage Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D50 stands for an unsteady output voltage signal from the on-board charger: the value jumps or drops out briefly instead of following the slowly changing battery voltage. No manufacturer documents P0D50 publicly.
Loose contact or cracked solder joint in the charger's measuring path
Electrical interference from the charger's power stage
Ageing voltage sensing electronics in the charger
Charge time noticeably longer than usual
P0D51: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Current Sensor Circuit
P0D51 covers a circuit fault of the sensor that measures the direct current the on-board charger pushes into the traction battery. No manufacturer documents P0D51 itself.
Current sensor or its evaluation circuit in the charger failed
Open signal path between sensor and charger controller
P0D52: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance
P0D52 flags an output current reading that lies inside the sensor's range yet cannot be right.
Zero point of the output current sensor has drifted
Charger or integrated charging unit (Kia ICCU) failed
DC fast charging may still work (Kia)
P0D53: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0D53 is set when the charger's output current sensor reports a value below its valid floor.
Current sensor output shorted to ground inside the charger
Supply of the current sensor missing
Charging fault indicated at the charge port or in the cluster
P0D54: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Current Sensor Circuit High

P0D54 marks a current reading at the charger's high-voltage output that exceeds the sensor's upper limit. The limit sits well above normal charging current, so the value counts as an electrical fault rather than real current.
Current sensor output shorted to supply voltage in the charger
Sensor output stuck at its upper end
Charge level stays unchanged after plugging in
P0D55: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Current Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D55 describes an output current signal from the charger that flickers, jumps or briefly drops out rather than tracking the regulated charging current. No manufacturer documents P0D55 publicly.
Intermittent contact in the current measuring path of the charger
Solder joints fatigued by charging heat cycles
Switching noise coupling into the sensor signal
Charging takes much longer than usual
P0D56: P0D56 is the general circuit fault of proximity detection circuit A, the line through which the vehicle notices that a charging plug sits in its inlet.
Damaged or corroded proximity contact in the charge inlet
Open or chafed wire between charge inlet and evaluating module
Evaluation input in the charger or control module failed
Charging does not start although the cable is plugged in
Vehicle refuses to drive or shows the cable as connected without a plug
P0D57: P0D57 means the plug-present signal of proximity circuit A is electrically within limits but its value or behaviour does not fit the situation, for instance a level between the defined states for plugged, unplugged and latch pressed.
Hybrid control software needs update (FCA HCP/AHCP)
Worn or contaminated proximity contact shifts the resistance
Charging cable or adapter with off-standard proximity resistor
Charging starts unreliably or not at all
P0D58: P0D58 reports a voltage on proximity circuit A that is too low while no plug can possibly be inserted.
Proximity signal wire shorted to ground or chafed against body
Loose low-voltage connector at the on-board charger (smart)
Moisture or contamination bridging the inlet contacts
Evaluation input of the control module failed
Vehicle will not start or shift because a plug appears connected
P0D59: P0D59 is logged when proximity circuit A shows a voltage above its expected resting level at a moment when the charge port must be empty.
Proximity signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Interrupted ground or reference path of the detection circuit
Loose connector at the charger or charge inlet
Inserted charging plug not recognised, no charging
P0D5A: P0D5A points to a proximity signal on circuit A that flips between states or jumps erratically, so the vehicle sees the plug come and go although nobody touched it. No manufacturer documents P0D5A publicly.
Loose contact in the inlet or at the charger connector
Worn latch switch or contacts in the charging plug
Plug status message appears and disappears
P0D5B: Battery Charger 14 Volt Output Power Performance

P0D5B checks whether the power leaving the charger's built-in 14 V output is physically possible. GM's charger module for the Volt and ELR multiplies the measured 14 V output voltage and current and compares the product with the AC input power times a factor of about 2 plus an offset: 2.5 W in the 2011 table, 125 W in the 2014 Volt/ELR and 2016 ELR tables.
Voltage or current measurement of the 14 V stage reads too high
AC input power measured too low
Low-voltage stage of the on-board charger faulty
12 V battery not supported while plugged in
P0D5C: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV Battery Output Power Performance

P0D5C judges the power the charger feeds into the traction battery against what it draws from the grid. GM's first-generation Volt and ELR charger module calculates high-voltage output power and flags it when it exceeds AC input power times about 2 plus 30 W (2011) or 120 W (2014 and 2016 ELR), for 1.6 of 2 s, Type A.
Power stage of the charger degraded, efficiency too low
Module software miscalculates power (Ford SOBDM update)
Output voltage/current or AC input measurement inaccurate
Insufficient cooling of the power electronics during charging
MIL on after a charging session
P0D5D: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV System Discharge Time Too Short

P0D5D concerns the active discharge of the charger's high-voltage side after charging ends: the stored voltage collapses faster than the circuit design allows. No manufacturer documents P0D5D publicly; GM's Volt only publishes the opposite case P0D5E.
Discharge switch inside the charger stuck closed
Charger voltage measurement reads falsely low
Charging system warning after the end of charging
Next charging session may not start
P0D5E: Battery Charger Hybrid/EV System Discharge Time Too Long
P0D5E means the high-voltage side of the charger did not drop to a safe level in time after it was disconnected.
Active discharge circuit of the charger not working
High-voltage contactor stuck closed keeps the bus energised
Lost communication between charger and hybrid controller
Charger voltage sensor reads falsely high
Further high-voltage codes such as contactor faults may be stored
P0D5F: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit/Open

Where a traction battery is cooled by two fans, each one can report its actual speed back to the controller on a separate sense line. P0D5F is the general circuit code for that return path of fan 2: the line is open or delivers nothing the controller can evaluate. No manufacturer documents P0D5F publicly.
Broken feedback wire or terminal pushed out at the fan 2 connector
Corroded or loose connector between fan 2 and the battery controller
Speed signal output inside the fan 2 motor electronics failed
Feedback input of the battery control module defective
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Reduced electric assist or charging power when the battery warms up
Often no noticeable change while fan 2 still runs
P0D60: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Range/Performance
P0D60 means the feedback of battery cooling fan 2 is electrically present but does not fit what the fan was told to do.
Fan 2 runs off its commanded speed due to worn bearing or debris on the impeller
Clogged intake grille, filter or duct of the battery cooling air
Drifting speed feedback stage in the fan electronics
High resistance in the feedback or supply connection of fan 2
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Fan noise that is louder, rougher or weaker than usual
Battery temperature rises faster and electric power is limited
P0D61: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit Low

P0D61 reports that the feedback signal of battery cooling fan 2 sits at or near zero. In Volkswagen's 2014 Touareg Hybrid the battery controller sets it once the fan 2 feedback voltage drops below 0.1 V; the matching fan 1 code is P0BC9.
Fan 2 feedback wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Fan 2 without supply (fuse, relay or supply wire), so no signal is generated
Feedback output of the fan 2 electronics failed low or motor seized
Feedback input of the battery control module defective
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Fan 2 audibly silent although battery cooling is requested
Reduced electric power, especially in warm conditions
P0D62: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit High

P0D62 is set when the feedback of battery cooling fan 2 rises above its plausible maximum. Volkswagen gives the threshold for the 2014 Touareg Hybrid as a fan 2 feedback voltage above 3.45 V, mirroring P0BCA for fan 1.
Fan 2 feedback wire shorted to a supply or neighbouring signal
Open ground at fan 2 letting the feedback line float high
Fan 2 electronics stuck at their upper feedback level
Feedback input of the battery control module defective
Hybrid system warning or check engine light
Electric power limited when the battery gets warm
P0D63: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan 2 Sense Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D63 flags a feedback signal from battery cooling fan 2 that drops out or jumps in steps no spinning fan could produce. The typical culprit is a loose pin or cracked wire that opens and closes with vibration, or interference coupled into the feedback line.
Loose or spread terminal in the fan 2 feedback connector
Cracked feedback wire that opens under vibration
Electrical interference from nearby high-current or high-voltage wiring
Unstable feedback stage in the fan 2 electronics
Warning light that comes and goes
Occasional short phases of reduced electric power
Often no noticeable change in fan operation
P0D64: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Enable Circuit/Open
Besides its speed command, a battery cooling fan can have a separate enable line that switches the fan electronics on. P0D64 means the controller has found this enable output open.
Broken enable wire between battery controller and fan
Fan connector unplugged or not latched, often after battery or trim work
Open enable input inside the fan electronics
Enable driver in the battery system module defective
Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan does not run
Reduced electric assist when the battery gets hot
P0D65: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Enable Circuit Low

P0D65 reports a short to ground on the enable output of the battery cooling fan: the line stays low even though the controller is trying to switch the fan on. GM's 2013 eAssist mild hybrid table 13OBDG05C detects it from the output driver's fault flag for the power pack fan, 20 failures in 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B.
Enable wire chafed and shorted to body ground
Shorted enable input inside the fan electronics
Moisture or corrosion bridging the enable pin to ground
Enable driver in the battery controller defective
Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan never switches on
Engine runs more and electric assist drops in hot weather
P0D66: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cooling Fan Enable Circuit High

P0D66 stands for a short to voltage on the enable output of the battery cooling fan. Because the line is pulled high from outside, the fan may run although the controller wants it off, or the controller simply loses authority over it.
Enable wire rubbed through and touching a 12 V supply wire
Moisture in the fan connector bridging enable and supply pins
Internal fault in the fan electronics feeding voltage back onto the enable line
Enable driver in the battery controller defective
Check engine light or hybrid warning after two trips
Battery cooling fan runs continuously, even with the vehicle off
P0D67: Battery Charger Control Module A Performance
P0D67 says that the control electronics of the on-board charger are not working properly.
Internal low-voltage supply of the on-board charger out of tolerance
On-board charger or integrated charging unit failed
Weak 12 V supply or poor ground at the charger
Charger software fault, fixed by an update where available
Plug-in charging stops or does not start
Electric vehicle system warning in the cluster, possibly MIL
Vehicle can still be driven on stored energy or fuel
P0D68: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit

An electric A/C compressor in a hybrid or EV runs its motor from the high-voltage battery through an inverter in the compressor housing, and a sensor there measures the incoming high voltage. P0D68 is the general circuit code for that sensor: its signal is missing or unusable as a whole, without a specific low or high reading.
Voltage measurement inside the electric compressor's inverter failed
Compressor reports its sensor value over a faulty data link
Poor high-voltage connection at the compressor
Warning message or warning light, depending on the vehicle
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
P0D69: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Performance
P0D69 is a plausibility check: the high voltage that the electric A/C compressor measures at its input should match the traction battery voltage, since both see the same supply.
Drifting high-voltage measurement inside the electric compressor
Fault on the data bus that carries the compressor voltage value
Hybrid or vehicle controller misjudging the comparison
Error in the battery voltage measurement used as reference
Air conditioning weak or switched off
P0D6A: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit High

P0D6A means the electric A/C compressor reports an input voltage higher than the high-voltage system can actually deliver. GM's 2011 Volt table sets it at 450 V or more (30 of 60 samples at 50 ms); the 2016 and 2019 Volt tables use more than 527.25 V, judged by the compressor itself and sent over the data bus (2019: 4 of 5 s).
Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reading too high
Hybrid controller or data link fault
P0D6B: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit Low

P0D6B reports that the high-voltage input reading of the electric A/C compressor sits below the plausible range. GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 ELR set it at 190 V or less in 30 of 60 samples at 50 ms, checked only with the contactors closed for over a second and fault-free.
Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reads too low
Faulty data link between compressor and hybrid controller (named by Mitsubishi)
Hybrid or vehicle controller evaluates the value incorrectly
Check engine light after two trips (GM) or immediately (Mitsubishi 2023)
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be restricted
P0D6C: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D6C covers a voltage-sensor signal from the electric A/C compressor that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong: single readings outside the expected window or abrupt steps that do not last long enough for the low or high code. No manufacturer documents P0D6C publicly.
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector at the compressor
Intermittent fault on the compressor's inverter board
Marginal high-voltage contact at the compressor connector
P0D6D: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage A Low
P0D6D concerns the high voltage actually reaching the electric A/C compressor motor rather than the sensor circuit: the supply is too low to run it.
Internal short in the compressor that has blown the A/C high-voltage fuse (Mazda)
Broken high-voltage cable in the supply path (Bentley, battery to on-board charger)
Open A/C fuse or poor high-voltage connection without a compressor defect
Air conditioning does not cool at all
Further codes such as lost communication with the compressor
High-voltage battery may not charge (cable fault)
P0D6E: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage A High

P0D6E means the high voltage supplied to the electric A/C compressor motor is above what the compressor is built to accept, as opposed to a sensor circuit reading too high (P0D6A). No manufacturer documents P0D6E publicly.
Voltage measurement in the compressor inverter reads too high
Voltage spikes on the high-voltage bus during charging or regeneration
Charger or DC/DC converter regulating the bus voltage incorrectly
Warning message depending on the vehicle
P0D6F: P0D6F flags excessive current drawn by the electric A/C compressor on its high-voltage DC link while the motor is running. GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR set it when the DC link current exceeds 27 A in 30 of 60 samples taken every 50 ms with a compressor speed request above zero; it is Type B, MIL after two trips.
Shorted winding in the compressor motor
Refrigerant overcharge or excessive high-side pressure
Failing power stage in the compressor inverter
Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning cuts out under load
P0D70: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit

The control electronics inside an electric A/C compressor carry a temperature sensor on the processor board, called internal sensor A; the compressor uses it to protect itself and reports the value to the vehicle. P0D70 is the general circuit code for it: the value is missing or invalid without a defined low or high reading.
Temperature sensor or its circuit on the compressor board failed
Value not transmitted correctly over the data link
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the compressor electronics
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
P0D71: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Performance

P0D71 is a plausibility test for the compressor control module's internal (CPU) temperature sensor: after a long rest, every temperature in the compressor should be close to its surroundings. GM's 2011 Volt compares it with intake air and with the output-stage sensor and fails above 6 °C in 35 of 40 samples at 250 ms.
Drifting internal temperature sensor in the compressor electronics
Outside air, intake air or IGBT sensor used for comparison is wrong
Compressor not fully cooled down when the test ran
Check engine light after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in A/C operation
P0D72: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P0D72 is the high-signal circuit code for the compressor module's internal temperature sensor. With the usual NTC thermistor a high signal means the reading looks extremely cold, and that is how GM defines it: every Volt and ELR table from 2011 to 2019 sets it when the reported CPU temperature is below −40 °C.
Open circuit in the internal temperature sensor path
Cracked solder joint on the compressor electronics board
