Faulty value transmission to the host controller
Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning limited or switched off
P0D73: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D73 is the low-signal circuit code for the internal (CPU) temperature sensor of the compressor control module. For an NTC sensor a low signal corresponds to an implausibly hot reading.
Short circuit in the internal temperature sensor path
Real overheating of the compressor electronics
Faulty value transmission to the host controller
Check engine light after two trips
Air conditioning reduced or switched off
P0D74: A/C Compressor Control Module Internal Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D74 reports an unsteady signal from the internal temperature sensor of the A/C compressor control module: the reading jumps or drops out in short bursts rather than sitting at one wrong value. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for P0D74.
Cold or cracked solder joint on the compressor board
Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the compressor
Electrical interference on the sensor signal
Air conditioning cuts out now and then
P0D75: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit

The output driver temperature sensor watches the power transistors (IGBTs) that switch the three motor phases of an electric A/C compressor; they heat up under load, and the compressor reduces speed or stops before they overheat. P0D75 is the general circuit code for this sensor without a defined low or high value.
Temperature sensor at the IGBT module or its circuit failed
Sensor value not transmitted correctly to the vehicle
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the compressor electronics
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
P0D76: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Performance
P0D76 checks whether the compressor's output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor agrees with other temperatures after a cold soak.
Drifting IGBT temperature sensor in the compressor inverter
Outside air or CPU temperature used for comparison is wrong
Power stage still warm when the test ran
Check engine light after two trips
Usually no noticeable change in A/C operation
P0D77: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit High

P0D77 is the high-signal circuit code of the output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor in the electric A/C compressor. As with an NTC sensor, the high signal shows up as an impossibly cold temperature: GM sets it when the IGBT reading is at or below −40 °C, in all Volt and ELR tables from 2011 to 2019.
Open circuit in the IGBT temperature sensor path
Cracked solder joint on the inverter board
Faulty value transmission to the host controller
Check engine light after two trips
P0D78: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit Low
P0D78 is set when the output driver (IGBT) temperature sensor of the electric A/C compressor signals low, which for an NTC sensor means an implausibly hot value.
Short circuit in the IGBT temperature sensor path
Real overheating of the power stage from high load or poor condenser cooling
Faulty value transmission to the host controller
Check engine light after two trips
P0D79: A/C Compressor Control Module Output Driver Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0D79 marks an erratic signal from the output driver temperature sensor, the sensor that guards the compressor's power transistors: values flicker or drop out briefly instead of staying wrong. No manufacturer publishes set criteria.
Cold or cracked solder joint at the IGBT sensor
Loose low-voltage connector or ground at the compressor
Switching noise from the inverter coupling into the sensor signal
P0D7A: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Low
Electric A/C compressors run a three-phase motor whose phase currents U, V and W are measured inside the inverter. P0D7A belongs to phase U.
Offset or failure of the phase U current sensor in the inverter
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit
Check engine light after two trips
P0D7B: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current High

P0D7B is the second phase U current code of the electric A/C compressor. In GM's first-generation Volt (2011–2015) and the 2016 Cadillac ELR it sets when the phase U current sensor reads −68 A or less although the motor is stopped and no speed is requested, counted as 30 failures in 60 samples at 50 ms; Type B, MIL after two trips, with a 12 V reset required…
Phase U current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current evaluation
Check engine light after two trips
P0D7C: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Low

P0D7C relates to phase V of the three-phase motor in an electric A/C compressor. GM documents it in the 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 ELR tables as a standstill check: with the compressor speed request at 0 rpm the measured phase V current should be near zero, and a value of +68 A or above in 30 of 60 samples (50 ms each) sets the code.
Offset or failure of the phase V current sensor in the inverter
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit
Check engine light after two trips
P0D7D: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current High

P0D7D marks a phase V current reading of the electric A/C compressor that is far negative while the motor should be idle. GM's first-generation Volt and the 2016 ELR set it at −68 A or less, judged in 30 of 60 samples every 50 ms whenever the speed request is zero, as Type B with MIL after two trips.
Phase V current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current evaluation
Check engine light after two trips
No cooling from the air conditioning
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
P0D7E: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Low

P0D7E applies to phase W, the third winding of the electric A/C compressor motor. GM's 2011–2015 Volt and 2016 Cadillac ELR check the W-phase current sensor while the motor is at rest: a reading of +68 A or more in 30 out of 60 samples at 50 ms sets the code, Type B with the MIL after two trips, and only a 12 V reset re-enables a pass.
Offset or failure of the phase W current sensor channel
Common supply or reference fault in the inverter (several phases affected)
Check engine light after two trips
P0D7F: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current High
P0D7F is the negative-direction current code for phase W of the electric A/C compressor motor.
Phase W current sensor reading negative at standstill
Fault in the inverter's current measuring circuit
Check engine light after two trips
P0D80: P0D80 means the on-board charger sees no usable AC supply at its input even though the charging handshake says power should be there.
Charging station or outlet delivers no AC after the handshake (fault, tripped breaker)
Open AC contact or wire between charge inlet and charger
Fault in the charger's input stage or voltage measurement
Vehicle does not charge although the cable is plugged in
Charging fault message or flashing fault pattern at the charge port
P0D81: P0D81 is the plausibility code for the charger's AC input: a signal is present and electrically valid, yet contradicts the stage the charging sequence has reached. No manufacturer documents this code publicly with thresholds.
Charging station switches AC on before the vehicle has closed S2 (faulty or welded EVSE relay)
Charger's input voltage measurement reports an implausible value
Improvised supply that feeds the inlet directly without a proper EVSE
Charging does not start or stops shortly after plugging in
P0D82: P0D82 reports that the charger's input circuit signal has dropped below the lowest value the module accepts as electrically valid. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Ford, for instance, folds missing input into P0D80 with its 85 VAC/30 s limit.
Input sense line or harness shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion at the charge inlet terminals
Failed input stage inside the on-board charger
P0D83: P0D83 is set when the charger reads its input circuit above the highest electrically valid level, i.e. a reading the measuring stage could not produce from a healthy mains connection. No manufacturer publishes a threshold for it.
Input sense line shorted to a voltage source
Damaged charge inlet with bridged or burnt contacts
Drifted or failed measuring channel in the charger
P0D84: P0D84 stands for an input signal that keeps jumping or dropping out during a charge rather than sitting steadily at a wrong value. There is no public manufacturer description of the code.
Worn, loose or heat-damaged charging plug or inlet contacts
Supply sagging under load, e.g. long extension lead
Loose connector between inlet and charger
P0D85: Battery Charging Output Voltage Too High

P0D85 means the charger is putting more voltage onto the traction battery side than it should. In Ford's 2019 plug-in hybrid OBD summary the battery controller compares the charger's output voltage with its own request and flags a surplus of 20.82 V lasting 20 seconds.
Voltage control fault inside the on-board charger/DC-DC unit
Open high-voltage fuse or P/N line between charger and battery (output unloaded)
Control unit software error (e.g. Porsche DME, reprogramming)
Hybrid system warning and check engine light
P0D86: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit A/Open

Many plug-in vehicles light up the charge inlet to show whether the plug is recognised, charging is running or a fault exists; a Ford summary describes a four-segment ring, a supplier patent multi-coloured LEDs at the port. P0D86 says the control module driving channel A of this indicator finds no continuity in that circuit.
Indicator connector at the charge inlet unplugged or not latched
Broken wire in the harness near the charge port flap
Failed LED or lamp element of channel A
Part of the charge port lighting stays dark
Charging status not visible at the inlet, charging itself works
P0D87: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit A Low

P0D87 flags channel A of the charge port status indicator as pulled low, which in practice means a short to ground somewhere between driver and lamp. Such a fault only shows when the channel is switched on: the driver tries to raise the line and current flows straight to ground.
Chafed wire of channel A touching body ground
Water ingress into the charge inlet lighting
Indicator channel A stays dark when it should light
Charging status hard to read at the port
P0D88: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit A High

P0D88 is stored when channel A of the charge port status indicator sits at a high level although the driver is holding it off, typically because the line touches a voltage-carrying wire or the driver stage leaks.
Channel A wire shorted to a voltage-carrying wire (pinched harness)
Bridged or corroded connector at the indicator
Leaking or failed output stage in the control module
Indicator channel A lights constantly or glows faintly
Port shows a misleading charging status
P0D89: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit B/Open

P0D89 reports lost continuity in the second output channel, B, of the charge port status indicator. Where an indicator has several channels, they usually stand for different colours or segments, as in the multi-colour port lighting of a supplier patent; which one is B depends on the vehicle, and no manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Break in the channel B wire or its connector pin
Failed LED or segment of channel B
Shared connector or ground at the inlet (when A and C are also affected)
One colour or segment of the port lighting missing
P0D8A: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit B Low
P0D8A means channel B of the charge port status indicator is held at ground level when it ought to rise, i.e. a short to ground on the B line or inside its lamp.
Wet or corroded contacts at the inlet lighting bridging to ground
Channel B wire chafed through to body ground
Shorted LED or segment of channel B
Colour or segment B stays dark
P0D8B: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit B High

P0D8B is set when the B line of the charge port status indicator carries voltage while its driver has it switched off. The detection logic mirrors what GM published for the Volt's charge-status LED (P0D2C): a short to battery is looked for during the off phase. No manufacturer documents P0D8B itself.
Insulation damage where the harness bends at the flap, contact with a supply wire
Driver output in the control module stuck on
Colour or segment B stays lit
Displayed charge level does not match the actual state
P0D8C: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit C/Open

P0D8C points to an open third channel, C, of the charge port status indicator. Only systems with at least three separately driven lighting outputs use it, for instance one per colour in an RGB-type port lamp of the kind a supplier patent describes, or individual ring segments. No manufacturer documents the code publicly.
Lamp connector left unplugged or pin pushed back after work at the inlet
Failed LED of channel C (on integrated inlets the whole inlet assembly)
One colour or segment of the port lighting missing
Fault appears after body or inlet repair
P0D8D: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit C Low

P0D8D marks channel C of the charge port status indicator as shorted toward ground: when the module switches C on, the line does not reach the expected level and the driver registers overcurrent or a low voltage.
Short to ground at the far end of the harness inside the inlet housing
Shorted LED or segment of channel C
Grounded driver output inside the control module
Colour or segment C stays dark
Whole port indicator may switch off
P0D8E: Battery Charger Coupler Status Indicator Control Circuit C High

P0D8E is recorded when channel C of the charge port status indicator shows a high level that the driver did not command, a short to a supply voltage or a driver that no longer turns off. Following the pattern GM published for the Volt's charge-status LED, this is checked while the output is meant to be inactive. No manufacturer documents P0D8E publicly.
Chafed channel C wire touching a supply wire at the flap mechanism
Output stage in the control module stuck on
Colour or segment C lit permanently
Port shows a fault or complete status that is not real
P0D8F: Battery Charger A Cooling System Performance
P0D8F means the cooling of on-board charger A is not keeping the unit within its temperature limits, so the charger has to restrict its function.
Low coolant level or air in the charger's cooling circuit
Coolant lines connected to the wrong circuit (Mercedes AMG GLE 53 Hybrid)
Failed coolant pump of the low-temperature circuit
Blocked low-temperature radiator or inactive cooling fan
AC charging stops after a short time or runs at reduced power
Warning that AC charging is inoperative
P0D90: P0D90 is stored when the AC supplied to the on-board charger does not have a believable mains frequency. No official manufacturer document available to the public names the code with a threshold.
Charging from a source with unstable frequency (small generator, inverter)
Faulty portable charging unit or wall box
Fault in the charger's frequency measurement
Often no noticeable effect apart from the stored code
Charging interrupted at certain supply points
P0D91: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit/Open

P0D91 means the module that drives the charge-plug latch sees its lock output as electrically open: when it commands the latch closed, no current flows through the wiring and actuator winding. Without a confirmed lock, the car normally refuses to start a charging session, because the plug could be withdrawn under load.
Connector at the lock actuator loose, corroded or backed out
Broken wire in the harness between control unit and inlet
Motor winding inside the lock actuator burnt through
Driver stage or software of the controlling module (Mercedes names both)
Vehicle does not charge on AC
Charging system warning in the instrument cluster
P0D92: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit Low

P0D92 says the voltage on the lock control output stays too low, typically because the drive line is shorted to ground or the actuator draws far too much current, so the module cannot energise the latch properly and shuts its driver off. No manufacturer publishes this exact code.
Lock drive wire chafed and shorted to body ground
Actuator jammed or binding, drawing excessive current
Water in the actuator connector at the inlet
Driver output of the controlling module defective
Charging session does not start after plugging in
Charge plug is not held in the inlet
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
P0D93: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit High
P0D93 reports a lock control circuit that reads higher than the module expects, classically a drive line shorted to a supply voltage.
Locking pin broken or missing after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Lock drive wire shorted to a supply voltage
Internal electrical fault in the lock actuator
Driver stage of the controlling module defective
Charger Service Required indicator in the cluster (Ford)
Locking pin visibly broken or absent at the inlet
P0D94: Battery Charger Coupler Lock Control Circuit Performance

P0D94 is the functional check of the locking step: the wiring tests fine, yet after a lock command the feedback from the actuator does not confirm that the pin arrived in its locked position. Two makers publish it.
Software fault in the on-board charger, fixed by update (Audi)
Actuator mechanism binding from dirt, ice or wear
Charge plug not fully seated, so the pin cannot engage
Charging aborts or does not start; DC fast charging unavailable
Charge cable cannot be removed except with the manual release
Charge LED changes from green to red, AC charging restricted message (Audi)
P0D95: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit/Open

P0D95 concerns the release direction: the output that withdraws the locking pin shows an open circuit when the module commands unlock. Because J2012 assigns lock and unlock separate control circuits, the module watches each drive direction on its own, and a break can disable only the release.
Open unlock drive wire or loose pin in the actuator connector
Motor winding or internal contact of the actuator open
Corrosion in the connector at the inlet from road splash
Unlock driver stage of the controlling module defective
Charge cable stays locked in the inlet after charging
Plug can only be freed with the emergency release
P0D96: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit Low

P0D96 indicates that the voltage on the unlock control output is too low, which usually means the release line is shorted to ground or the actuator pulls an overcurrent as soon as it is energised in the release direction. To protect its driver, the module stops commanding, so the pin stays where it is.
Unlock drive wire shorted to ground at a chafe point
Actuator seized, for example by ice or dirt, causing overcurrent
Unlock driver stage of the module defective
Charge plug cannot be unplugged after charging
Emergency release needed to free the cable
P0D97: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit High
P0D97 reports that the unlock control output sits higher than it should while the module is not driving it, or does not follow the command, which points to a release line touching a supply voltage.
Unlock drive wire shorted to a supply wire in the harness
Internal short inside the lock actuator
Unlock driver stage of the module stuck on
Charging session stops or does not start
Plug is not held firmly in the inlet
P0D98: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Control Circuit Performance
P0D98 is set when the release command is carried out electrically but the feedback does not confirm that the pin has retracted, or the actuator never reaches its open end stop.
Actuator pin damaged by pulling the plug while latched (Ford)
Release movement blocked by ice, dirt or a worn gear train
Plug hard to remove or held in the inlet
P0D99: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit

P0D99 flags a general electrical fault in temperature sensor A of the charging inlet, the element that tells the car how hot the power contacts are. At high current, contact resistance heats the pins; the reading lets the car throttle or stop charging (TE Connectivity, US10960781B2).
Loose low-voltage connector at the on-board charger (smart)
Damaged sensor wiring between inlet and charger
Temperature element in the inlet failed (usually replaced with the inlet harness)
Evaluation input in the charger module defective
P0D9A: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P0D9A covers a coupler temperature signal that is electrically valid but does not make sense, for example a rise that the charging current cannot explain or a value that disagrees with the rest of the system.
Oversized or damaged terminals in the charging station plug (GM)
Charging software calibration, update pending or available (GM)
Raised contact resistance at the vehicle inlet pins
Temperature element drifting out of its characteristic
Charging fails or stops, often at busy public stations
Code returns only after a drive of about 10 minutes (GM)
P0D9B: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low
P0D9B means the voltage of coupler temperature sensor A has dropped below its valid window.
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or corrosion bridging the sensor contacts in the inlet
Diagnosis misled by swapped fault texts in the charger (Bentley)
Fault stored as intermittent or static in the charger
P0D9C: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit High
P0D9C is stored when the signal of coupler temperature sensor A climbs above its valid window, the typical result of an open sensor loop, an unplugged connector or a short to a supply voltage.
Open sensor wire or connector at the inlet or charger
Sensor signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Temperature element open inside the inlet
Diagnosis misled by swapped fault texts in the charger (Bentley)
Charging stops immediately or does not start
Fault stored as intermittent or static in the charger
P0D9D: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0D9D is logged when the signal of temperature sensor A in the charging inlet jumps or drops out for short moments instead of failing for good.
Sensor wiring between inlet and charger with a loose or chafed contact
Low-voltage connector at the on-board charger not fully seated (seen on smart for sibling codes)
Moisture or corrosion in the inlet harness connector
Temperature element in the inlet with an internal intermittent break
Charging stops now and then and resumes on a later attempt
Charging power reduced for a while without an obvious reason
Charging fault message that comes and goes
P0D9E: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit

The lock position sensor tells the vehicle whether the pin that holds the charging plug in the inlet is extended or retracted. Without that feedback the car cannot confirm a latched plug and refuses fast charging. A GM patent, US8936482B2, measures how far the actuator has moved the pin, with a Hall element, a potentiometer or an end-stop switch as options.
Actuator pin broken or missing after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Open or shorted feedback wire between lock actuator and control module
Corroded or loose connector at the lock actuator
Evaluation input of the controlling module defective
Charger Service Required message in the cluster (Ford)
Locking pin visibly damaged or absent at the inlet
P0D9F: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P0D9F covers a lock position signal that is electrically in range but does not fit the situation: the pin is reported in a position the actuator was not told to reach, or it gets there too late. The sensing principle in GM patent US8936482B2 works on pin travel, so a jammed or worn mechanism shows up here as well as a drifting sensor.
Loose low-voltage contacts at the 22 kW on-board charger (smart)
Lock mechanism sluggish from ice, dirt or a worn gear train
Position sensor in the actuator drifting or misaligned
Vehicle will not start and reports a connected charging cable (smart)
Fault may appear only at the start or end of charging, with cold or warm parts
P0DA0: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Low

P0DA0 means the lock position feedback sits at the bottom of its range, typically from a signal wire shorted to ground. Mitsubishi documents it for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: with the IGCT supply on, the PHEV-ECU detects a low input from the lock position reading.
Lock position signal line shorted to ground (Mitsubishi)
Actuator pin broken after the plug was pulled while latched (Ford)
Position sensor in the inlet harness outside its resistance specification
Plug is not latched or charging ends right after start
P0DA1: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit High

P0DA1 is the high-side fault of the lock position feedback: the signal stays near its upper limit, which points to an open circuit somewhere in the sensor loop rather than a grounded wire. In the 2023 Outlander PHEV, Mitsubishi sets it in the PHEV-ECU when the supply is on and a high input from the lock position reading is seen.
Ground connection of the lock actuator connector interrupted
Open signal line between inlet harness and PHEV-ECU
Position sensor in the inlet harness open or far above 16.8 kOhm
Charging plug lock not confirmed, DC charging refused
Charging system message, no MIL documented
P0DA2: Battery Charger A Coupler Lock Position Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DA2 is stored when the lock position feedback flickers or drops out briefly, while it never sits at one limit long enough for the low or high verdict. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Loose or corroded contact at the lock actuator connector
Inlet harness chafed where it moves with the charge port flap or body
Worn lock mechanism letting the pin rattle near a switching point
DC fast charging aborts at random
Lock status message that appears and clears again
P0DA3: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit

The inverter of drive motor B, usually the rear electric motor in all-wheel-drive hybrids, measures its own DC link voltage; sensor A delivers that value to the motor controller. P0DA3 is the general circuit fault for this channel, with no finer verdict such as low or high. No manufacturer documents P0DA3 publicly.
Voltage sensing circuit inside the rear motor control unit defective
Loose high-voltage cable or terminal at the rear inverter
Low-voltage connector or harness to the inverter controller faulty
Rear electric drive reduced or unavailable
Reduced power or no READY state
P0DA4: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0DA4 flags a rear inverter voltage that is electrically valid but disagrees with the other voltage readings on the same high-voltage bus.
Rear inverter voltage sensing drifts against the other bus readings
Power drive unit faulty (Mitsubishi final repair step)
Underlying fault in the rear motor control unit (P0C7A, P0DA5, P0DA6, P30D1)
Plug-in hybrid system warning and MIL on
Code returns only after the OBD-II drive cycle
P0DA5: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Low
P0DA5 reports that the rear inverter voltage signal sits at the bottom of its range, the classic result of an open circuit, a short to ground or no high voltage arriving at all.
Rear high-voltage battery cable (P and N lines) loose or damaged
High-voltage fuse not seated or loose bus bar in the battery
Sensing circuit in the rear motor control unit failed
Fault inside the traction battery pack
MIL and plug-in hybrid warning on
Possible no-READY condition if other units also lose voltage
P0DA6: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit High
P0DA6 is the upper-limit fault of the rear inverter voltage signal: the reading sticks near the top, as with a short to the sensor supply, or the bus really is overvolted.
Rear motor control unit sensing faulty when no other unit reports high voltage (Mitsubishi)
Fault in the high-voltage circuit or battery when front and generator units also report high
Signal shorted to the sensor supply inside the inverter
MIL and plug-in hybrid warning on
Rear motor drive switched off, reduced power
P0DA7: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0DA7 is meant for a rear inverter voltage reading that jitters or drops out briefly without staying out of range long enough for P0DA5 or P0DA6. No manufacturer documents this code publicly.
Low-voltage connector at the rear inverter with intermittent contact
High-voltage terminal at the rear inverter not tightened properly
Voltage sensing electronics failing with temperature or vibration
Hybrid warning that appears and clears
Brief loss of rear drive power
P0DA8: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage/Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Correlation

P0DA8 compares the traction battery voltage with the voltage measured at the inverter of drive motor A; both should match closely once the contactors are closed. Denso cites earlier diagnostics that blame a voltage sensor when the two differ by more than a set amount (US9819293B2).
Cracked solder joint in the motor power inverter (Honda Civic/ILX Hybrid)
Battery cell voltage sensor software misreading inverter noise (Honda Accord Hybrid recall)
High-voltage battery junction box faulty (Ford Mach-E)
Battery-side or inverter-side voltage sensor drifting
Fail-safe electric mode with strongly limited speed (Honda)
P0DA9: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage/Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Correlation

P0DA9 is the motor B counterpart of P0DA8: the controller compares traction battery voltage with the voltage seen at the inverter of drive motor B, typically the rear motor, and logs the code when the two drift apart with the contactors closed. No manufacturer documents P0DA9 publicly.
Voltage sensing in the motor B inverter drifting
Battery pack voltage measurement in the battery management faulty
High resistance in a contactor, fuse or cable between battery and rear inverter
Rear electric drive limited or disabled
P0DAA: P0DAA reports that the resistance between the charging-side HV bus and chassis ground has fallen too low, so the charging path or the battery is no longer safely insulated.
Coolant leaking into the battery pack (GM)
Insulation loss within battery cells or sections (GM)
Damaged insulation in the on-board charger or charging cables
Low coolant level in the battery coolant reservoir
P0DAB: P0DAB is the overall verdict on cell balancing: the battery controller sees that bleeding charge off the fuller cells no longer brings the pack back into line, so the spread between cells stays too wide. CARB 13 CCR 1968.2 (e)(15.2.3) requires hybrids to check exactly this.
Battery controller software that judges balancing too strictly (FCA BPCM and Mazda MSP66 reflash)
Cells aged unevenly so the spread grows faster than balancing can correct it
Internal fault in the battery assembly (Mazda 48 V battery replaced when the code returns at once)
One or more balancing switches or resistors no longer working
Check engine light and hybrid system warning in the cluster
Mild hybrid assist, start-stop and regeneration switched off (engine-only operation on Mazda)
Reduced electric range or usable battery capacity
P0DAC: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A

P0DAC reports an electrical fault in balancing circuit A, meaning the wiring, switch or monitoring chip behind it, not a balancing result. Audi uses it on the e-tron GT (2022-2026) in battery management address 008C and spells it out as an electrical fault of cell controller 1.
Brief 12 V supply interruption, e.g. while reconnecting the 12 V battery (Audi e-tron GT)
Defective cell monitoring controller or balancing switch of circuit A
Loose or corroded sense/balancing lead connector at the module
Battery management warning or red onboard supply lamp
Vehicle may refuse to start or enter drive readiness
Diagnostic tester proposes replacing HV battery modules
P0DAD: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A Stuck On
P0DAD means balancing circuit A keeps draining its cells although the controller has not asked for it: the bleed switch is stuck closed and the resistor keeps pulling those cells down.
Balancing transistor of circuit A shorted (fails closed)
Monitoring chip or its drive output keeps the switch enabled
Controller software leaving a balancing request active
Hybrid or EV battery warning with the MIL
Cells of one group noticeably lower after the car has been parked
Range or electric assistance decreasing over days
P0DAE: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A Stuck Off
With P0DAE the controller has commanded balancing on circuit A, yet nothing happens: the switch stays open or the bleed resistor is broken, so the targeted cells keep their charge.
Bleed resistor of circuit A open or its solder joint cracked
Broken balancing/sense lead or terminal between module and cells
Charging ends early because individual cells reach full first
Growing cell voltage spread in the live data
P0DAF: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit A Range/Performance

P0DAF is a plausibility code: circuit A switches and is electrically intact, but the effect on the cell voltages does not match what the controller expects. FCA is the visible user. Ram 1500 pickups with the 48 V eTorque system (2019-2024, bulletin 08-030-24 and its yearly versions) list P0DAF among the MIL codes fixed by new BPCM software.
Battery pack control module software with an oversensitive check (FCA bulletins 08-030-24, 08-186-26)
Weak or deeply discharged cells that respond differently to balancing, e.g. after cold cranking
Bleed resistor or switch of circuit A with changed resistance
MIL on, often together with other battery codes
Vehicle may not start or cannot be switched off (Jeep Cherokee hybrid)
P0DB0: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B

P0DB0 flags an electrical defect in the second balancing circuit, B. The battery controller finds an open, short or implausible voltage on the switch, resistor or lead serving that cell group, independent of whether balancing would be needed right now.
Damaged balancing/sense lead or connector of cell group B
Cell monitoring chip or controller of group B defective
Short 12 V supply dropout during service work
Electric drive or assistance possibly limited
P0DB1: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B Stuck On

P0DB1: in circuit B the bleed path stays closed even after the controller withdrew the command. The cells of group B are drained without pause, so their voltage falls behind the others, worst during long standstill.
Shorted balancing transistor in circuit B
Drive output of the monitoring chip stuck active
Moisture or contamination on the module board creating a leakage path
Group B cells clearly low after parking
P0DB2: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B Stuck Off

Stuck off on circuit B (P0DB2) is the passive failure: the command arrives, but the bleed resistor of that group carries no current, so its high cells are never trimmed. LG Chem's patent EP2730933A1 tests for this by switching the balancing circuit on and off and watching how the voltage across a diagnosis resistor reacts; no change means a dead circuit.
Bleed resistor of group B burnt open
Balancing transistor of circuit B no longer switching
Open terminal or cell tap connection in group B
Charging stops before the expected state of charge
High cell voltages in group B in live data
P0DB3: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit B Range/Performance

P0DB3 concerns how well circuit B works rather than whether it switches. The controller balances group B for a set time and then checks the outcome; if the cells moved too little, too much or in an unexpected direction, the result is called implausible.
Controller software with too narrow expectations (cf. FCA updates for P0DAF)
Aged or high-resistance cell in group B reacting atypically
Bleed resistor value drifted so balancing current is wrong
MIL, sometimes without any noticeable drivability change
Cell spread in group B not shrinking after charging
P0DB4: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C
P0DB4 belongs to the third balancing channel, C, and points to its hardware: an interrupted or shorted lead, a failed switch or a monitoring chip reporting nonsense for that cell group.
Fault in a lead shared by voltage sensing and balancing in group C
Cell monitoring chip of group C defective
Corroded module connector after water ingress
MIL with battery or hybrid warning
Further cell voltage codes stored alongside
P0DB5: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C Stuck On

Circuit C stuck on (P0DB5) means the cells of group C bleed energy permanently, also with the car switched off. Designers guard against exactly this: the LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 lets every balance enable expire on a timer unless the central controller renews it, so a lost command cannot leave a switch on.
Balancing transistor in circuit C failed closed
Enable or watchdog logic of the module not releasing the switch
Leakage path on the module board
MIL with battery warning, often after standing
Low cell voltage codes in group C as a follow-up
P0DB6: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C Stuck Off

P0DB6 says that the bleed function of group C does not respond: commanded on, circuit C stays dead. In LG Chem's US20110285539A1 such a case shows up because a test capacitor charged to cell voltage is not emptied through the balancing path and keeps a high residual voltage.
Bleed resistor of circuit C open
Balancing transistor of circuit C not conducting
Broken cell tap or weld in group C
Shorter charging sessions and lower usable capacity
P0DB7: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit C Range/Performance

P0DB7 covers a circuit C that works electrically but whose outcome does not add up. A typical trigger is a cell in group C that needs trimming far more often or far less often than its neighbours. Southwest Electronic Energy's patent US9097774B2 counts balancing events per cell and flags one whose count runs away, because that hints at an internal short.
Cell in group C with rising self-discharge or an internal short
Controller software with unsuitable plausibility limits
Bleed resistor of circuit C out of tolerance
MIL, often with no other immediate effect
One cell in group C repeatedly lower than the rest
P0DB8: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D

P0DB8 is the circuit code for balancing channel D. Here the controller sees a hardware problem: the switch, resistor or cell tap of group D reports a state that cannot be valid, typically an open lead or a short to a neighbouring line.
Open balancing terminal or lead in group D
Monitoring chip of group D defective
P0DB9: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D Stuck On

A stuck-on circuit D (P0DB9) drains group D continuously. The usual check is simple: does the switch state reported back equal the state the controller asked for? GM applies this on the eAssist battery for a related code, sampling every 200 ms and logging a Type B fault after 7 mismatches in 10. Here the reported state stays on while the command says off.
Balancing transistor of circuit D shorted
Status feedback of the module wrong, switch actually fine
Drive output of the monitoring chip stuck on
Group D cells and their local temperature deviating
P0DBA: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D Stuck Off

P0DBA: circuit D refuses to bleed. Toshiba's patent US20130026994A1 lists an open balancing terminal as one of the faults a monitoring chip should report, and this is the typical root of a stuck-off result.
Open balancing terminal or cell tap in group D
Bleed resistor of circuit D open
Balancing transistor of circuit D failed open
Range slowly decreasing, charging finishing early
P0DBB: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit D Range/Performance

For P0DBB the controller judges the effect of balancing in circuit D as implausible. A clear reference is GM's eAssist key-off test for a related code: engaging the bleed load has to pull the cell at least 0.1 V away from its rest value. A result outside the expected window, even with intact wiring, is what a performance code captures.
Cell in group D with changed internal resistance or capacity
Plausibility limits in the controller software too tight
Bleed resistor of circuit D drifted
Cell spread in group D persisting after long charging
P0DBC: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E

P0DBC is set for an electrical fault in the fifth balancing channel, E: the controller cannot trust the path through which group E would be bled, because a lead, switch or resistor reads open, shorted or out of range.
Open or shorted balancing lead in group E
Monitoring chip responsible for group E faulty
Module connector of group E loose or corroded
P0DBD: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E Stuck On

With P0DBD the controller finds circuit E active when it should be idle. LG Chem's EP2730933A1 offers a way to see it: with the balancing circuit commanded off, the voltage across the diagnosis resistor should match the idle pattern; if it looks like the active pattern, current is still flowing.
Balancing transistor of circuit E shorted
Drive line of the switch held active by the monitoring chip
Leakage on the module board after moisture
Power reduced as group E cells drop
Charge loss after a few days parked
P0DBE: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E Stuck Off

P0DBE means circuit E does nothing when told to bleed. The LaunchPoint patent US8598840B2 describes reading the cells while a planned bleed phase is running and treating a balancing side that shows no effect as faulted; this is the logic behind a stuck-off verdict.
Bleed resistor of circuit E open
Balancing transistor of circuit E does not turn on
Enable signal for group E not reaching the module
Apparent loss of capacity over weeks
P0DBF: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit E Range/Performance

P0DBF tells that balancing in circuit E produces results the controller cannot explain, though the circuit switches. One reason can be a cell that keeps needing correction: the Southwest Electronic Energy patent US9097774B2 tracks how often each cell gets balanced and treats an outlier as a warning of internal shorting, well before overheating.
Cell in group E with increased self-discharge
Software limits for the balancing check too narrow
Bleed resistor of circuit E out of tolerance
MIL, usually without immediate drivability change
Recurring deviation of a single cell in group E
P0DC0: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F

P0DC0 marks an electrical fault in balancing circuit F, the sixth cell group whose bleed path the battery controller can switch. Audi lists P0DC000 for the 2016 A3 e-tron in bulletin 93 17 04 (2046556/1), together with the circuit codes for groups A to H and B200000.
Battery controller software that starts CAN communication too late (Audi A3 e-tron, J840/JX1 update)
Open or chafed balancing/sense lead of cell group F
Defective cell monitoring chip serving group F
Cluster shows a connected charger although no cable is plugged in
Several balancing circuit codes stored at the same time
P0DC1: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F Stuck On

P0DC1 says that the bleed path of cell group F appears to stay engaged. Ford lists it for the BECM of its full and plug-in hybrids in the OBD system summaries of model years 2014 to 2019. The battery there is split into fourteen balancing circuits, A to N, each looking after six cells.
Bleed transistor of group F shorted, so the resistor stays connected
Monitoring chip output keeps the switch of circuit F enabled
A cell of group F with high self-discharge mimicking a drained group
Check engine light with hybrid battery warning after a cold start
Cells of group F clearly below the pack average after standstill
P0DC2: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F Stuck Off
With P0DC2 the controller concludes that circuit F does not bleed when asked to, so the fullest cells of group F are never trimmed.
Bleed resistor of group F burnt open
Bleed transistor of circuit F no longer conducting
Loose cell tap or connector pin on the balancing lead
Charging ends earlier than usual, displayed full charge gives less range
Cells of group F remain highest after charging
Check engine light, usually without noticeable driving change
P0DC3: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit F Range/Performance

P0DC3 is the plausibility code for balancing circuit F, and Volvo is a documented user. On the SPA Twin Engine plug-in hybrids (XC90, XC60, S90, V90, model years 2016-2019) the BECM stores P0DC300 as an intermittent fault, listed alongside the range/performance codes of circuits A to E.
BECM software version with faulty balancing evaluation (Volvo TJ 33931)
Cells of group F with changed capacity respond differently to bleeding
Bleed resistor value drifted so the balancing current is off target
Displayed electric range fluctuates or is unreasonably low
Combustion engine runs more often than expected in hybrid mode
Check engine light, fault often stored as intermittent
P0DC4: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G

P0DC4 points to the hardware path of balancing circuit G: lead, switch, resistor or the chip that drives them. On the 2016 Audi A3 e-tron it appears as P0DC400 in bulletin 93 17 04, never alone but in a row with the circuit codes of groups A to H.
Common software or communication cause when circuit codes A to H appear together (Audi A3 e-tron)
Bleed FET of channel G failing the on-state check
Corroded or loose connector on the cell harness of group G
Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
External charging refused now and then
Scan tool lists several circuit codes plus a control module fault
P0DC5: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G Stuck On

P0DC5 reports that the bleed switch of group G seems to stay closed. Ford lists the code for the BECM of its 2018 hybrids and plug-ins; there, a sticking circuit is inferred at start-up, with contactors open, from any of its six cells straying more than 75 mV from the pack average. A more direct test can sit in the monitoring chip.
Balancing switch of group G stuck in conduction
Enable signal from the controller or chip never withdrawn
Moisture or contamination forming a leakage path on the module board
Check engine light and hybrid battery warning
Low cell voltage codes may follow after longer parking
Electric range decreasing from day to day
P0DC6: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G Stuck Off

P0DC6 is set when circuit G stays idle although balancing is requested, so group G cannot give up charge. Ford names the code in its 2015 hybrid OBD summary and decides it from the start-up voltage comparison of the six cells per circuit.
Shunt resistor of group G open, no current can bypass the cells
Balancing switch of group G does not close on command
Pin backed out of the cell harness connector
Electric range shrinks gradually over weeks
Charging stops before the indicated target
Check engine light without immediate drivability change
P0DC7: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit G Range/Performance
P0DC7 means circuit G switches but its effect on the cells does not fit the controller's model. The code is not tied to passive bleeding.
Controller software with too tight plausibility limits
Weak transfer stage in active balancing (capacitor or transformer aged)
Cells of group G aged so that they react differently to correction
Check engine light with hybrid system message
Cell spread in group G does not shrink after balancing
P0DC8: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H

P0DC8 covers an electrical fault of balancing circuit H. Audi's bulletin 93 17 04 for the 2016 A3 e-tron lists P0DC800 as the last of its circuit codes; no letter beyond H appears there, which suggests eight circuits in that pack.
Cell electronics not answering in time after wake-up (Audi software fix)
Damaged internal bus or supply wiring to the monitoring board of group H
Open bleed path or lead in circuit H
Hybrid battery warning and check engine light
Fault returns after clearing until software is updated
P0DC9: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H Stuck On

P0DC9: the bleed path of group H keeps conducting. Ford lists the code for its 2016 hybrid and plug-in BECM, judged at start-up from the cell spread within the six-cell circuit. Besides draining charge, a switch that cannot open turns energy into heat around the clock.
Bleed FET of group H shorted and unaffected by thermal pause
Heat damage on the monitoring board around the bleed resistors of H
Chip logic keeping the balancing enable of channel H active
Check engine light and hybrid battery warning
Group H noticeably lower than the rest after parking
Locally raised temperature reading in the battery module
P0DCA: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H Stuck Off

P0DCA flags circuit H as inactive: balancing was ordered, but group H keeps its charge. Ford includes the code in its 2017 hybrid OBD summary, again decided by the start-up comparison of six cells per circuit with the pack average. Not every pause is a fault, which makes this code tricky.
Bleed resistor of group H open
Broken cell tap or weld on the balancing lead of H
Intended stop (timer, thermal pause) wrongly judged as no response by the software
Full charge reached earlier, with less range than before
Cells of group H stay at the top of the cell list
P0DCB: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit H Range/Performance
P0DCB is raised when circuit H works electrically but the result of a balancing run does not match the plan.
Wrong capacity or state-of-charge estimate for the cells of group H
Battery controller software (update first, as Volvo does for P0DC3)
Bleed resistor of H drifted from its nominal value
Check engine light, often only after charging sessions
Group H remains out of line after a full charge
P0DCC: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I

P0DCC concerns the hardware of balancing circuit I, the ninth group, so only packs split into at least nine balancing channels can raise it. No maker publishes this exact code: Ford's hybrid summaries assign letter I only to the stuck codes P0DCD and P0DCE, and Audi's A3 e-tron bulletin stops at H.
Broken balancing or sense lead of group I
Corroded connector between cell group I and its monitoring board
Defective monitoring chip for channel I
Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Electric drive or charging limited by the battery controller
P0DCD: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I Stuck On

P0DCD tells that circuit I is drained although no balancing is wanted. In Ford's 2014 hybrid OBD summary the code belongs to the start-up check with open contactors; that early version only sets it after the 75 mV spread within the six-cell group has shown up on two consecutive power-ups. A diagnosis must also know when a switch is on deliberately.
Balancing switch of group I permanently conducting
Software leaving a deliberate switch activation (e.g. chip warming) active
Driver stage of the monitoring chip stuck active on channel I
Check engine light with hybrid battery warning at start-up
Group I lower than the rest after longer standstill
P0DCE: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I Stuck Off

P0DCE means the bleed path of group I does not respond to a balancing request. Ford lists it in the 2019 OBD summary for its full and plug-in hybrids, where the BECM discharges only the highest cells to match the rest and runs this check for 100 ms at power-up before the contactors close.
Open bleed resistor in circuit I
Balancing switch of group I that no longer closes
Cell tap of group I loose at the busbar
Electric range decreases over many charging cycles
Cells of group I highest at the end of charging
Check engine light without noticeable effect while driving
P0DCF: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit I Range/Performance

P0DCF closes the series for the ninth balancing group: circuit I is electrically intact, yet balancing does not bring its cells to where the controller intended. No maker publishes this code. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries cover letter I only with the stuck codes P0DCD and P0DCE.
Cells of group I aged differently, so the planned balancing time no longer fits
Battery controller calibration with an unsuitable target or time window
Bleed resistor of circuit I off its nominal value, giving too little current
Check engine light, typically noticed after charging
Group I stays apart from the other cells after a full charge
P0DD0: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J

P0DD0 reports an electrical fault in balancing circuit J, the tenth group. Only packs split into ten or more balancing channels can set it; Audi's A3 e-tron bulletin ends its circuit codes at H and Volvo's SPA Twin Engine journal at F, so those packs never reach J. No manufacturer documents P0DD0 publicly, and Ford uses J only for stuck faults.
Open balancing or sense terminal of group J (lead, crimp or weld)
Loose or corroded connector between group J and its monitoring board
Faulty monitoring chip channel serving circuit J
Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
Charging or electric drive limited by the battery controller
P0DD1: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Stuck On
P0DD1: group J's bleed path keeps drawing current after balancing should have ended.
Balancing transistor of group J shorted and conducting permanently
Balancing enable for channel J not withdrawn by the monitoring electronics
Cell in group J with high self-discharge producing the same voltage pattern
Check engine light and hybrid battery warning after switching on
Group J clearly lower than the rest after parking
P0DD2: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Stuck Off

P0DD2 marks circuit J as unable to bleed: balancing is commanded, but the six cells of group J keep their charge. Ford lists the code in its 2015 hybrid OBD summary with the same power-up test as for the stuck-on case, run for 100 ms with the contactors still open, two consecutive power cycles and the 75 mV limit against the average cell voltage.
Bleed resistor of circuit J open or burnt
Balancing switch of group J no longer closing
Interrupted balancing lead between cell tap and board
Check engine light without noticeable change in driving
Cells of group J at the top of the cell list at the end of charging
Usable battery capacity declining over time
P0DD3: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit J Range/Performance

P0DD3 is a plausibility verdict on circuit J: the switch reacts, but the effect of balancing on group J does not match what the controller expected. No maker documents this code publicly, so the reasoning rests on CARB and on how balancing is planned.
Wrong charge estimate for the cells of group J
Battery controller software or calibration (check for updates first)
Balancing path of J with raised resistance, so less charge moves than planned
Check engine light, often only after several charges
Group J remains out of line despite balancing
P0DD4: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K

P0DD4 is the electrical fault code for balancing circuit K, the eleventh group, so it only exists on packs with at least eleven balancing channels. Public maker documents for this exact code were not found; Ford's summaries give K only to the stuck faults P0DD5 and P0DD6.
Open wire or loose cell tap in group K
Corrosion or moisture at the connector of the monitoring board for K
Defective monitoring chip or external balancing part of channel K
Check engine light and hybrid system warning
Missing or implausible cell voltages for group K in the scan tool
P0DD5: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Stuck On

P0DD5 tells that circuit K is discharging its cells without a balancing request. Ford's 2016 hybrid OBD summary links the code to the BECM start-up check: before the contactors close it looks at the six cells of the circuit for 100 ms and fails it when one of them is more than 75 mV away from the average, confirmed on a second power cycle.
Shorted balancing switch of group K
Heat damage or contamination bridging the balancing path of K on the board
Driver stage of the monitoring chip holding channel K on
Group K drops faster than the other cells while parked
P0DD6: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Stuck Off

P0DD6: group K's bleed path stays dead when balancing is called for. Ford includes it in its 2017 hybrid OBD summary; the BECM decides at power-up with open contactors, within 100 ms and over two power cycles, using the 75 mV deviation of one of the six cells from the average.
Open bleed resistor in circuit K
Balancing switch of group K failing to turn on
Cracked solder joint in the balancing path of K
Check engine light while the car drives normally
Group K highest at the end of charging
Electric range decreasing over many charges
P0DD7: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit K Range/Performance
P0DD7 points to balancing of group K that works, but not within the expected limits. No maker publishes this code.
Balancing current of K below the expected value (aged resistor, raised contact resistance)
Controller calibration with too short balancing time for group K
A cell in group K drifting faster than balancing can compensate
Check engine light, often after charging
Spread of group K returns soon after a balancing session
P0DD8: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L

P0DD8 concerns the hardware of balancing circuit L, the twelfth group. No manufacturer documents it publicly; Ford, whose hybrid BECM runs through letter N, uses L only in the stuck codes P0DD9 and P0DDA.
Open resistor, switch or solder joint in circuit L
Poor connection of the cell taps of group L
Faulty voltage measuring channel next to circuit L
Hybrid battery warning and check engine light
P0DD9: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Stuck On

P0DD9: the balancing path of group L will not switch off. The 2018 edition of Ford's hybrid OBD summary contains the code; the BECM catches it at power-up with the contactors still open, in a 100 ms check that compares each of the six cells of circuit L with the average and fails above 75 mV, again over two power cycles.
Balancing switch of group L shorted
Switch status feedback of channel L reporting on although the switch is open
Balancing command for L not cleared by the monitoring electronics
Check engine light after switching on
Group L lower than the others after standing
P0DDA: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Stuck Off

P0DDA says circuit L does not discharge when it is told to. In Ford's 2019 hybrid OBD summary the start-up test has been simplified: it still runs for 100 ms before the contactors close, but the requirement of two consecutive power cycles is gone, and the 75 mV deviation of a cell from the average must instead persist for 0.1 s.
Balancing switch of group L stays open when commanded on
Bleed resistor of circuit L open
Missing gate drive for the balancing switch of L
Check engine light with no change in drivability
Group L reaches full charge before the rest
P0DDB: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit L Range/Performance
P0DDB stands for balancing of group L whose result is out of range although the circuit answers. No maker documents P0DDB publicly.
Cell in group L with an internal soft short, needing balancing again and again
Controller calibration of expected balancing effect for L
Drifted bleed resistor of circuit L
Check engine light, sometimes only after long parking

Range estimate varying from day to day
P0DDC: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M

P0DDC reports an electrical fault of balancing circuit M, the thirteenth group, which only large packs with at least thirteen channels possess. No maker publishes this exact code; in Ford's BECM documents M appears only as stuck on (P0DDD) and stuck off (P0DDE).
Broken sense or balancing wire of group M
Damaged or poorly seated connector at the board for M
Fault in the monitoring electronics of channel M
Check engine light and hybrid warning
Battery controller restricting power or charging
P0DDD: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Stuck On

P0DDD reports a balancing path of group M that keeps conducting. Ford's 2015 hybrid OBD summary places it in the BECM monitor, judged at power-up before the contactors close: 100 ms, six cells per circuit, more than 75 mV from the average, two consecutive power cycles. A properly working chip should never leave a channel on indefinitely.
Shorted balancing switch of group M that no timer can stop
Damaged external balancing transistor on the board for M
High self-discharge cell in group M imitating a stuck switch
Group M noticeably low after overnight parking
Raised module temperature near group M
P0DDE: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Stuck Off

P0DDE means group M is not bled when it should be. Ford carries the code in its 2016 hybrid OBD summary with the usual BECM start-up rule: 100 ms with open contactors, six cells per circuit, a 75 mV gap to the average, confirmed over two power cycles. A balancing channel can also be stopped on purpose, which a diagnosis must keep apart from a real failure.
Bleed resistor of circuit M open
Balancing switch of group M that no longer turns on
Intended balancing stop for M misjudged as no response by the software
Check engine light while driving feels normal
Group M highest at the end of each charge

P0DDF: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit M Range/Performance
P0DDF covers group M when balancing responds but its outcome is not credible. No manufacturer publishes this code.
Stored capacity value for cells of group M out of date
Check engine light following charging sessions
Group M not aligned with the rest after full charge
P0DE0: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N

P0DE0 flags a wiring or driver fault in balancing circuit N, the fourteenth and last letter of the series; the next code, P0DE4, belongs to a different system. Packs with more balancing groups than fourteen must therefore map several groups to one letter or use their own codes.
Open balancing terminal or lead of group N
Corroded or loose connector at the last module board
Monitoring chip channel for N defective
Hybrid battery warning with check engine light
P0DE1: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Stuck On
P0DE1 is the last stuck-on code of the series: group N keeps bleeding when it should rest.
Balancing switch of group N permanently conducting

Monitoring electronics keeping the balancing command for N active
Check engine light after switching on
Group N drops while the car is parked
P0DE2: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Stuck Off

P0DE2 closes Ford's list of balancing codes: circuit N does not discharge when commanded. Ford's 2018 hybrid summary has the BECM judge this during a 100 ms window at key-on, contactors still open, comparing each of the six cells with the average against 75 mV over two power cycles.
Open bleed resistor in circuit N
Balancing switch of group N not turning on
Cell tap of group N detached from the busbar
Check engine light without driving complaint
Charging ends early because group N is full first
P0DE3: Hybrid/EV Battery Cell Balancing Circuit N Range/Performance
P0DE3 is the final code of the balancing series and judges whether balancing of group N achieves a believable result. No maker documents it publicly.
Cells of group N aged unevenly
Controller estimates or calibration for group N off
Bleed path of N with too little current
Check engine light, mostly after charging
Group N never quite levels with the other groups
P0DE4: Electric/Auxiliary Transmission Fluid Pump A Motor Over Temperature

P0DE4 reports that the electric motor of auxiliary transmission fluid pump A has run too hot. Such a pump keeps the transmission pressurised while the engine is stopped, either by start-stop or during electric driving in a hybrid. No manufacturer documents P0DE4 publicly.
Low, aged or wrong transmission fluid making the pump work harder
Binding rotor or worn bearing in the pump motor
Transmission running hot (towing, heat, restricted fluid cooler)
Faulty temperature evaluation in the pump controller or outdated software
Start-stop no longer shuts the engine off
Electric driving limited, engine keeps running
Harsh engagement when pulling away after a stop
P0DE5: Charge Status Indicator B Control Circuit/Open

P0DE5 flags an interrupted drive circuit for charge status indicator B, a second lamp or LED that tells the owner whether the vehicle is charging, for instance one at the charge port next to the one on the dashboard. Which light gets the letter B is up to the maker. No manufacturer documents P0DE5 publicly.
Broken wire or unplugged connector to indicator B
Burnt-out LED or failed indicator unit
Corroded contacts in the weather-exposed charge port area
Failed output driver in the controlling module
Charge status indicator B stays dark while charging
Warning lamp possible depending on the manufacturer
P0DE6: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cell Voltage Low

P0DE6 means the battery controller has measured at least one cell of the high-voltage pack below its lower voltage limit. It concerns a real reading, not the sensing lines (P0B3D and similar), and it looks at the weakest cell rather than the charge of the whole pack (P0A7D).
Pack deeply discharged after long standing or repeated failed starts
Battery controller software judging too strictly (e.g. cold cranking)
Single weak cell with high self-discharge or lost capacity
Cell balancing circuit draining one cell
Vehicle will not start or switch to ready
P0DE7: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Cell Voltage High

P0DE7 is stored when a single cell of the high-voltage pack climbs above the upper voltage limit the battery controller permits. Overcharged lithium-ion cells age quickly and can become unsafe, so the controller usually restricts charging and regenerative braking until the cell is back in range.
Battery controller software or calibration (documented by Ram)
Cell balancing no longer bleeding off the highest cell
Aged cell with raised internal resistance overshooting during regen
Drifting cell monitoring chip reporting too high a value

P0DE8 reports an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit for coolant control valve C, a third switchable valve in the coolant loop of the hybrid or EV battery. What it switches depends on the layout, for example whether coolant passes through the radiator, the air-conditioning chiller or a heater, and the maker decides which valve is called C.
Broken wire or loose connector at valve C
Open coil or motor winding inside valve C
Corroded pins from coolant or water ingress
Failed driver stage in the controlling module
Battery temperature control works only in a fallback mode
Charging or drive power reduced when the pack is too hot or cold
P0DE9: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Performance/Stuck Off
P0DE9 says coolant control valve C is electrically fine but does not do its job: it fails to reach the commanded position or remains in its off state. No manufacturer documents P0DE9 publicly.
Valve body seized or sluggish from deposits
Worn actuator motor or gearing in valve C
Low coolant or air in the battery loop distorting the temperature check
Battery heats up faster under load or while fast charging
Charging power or drive power limited
P0DEA: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Stuck On

P0DEA means coolant control valve C stays in its active position even though the controller has asked it to return. A wiring check cannot see this, because the circuit is intact; the controller needs a position feedback, as on GM's Volt valve with its own sensor codes, or it infers the state from coolant and pack temperatures that keep moving the wrong way.
Valve jammed in the active position by debris or wear
Driver stage that does not switch off
Pack too cold in winter or too warm in summer
P0DEB: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Control Valve C Control Circuit Low

P0DEB is set when the drive line of coolant control valve C reads too low, which almost always means a short to ground somewhere between controller and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DEB publicly.

P0DEC is the short-to-voltage case for coolant control valve C: its drive line reads high at a moment when the controller expects it low. No manufacturer documents P0DEC publicly. P0DEE: Pedestrian Alert Control Module Circuit Low

P0DEE is set when the hard-wired circuit to the pedestrian alert control module sits below its expected voltage, typically from a short to ground. No manufacturer documents P0DEE publicly, so the exact signal behind it, whether supply, wake-up or a command line, is not known in detail.

P0DEF: Pedestrian Alert Control Module Circuit High

P0DEF reports a voltage above the permitted window on the wired link to the pedestrian alert control module, most often because a wire touches a supply line or the line has lost its ground reference. No manufacturer documents P0DEF publicly.

P0DF0 is the catch-all circuit code for temperature sensor B in the generator inverter, the power stage that drives the generator of a two-machine hybrid. P0DF1 means the signal of generator inverter temperature sensor B drops out or jumps for short moments and then looks normal again. Typical triggers are temperature steps faster than the power module could physically heat or cool, or brief readings that resemble an open line.

Fault often not reproducible at the workshop
P0DF2: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit
P0DF2 covers an electrical fault on temperature sensor C of the generator inverter that the controller cannot assign to a more specific low, high or intermittent code.

P0DF3: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0DF3 is logged when sensor C in the generator inverter delivers an unsteady signal: short spikes, gaps or values that change faster than the module temperature ever could. P0DF4: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0DF4 reports that temperature sensor B of the generator inverter delivers an electrically valid signal whose value does not fit the other sensors.
Control software misdetection (Volvo T8, ECM update available)
Sensor in the power module drifted or stuck at one value
Internal fault in the power drive unit (Mitsubishi replaces the unit)
Message such as Propulsion System Service Required

P0DF5: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P0DF5 sets when the signal voltage of generator inverter temperature sensor B stays below its valid window. Mitsubishi's Outlander PHEV checks this continuously: if the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor reads at most 1.25 V during 0.08 s while the generator control unit has at least 8 V supply, P0DF5-00 is stored.
Shorted thermistor inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit
Engine or hybrid warning light on
Generator output limited, engine runs more often
P0DF6: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P0DF6 is the high-signal case for sensor B in the generator inverter. In the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi stores P0DF6-00 when the V-phase high-side IGBT sensor voltage reaches at least 3.75 V during 0.08 s, again only with a GCU supply of at least 8 V.
Open signal line or backed-out terminal
Cracked sensor element or internal fault of the power drive unit
Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature shown far too low
P0DF7: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P0DF7 is the plausibility code for temperature sensor C of the generator inverter. The idea behind it: after a long rest every power switch should be at roughly the same temperature, so a sensor that stands out is suspect.
Sensor C drifted or stuck inside the IGBT module
Internal fault of the power drive unit
Engine warning light on after a cold start
Usually no noticeable change in driving
P0DF8: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low

P0DF8 tells that temperature sensor C in the generator inverter delivers a voltage below its valid range. Mitsubishi uses the code in the Outlander PHEV for the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor: a reading at or under 1.25 V for 0.08 s, with at least 8 V GCU supply, stores P0DF8-00, and the check runs all the time.
Signal line of sensor C shorted to ground
Coolant or moisture inside the inverter electronics
Shorted sensor or internal fault of the power drive unit
Hybrid or engine warning light on
Implausibly high inverter temperature in live data
P0DF9: Generator Inverter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High

P0DF9 is stored when the C temperature sensor of the generator inverter reports a voltage at or beyond the upper end of its window. For the Outlander PHEV Mitsubishi defines the limit as 3.75 V for 0.08 s on the W-phase high-side IGBT sensor, monitored continuously whenever the GCU has at least 8 V.
Open signal line of sensor C
Terminal pushed back in the inverter connector
Broken sensor element inside the power drive unit
Engine or hybrid warning light on
Inverter temperature stuck at a very low value
P0DFA: Generator Phase U-V-W Current Sensor Correlation

In a three-phase machine the currents of phases U, V and W add up to nearly zero at every instant, so a sum far from zero shows that at least one current sensor is wrong. P0DFA is the code for this cross-check on the generator side.
12 V voltage drop at key-on (Ford SSM 50151)
One phase current sensor with offset or gain error
Internal fault of the inverter or power drive unit
Stop Safely Now or hybrid system warning
Vehicle may not start or ready mode is refused

Offset learning interrupted or run under wrong conditions

Fault or wrong software in the generator control unit
Hybrid system warning and engine warning light

Code returns after clearing until relearned
P0DFC: P0DFC is stored when the controller has no valid learned position offset for the generator resolver.
Inverter or hybrid controller replaced without resolver learning
Software fault in the inverter generator module (Volvo, update available)
Stored offset lost or corrupted in EEPROM
Sometimes only stored as history code without symptoms
P0DFD: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit/Open

P0DFD flags an open or otherwise faulty drive circuit of the valve that controls coolant flow through the on-board charger. Such a valve lets the thermal system send coolant to the charger during AC charging and bypass it while driving. No manufacturer documents P0DFD publicly.
Broken wire or unplugged connector at the valve
Open coil or motor winding in the valve
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
Charging slower than usual or interrupted
P0DFE: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit Low
P0DFE means the control line of the charger coolant valve reads low, usually because it is shorted to ground somewhere between driver and valve. No manufacturer documents P0DFE publicly.
Control wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Coolant or water in the valve connector
Internal short in the valve actuator
Reduced charging power, longer charging time
P0DFF: Battery Charger Coolant Control Valve Control Circuit High

P0DFF is the short-to-voltage case for the valve that cools the on-board charger. The controller sees the drive line high while commanding it low. No manufacturer documents P0DFF publicly. The closest published logic is GM's 2011 Volt monitor for battery coolant valve A (P0CE3).
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Output stage in the controlling module will not switch off
Internal fault in the valve actuator

P0E00: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit

P0E00 is the general circuit code for the current sensor in phase U of the generator. Each phase sensor, usually a Hall-type device inside the inverter, outputs a voltage around a mid-point when no current flows. No manufacturer documents P0E00 publicly.
Supply or reference fault of the current sensor
Defective phase U current sensor inside the inverter
Faulty internal connection between sensor and control board
Hybrid system warning and engine warning light
Vehicle may not reach ready mode
P0E01: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P0E01 flags an implausible zero point of the U-phase current sensor inside the generator inverter. Sensors of this kind put out a voltage near the middle of their span while no current flows, so the test is only run when the machine cannot carry current.

Unstable sensor supply or reference voltage inside the inverter
Evaluation circuit of the generator control unit faulty
MIL and hybrid system warning light on

P0E02: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low
P0E02 is stored when the output of the generator inverter's phase U current sensor falls to the bottom of its range, a level no real current would produce.
Sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor output failed low

Input stage of the generator control unit faulty
MIL and hybrid system warning light on

P0E03: Generator Phase U Current Sensor Circuit High
P0E03 is the upper-limit fault of the current sensor that measures phase U of the generator inverter: its signal is pinned near the supply rail.
Sensor signal shorted to its supply voltage
Current sensor in the power drive unit failed with high output
Lost sensor ground or reference inside the inverter
MIL and hybrid system warning light on

P0E04: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit

P0E04 is the general circuit code for the generator inverter's V-phase current sensor, meant for an electrical fault that is not narrowed down to offset, low or high. No manufacturer documents P0E04 publicly.
Electrical fault in the V-phase sensor circuit inside the inverter

Hybrid or engine warning light on
P0E05: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P0E05 reports an implausible zero point of the current sensor in phase V of the generator inverter. Mitsubishi describes it only for the 2023 Outlander PHEV, the first of its generator units with a sensor in phase V; the earlier model measured just U and W.
Zero point of the phase V current sensor drifted
Disturbed sensor supply or reference in the power drive unit
MIL and hybrid system warning light on
Possibly also the phase sum code P0DFA stored
Less generator support during hybrid driving
P0E06: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low

P0E06 means the phase V current sensor of the generator inverter delivers a signal at the floor of its range. The 2023 Outlander PHEV is the only documented user: Mitsubishi's generator control unit, running on 8 V or more, stores P0E06-00 when the V-phase voltage remains at 0.5 V or below for 0.2 s, and the MIL comes on.
V-phase sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor failed low

Input of the generator control unit faulty
MIL and hybrid system warning light on
P0E07: Generator Phase V Current Sensor Circuit High

P0E07 is set when the phase V current sensor in the generator inverter reports a signal stuck high. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV has its generator control unit flag P0E07-00 as soon as the V-phase voltage is at 4.5 V or above for 0.2 s while its own supply is at least 8 V; MIL and hybrid warning both illuminate.
V-phase sensor signal shorted to its supply
Common sensor supply in the power drive unit too high or faulty
Current sensor failed with high output

P0E08: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit
P0E08 covers an electrical fault of the generator inverter's W-phase current sensor that falls outside the offset, low and high categories. No manufacturer documents P0E08 publicly.
