Hybrid or engine warning light on
Reduced generator output, battery charged less while driving
P0E09: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

P0E09 is the zero-point check of the phase W current sensor in the generator inverter. Mitsubishi uses it on two Outlander PHEV generations. The 2018 code chart lists it as an offset fault of current sensor 2, the second of only two generator current sensors.

P0E0A: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Low
With P0E0A the phase W current sensor of the generator inverter reports a signal at or near zero volts.
W-phase sensor signal shorted to ground or sensor failed low

P0E0B: Generator Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High
P0E0B marks a phase W current sensor signal in the generator inverter that sits at the top of its range.
W-phase sensor signal shorted to its supply voltage
Current sensor in the power drive unit failed with high output

P0E0C: P0E0C concerns the three power phases between generator inverter and generator, not the current sensors.

No manufacturer documents P0E0D publicly.
Phase cable or winding insulation damaged, leakage to ground
Lower IGBT of one phase leaking or shorted
Phase voltage evaluation in the inverter faulty
Hybrid system warning light, possibly with insulation fault message
P0E0E: P0E0E reports a generator phase line that reads high: one of the U, V or W connections is held near the positive high-voltage potential, typically by an upper power switch that stays on or by a short to the positive rail.
Upper IGBT of one phase shorted or not switching off
Phase line shorted to the positive high-voltage rail
Phase monitoring in the inverter faulty
Hybrid system warning light and MIL on

P0E0F: Generator Inverter Power Supply A Circuit/Open

P0E0F is set when the generator inverter loses one of its internal supplies, supply A, or the line to it is interrupted. Which supply carries the letter A is up to the manufacturer; usually it is the low-voltage feed of the gate drivers that switch the power transistors. No manufacturer documents P0E0F publicly.
Gate driver supply inside the inverter failed
12 V feed, fuse or connector of the inverter interrupted
Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator out of operation, vehicle may not reach ready state
P0E10: Generator Inverter Power Supply A Circuit Low

P0E10 means supply A of the generator inverter is present but too low. Ford lists the code in the HEV OBD system summary for its power-split hybrids (OBDSM1901): in the paragraph on the gate signal lines of motor and generator, P0E10 appears with P0BCE and P0BCF among the generator-side open-circuit faults, while the motor side is covered by P0C0C.
Gate drive supply or gate signal path in the inverter faulty (Ford)

Hybrid system warning light and MIL on

P0E11: Generator Inverter Power Supply A Circuit High

P0E11 is stored when supply A of the generator inverter is above its permitted range. Overvoltage on the gate driver feed can overstress the control inputs of the power transistors, so controllers usually react by blocking the inverter. No manufacturer documents P0E11 publicly.
Voltage regulator of the gate driver supply in the inverter faulty
Short between two internal supply rails
Overvoltage in the 12 V system (DC/DC converter or charging fault)
Hybrid system warning light and MIL on
Generator blocked, no charging while driving
P0E12: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater A Control Circuit/Open

P0E12 concerns the command circuit of battery coolant heater A, the electric element that warms the coolant sent to the hybrid or EV battery when the pack is too cold for charging or full power. The controller flags it when this circuit is open or otherwise electrically faulty. No manufacturer documents P0E12 publicly.
Broken or chafed wire in the heater A command circuit
Loose, corroded or unlocked connector at the heater or controller
Open circuit inside the heater A assembly
Failed output driver in the controlling module
Slow or reduced charging in cold weather
Engine runs more often than usual on cold days
Reduced electric power until the pack warms up
P0E13: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater A Control Circuit Low

P0E13 is the low-signal case on the command line of battery coolant heater A: the controller reads the line near ground at a moment when it expects a higher level, which points to a short to ground or a driver that cannot pull the circuit up. No manufacturer documents P0E13 publicly.
Command wire shorted to ground, e.g. chafed against the body
Moisture or coolant in the heater connector
Internal short in the heater's control input
Output driver in the controller stuck low
Battery heater does not work at low temperatures
P0E14: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater A Control Circuit High

P0E14 is logged when heater A's control wire sits too high, typically because it touches a supply voltage or because a pulled-up input has lost its connection. No manufacturer documents P0E14 publicly; GM's 2016 Volt reports open, ground and voltage faults of its heater transistor together as P1EC3 (Type B).
Command wire shorted to a supply or neighbouring live wire
Open connection on a pulled-up heater input reading as high
Output driver in the controller that will not switch off
Heater shut down by its own overheat protection
Battery heating unavailable or erratic in cold weather

P0E15 means heater A can be addressed electrically but does not deliver the heat it was asked for. Stellantis uses the code on Chrysler Pacifica plug-in hybrids from 2017 onward and the 2021–2023 Jeep Wrangler 4xe for the high-voltage electric coolant heater (ECH), a LIN-controlled unit that on these models heats the cabin loop.
Low coolant, leaks or trapped air in the heater loop
Hybrid control software that needs an update (Stellantis HCP/AHCP)

Faulty auxiliary coolant pump or restricted hoses

P0E16 is the open-circuit code for a second battery coolant heater, B. Why a car has two: some thermal systems pair the pack heater with another heater, for example one for the cabin loop, and can route its heat to the battery.

P0E18: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Heater B Control Circuit High

P0E1C: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Control Circuit High

P0E1C is set when the command signal to battery coolant pump B stays above what the controller allows, for instance because the line is shorted to battery voltage or, on a pulled-up PWM input, interrupted. No manufacturer documents P0E1C publicly.

P0E1D: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Coolant Pump B Control Performance

P0E1D says pump B accepts its command electrically but the effect the controller looks for does not appear, such as the expected flow, speed or temperature change in its loop. No manufacturer documents P0E1D publicly.

P0E31: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A Circuit

P0E31 is the general circuit code of voltage sensor A in a DC/DC converter, the measurement the converter or its controller uses to regulate output voltage. P0E32 flags a voltage reading of DC/DC converter sensor A that is electrically valid but does not match a reference.

P0E33: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A Low
P0E33 means the controller reads an implausibly low value from voltage sensor A of a DC/DC converter, typically because the signal wire is shorted to ground.

P0E34: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A High

With P0E34 the controller sees a voltage on sensor A of the DC/DC converter that is too high to be real, which points to the signal being shorted to a battery feed or another live wire. In GM's 2025 tables (25OBDG03A) the ECM flags it when raw voltage value 1 exceeds 28 V, far above anything a 12 V converter output should reach.
Signal wire shorted to a battery feed or other live circuit
Lost reference ground of the measurement, signal floats high
Faulty measuring circuit in the converter
P0E35: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor A Intermittent/Erratic

P0E35 is reserved for a voltage sensor A signal that jumps or drops out briefly instead of staying wrong: the reading is erratic, but not low or high long enough for P0E33 or P0E34 to mature. No manufacturer documents P0E35 publicly.
Loose or spread terminal in the converter connector
Ground connection that fails under vibration
Cracked solder joint in the converter's measuring circuit
Warning light that appears and disappears
Start-stop works only now and then
P0E36: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Circuit

P0E36 is the catch-all circuit code for the second voltage measurement of a DC/DC converter, sensor B. Where a converter reads both its input and its output, or monitors one rail twice, the second path gets the letter B; FCA names it voltage sensor 2 on the 2021 Ram 1500 eTorque. No manufacturer documents P0E36 itself in public sources.
Open sense wire or unplugged connector
Second measuring path inside the converter failed
Warning light, possibly 12 V battery warning
Start-stop disabled or converter output reduced
P0E37: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Range/Performance

P0E37 says that voltage sensor B delivers a believable number which nevertheless disagrees with what the vehicle measures elsewhere. GM's 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) check raw voltage value 2 of the converter against the ECM run/crank voltage: in bypass mode a gap above 2 V counts, and 320 failed samples out of 400 at 12.5 ms set a Type B code.
Second voltage measurement in the converter drifting
Voltage drop on supply or ground wiring distorting the comparison
Controller software needing an update (FCA eTorque)
MIL on, after one or two trips depending on maker and software
P0E38: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Low

P0E38 is stored when the second voltage reading of the DC/DC converter, sensor B, sits at the bottom of its scale. GM uses it in the 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) with the same limits as on sensor A, only applied to raw voltage value 2: under 1 V, confirmed by 320 of 400 samples taken at 12.5 ms intervals and only checked at 6.6 V battery voltage or more.
Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Failed second measuring circuit in the converter
Bent or corroded pin in the converter connector
P0E39: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B High

P0E39 reports that sensor B of the DC/DC converter reads far too high, a pattern GM attributes to a short to battery. The 2025 engine tables (25OBDG03A) set the bar at more than 28 V for raw voltage value 2, again needing 320 failing samples within 400 at 12.5 ms and a battery voltage of at least 6.6 V, with Type B confirmation over two trips.
Sensor B signal shorted to a voltage-carrying wire
Open reference ground letting the signal float high
Failed measuring circuit for sensor B
P0E3A: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor B Intermittent/Erratic

P0E3A covers an unsteady signal from voltage sensor B of a DC/DC converter: short spikes, dropouts or noise that never last long enough for the hard low or high codes. Publicly, no manufacturer documents P0E3A.
Harness rubbing intermittently where it moves with the engine
Poor terminal tension in the sensor B circuit
Electrical interference on an unshielded sense line
Sporadic warning light, sometimes cleared on its own
Start-stop unavailable from time to time
P0E3B: P0E3B indicates that the electric pump circulating coolant through the high-voltage battery turns faster than commanded. A pump that suddenly spins too freely has usually lost its load, because it is moving air instead of coolant after a leak, a low reservoir or a poorly bled system. No manufacturer documents P0E3B publicly.
Low coolant level or leak, pump running partly dry
Air left in the battery loop after a repair
Faulty pump electronics or speed feedback signal
Reduced charging or drive power when the battery warms up
P0E3C: P0E3C is set when the battery coolant pump stays below the speed it has been asked for. GM documents it specifically for the 2024–25 Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray: the battery energy control module (K16) stores P0E3C, and the ECM may add P0A7B to switch on the MIL.
Air trapped around the pump after earlier service (GM 24-NA-160)
Worn pump bearing or debris slowing the impeller
Low supply voltage or poor ground at the pump
MIL on, with P0A7B stored in the ECM (Corvette E-Ray)
Electric front-axle drive limited when the battery gets hot
P0E3D: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit Low

P0E3D concerns the lamp or LED that shows the state of the pilot connection to the charging station, not the pilot signal itself. Low means the driver circuit reads too little voltage, typically because the line to the LED is shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents P0E3D publicly.
Wire to the indicator LED shorted to ground at the charge port
Faulty output driver in the controlling module
Pilot indicator stays dark when it should light
P0E3E: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit High

P0E3E is the high-side counterpart for the control pilot indicator circuit: the module senses voltage on the LED line when there should be little or none, the classic sign of a short to a supply wire. Publicly, no manufacturer documents P0E3E.
Indicator wire chafed against a supply wire near the charge port
Output stage in the module stuck on
Water in the charge port connector bridging pins
Pilot indicator lit or flickering without reason
Misleading charge port light while charging works
P0E3F: Charge Status Indicator A Control Circuit Low

P0E3F reports that the output feeding charge status indicator A sits too low in voltage. That light confirms to the owner that the vehicle is charging, and the expected cause is an LED line touching ground. No manufacturer documents P0E3F publicly.
LED supply wire pinched or chafed to ground
Failed driver in the controlling module
Charge status light stays off during charging
P0E40: Charge Status Indicator A Control Circuit High

P0E40 is logged when the drive circuit of charge status indicator A carries voltage although the light is commanded off, typically because the line touches a live wire. P0E40 has no public documentation from any manufacturer.
Indicator wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Output driver no longer switching off
Moisture bridging pins in the indicator connector
Charge status light on although nothing is charging
Owner misled about the actual charge state
P0E41: Charge Status Indicator B Control Circuit Low

P0E41 refers to a second charge status light, indicator B, whose driver circuit is pulled too low, usually by a short to ground. Which light carries the letter B is the maker's choice; a lamp at the charge port alongside the dashboard light would be a typical pair.
Indicator B wire pinched to ground near the charge port flap
Water ingress into the charge port light assembly
Second charge light (e.g. at the port) stays dark
Main charge indicator and charging unaffected
P0E42: Charge Status Indicator B Control Circuit High

P0E42 means the driver circuit of charge status indicator B shows voltage at a moment when the light should be switched off, pointing to a short to a supply wire or a driver that stays on. P0E42 appears in no public manufacturer document.
Indicator B wire touching a live wire at the charge port
Wet or corroded contacts bridging to a supply pin
Output driver for indicator B stuck on
Second charge light glowing or flickering when not charging
P0E43: P0E43 is the module-B counterpart of P0A1D: it reports that a second hybrid/EV powertrain controller has detected an internal failure or can no longer be trusted. Vehicles with two such processors, for example GM's Bolt EV with a second powertrain module labelled K114B (HPCM2), are where the letter B makes sense. No manufacturer documents P0E43 publicly.
Internal processor or memory fault in module B
Supply, ground or internal bus fault at the module
MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Reduced propulsion power or no ready mode
P0E44: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit
P0E44 is the basic circuit code for the fifth pack voltage measurement, channel E, which follows channels A to D (P0ABA, P0B14, P0B19, P0B1E) in the code list.
Open or unplugged voltage sense lead or connector inside the pack
Faulty measuring stage or input of the battery controller
Blown fuse or open resistor in the sense path
Hybrid or high-voltage system warning lit
Reduced electric assist or limited battery power
Vehicle may not switch to ready mode
P0E45: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit Range/Performance

P0E45 says pack voltage measurement E delivers a value that is electrically valid but does not fit the rest of the battery data. Such a rationality test usually compares the channel with the summed block or cell voltages, or with a second pack measurement. No manufacturer documents P0E45 publicly.
Corroded or loose sense connection adding resistance and skewing the reading
Drifting measuring stage or outdated software in the battery controller
Fault in the reference value, e.g. a block or cell voltage channel
Warning light with reduced hybrid or electric power
Displayed state of charge or range jumps unexpectedly
P0E46: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit Low

P0E46 is stored when pack voltage measurement E reads below the lowest value the connected battery could physically present. That points to the measuring path, such as a sense lead shorted to ground, a blown sense fuse or a failed input stage, not to an empty battery. No manufacturer documents P0E46 publicly.
Sense lead of channel E shorted to ground or chassis
Blown fuse or open resistor in the sense path pulling the reading down
Defective input stage of the battery controller
Vehicle does not become ready to drive or drops out of ready mode
Hybrid system warning and MIL lit
Electric drive or engine assist unavailable
P0E47: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit High

P0E47 means pack voltage measurement E reports more voltage than the pack can reach even when fully charged. A sense lead touching a higher potential, a broken divider resistor or a damaged input of the measuring chip are the usual explanations; real overcharging is unlikely when only one channel shows it.
Sense lead of channel E chafed through and touching a higher potential
Broken divider resistor or lost reference in the measuring circuit
Damaged measuring input or software fault in the battery controller
P0E48: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense E Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0E48 marks pack voltage measurement E as unsteady: the signal jumps, drops out for fractions of a second or changes faster than a battery voltage can, and then returns to normal. Because the fault comes and goes, it is often found only as a stored code after a brief warning.
Loose, pushed-back or corroded terminal on the channel E sense lead
Chafed sense lead that shorts briefly under vibration
Intermittent fault in the battery controller input
Warning light that comes and goes
Brief losses of electric power, often on rough roads
Stored code without a current fault
P0E49: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit
Channel F is the sixth and last pack voltage measurement in this series and comes after channel E (P0E44 to P0E48).
Open sense lead or disconnected connector of channel F
Internal fault of the voltage measuring chip or battery controller
Moisture or corrosion in the pack-side connector
Vehicle may refuse to become ready
P0E4A: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Range/Performance
P0E4A reports that pack voltage measurement F lies within its electrical range but disagrees with a reference value. No manufacturer documents P0E4A publicly.
Contact resistance at a sense terminal distorting the channel F value
Fault in the comparison value, such as the inverter bus or cell voltage measurement
Measuring drift or software issue in the battery controller
MIL on in the first trip with reduced battery power
P0E4B: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Low

P0E4B sets when pack voltage measurement F falls below its plausible minimum, which normally points to a sense path shorted to ground, an open sense fuse or a defective input of the battery controller. No manufacturer documents P0E4B publicly.
Channel F sense lead shorted to ground or pack housing
Open fuse or resistor in the channel F sense path
Failed analog input of the battery controller
No ready mode or contactors do not close
P0E4C: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit High

P0E4C means pack voltage measurement F reports a value above anything the battery can produce. Common reasons are a sense line in contact with a higher potential, a lost ground reference in the measuring circuit or a faulty analog input, so the channel rather than the cells is suspect. No manufacturer documents P0E4C publicly.
Channel F sense line touching a higher potential
Lost ground reference or broken divider in the measuring circuit
Faulty analog input or software of the battery controller
Warning lamp and limited electric drive
P0E4D: Hybrid/EV Battery Pack Voltage Sense F Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E4D flags pack voltage measurement F as intermittent: short dropouts, spikes or steps that a real high-voltage battery cannot make, followed by normal readings again.
Loose or corroded terminal in the channel F sense circuit
Sense lead that loses contact when the harness moves
Interference or intermittent fault in the measuring electronics
P0E4E: P0E4E reports that the hybrid system commanded an engine start but the crankshaft did not turn, or did not reach the cranking speed it expected. It differs from P0A0F, where the engine is turned over but does not fire and keep running.
High-voltage battery too low to crank, often after repeated failed starts
Mechanically seized engine or blocked transaxle
Fault in the cranking motor-generator, its inverter or a conventional starter
Crankshaft speed not detected because of a sensor or signal fault
Engine does not turn over when the hybrid system calls for it
Vehicle runs electrically only or shows a stop-safely warning
No start at all once the battery is depleted
P0E4F: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0E4F covers coolant pump A of the motor electronics loop, which cools the inverter and drive motor, and sets when the signal exchanged with the pump becomes unstable rather than permanently open or shorted.
Loose, corroded or wet pins in the pump A connector
Chafed command or feedback wire that loses contact intermittently
Failing electronics inside the pump sending an unstable feedback signal
Unstable 12 V supply or poor ground at the pump
Power reduction when inverter or motor temperature rises
Fault may clear itself and return later
P0E50: Motor Electronics Coolant Pump B Control Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0E50 is the intermittent or erratic fault of the control circuit for coolant pump B, the second electric pump some hybrids use in the inverter and motor electronics cooling. No manufacturer documents P0E50 publicly.
Intermittent contact at the pump B connector or a harness splice
Pump B electronics producing an unstable signal
Control module software evaluating the pump signal too strictly
Warning light that appears now and then
Temporary power reduction under high load or heat
P0E51: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit

P0E51 is the general circuit fault of current sensor A in a DC/DC converter, the element that tells the converter's controller how many amps flow through its power stage. The code covers a signal path that is broken in a way the controller cannot sort into low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E51 publicly.
Current sensor inside the converter defective (usually not replaceable separately)
Loose, corroded or damaged sensor connection or harness
Fault on the converter control board or its sensor supply
Converter or hybrid control software needs an update
Hybrid or 12 V battery warning in the instrument cluster
12 V battery is charged poorly or not at all
Reduced electric power or limited hybrid functions
P0E52: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance
P0E52 is the plausibility test of current sensor A: the signal is electrically valid, yet the measured current does not fit what the converter is doing. Two makers name it.
Control software with unsuitable limits (FCA eTorque HCP update)
Internal fault of the inverter system controller (Ford hybrid)
Current sensor drifting or offset out of tolerance
High resistance at sensor connector or ground
MIL on, often after only one drive
Limited power with Stop Safely Now or Service Vehicle Soon message
Reduced eTorque assist or start/stop function
P0E53: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Low

P0E53 means the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor A sits below its valid window. On a Hall-type sensor with a mid-scale zero point, that usually points to a short to ground, a missing sensor supply or an open signal wire pulled low, not to a real drop in current. No manufacturer documents P0E53 publicly.
Sensor supply missing or too low
Current sensor or converter electronics defective
12 V battery discharges because the converter does not supply it
Reduced power or electric drive not available
P0E54: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit High

P0E54 reports a current sensor A signal above the range the DC/DC converter accepts. Mercedes-Benz uses it explicitly: its bulletin LI54.10-P-079533, covering the EQB (series 243) and the G-Class including the electric G 580 (series 465), defines P0E5400 as a short to positive of the converter's current sensor A.
Converter stuck in a fault state after incorrect wake-up (Mercedes 243/465)
Signal line shorted to a supply voltage
Current sensor or converter electronics defective
White or yellow high-voltage system warnings
P0E55: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0E55 deals with a current sensor A reading that flickers or vanishes for moments instead of failing for good. FCA documents it repeatedly for the Ram 1500 with eTorque mild hybrid, where the DC/DC converter sits in the 48 V battery pack and is run by the battery pack control module (BPCM).
Battery pack control module software (FCA eTorque, reflash)
Loose or corroded contact in the sensor path
Current sensor or converter electronics failing intermittently
12 V battery not charging, flat soon after driving
P0E56: DC/DC Converter Input Voltage Too Low

P0E56 says the voltage arriving at the input of the DC/DC converter, normally the high-voltage bus of the traction battery, is lower than the converter needs to work. Unlike the sensor codes, the reading itself is believed; the supply is the problem. No manufacturer documents P0E56 on an official public server.
Traction battery deeply discharged or limited by its management system
Main contactor not closing or high-voltage cable/connector fault
Input voltage measurement inside the converter faulty
12 V battery warning, battery discharges while driving
Hybrid system warning, vehicle may not reach ready mode
P0E57: DC/DC Converter Input Voltage Too High

P0E57 is set when the DC/DC converter sees more voltage on its input than it is rated for. Excess input voltage stresses the switching transistors and input capacitors, so a converter typically stops working to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E57 on an official public server.
High-voltage bus driven too high by boost stage, regeneration or charging
Input voltage measurement in the converter reads too high
Hybrid or battery control software needs an update
Hybrid system or 12 V battery warning
Converter switches off temporarily, 12 V voltage drops
P0E58: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit

P0E58 stands for a general circuit fault of the third temperature sensor in a DC/DC converter, after sensors A (P0C38 ff.) and B (P0C3D ff.). Which part of the converter sensor C watches is up to the maker.
Sensor connection or wiring damaged or corroded
Temperature sensor in the converter defective
Sensor reference or evaluation circuit in the converter faulty
P0E59: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P0E59 is the best-documented member of this group. Ford's hybrid OBD summaries from 2015 to 2019 assign it to the inductor temperature sensor of the variable voltage converter and monitor it without pause once 500 ms have passed since power-up, provided the 12 V supply lies between 6 and 19 V.
Inductor temperature sensor drifting, reading off after cold soak
Inductor really overheating, e.g. due to weak electronics cooling
Short or open in the sensor circuit (Ford range limits)
MIL on, at FCA after one faulty drive
Reduced hybrid assist or electric driving
P0E5A: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Low

P0E5A means the voltage from DC/DC converter temperature sensor C has fallen below its valid window. With the NTC thermistors common in power electronics, a low voltage translates into an implausibly hot reading, so a grounded signal wire or a failed sensor is far more likely than genuine overheating. No manufacturer documents P0E5A publicly.
Evaluation circuit in the converter faulty
P0E5B: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit High

P0E5B is stored when the signal of DC/DC converter temperature sensor C rises above its valid window. On an NTC circuit with pull-up resistor, that is the typical picture of an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a short to a supply voltage, and it reads as a converter far colder than possible. No manufacturer documents P0E5B publicly.
Connector unplugged or sensor wire broken
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
P0E5C: DC/DC Converter Temperature Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0E5C flags a sensor C signal that changes faster than the part it watches could heat or cool. A converter inductor or heat sink has thermal mass, so a jump of many degrees within a few milliseconds points to a contact problem in the circuit, not to the converter itself. No manufacturer documents P0E5C publicly.
Loose or widened terminal at the sensor or converter connector
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short episodes of reduced electric power
P0E5D: P0E5D adds the intermittent case to the DC/DC converter enable codes P0A11 (open), P0A12 (low) and P0A13 (high). Through the enable line a hybrid or body controller switches the converter on and off; if that line flickers, the converter keeps stopping and restarting.
Loose or corroded terminal on the enable line
Poor ground reference between controller and converter
Chafed enable wire touching ground intermittently
Output stage in the commanding controller faulty
12 V battery warning that comes and goes
P0E5E: Battery Charger Control Module A Processor Performance

P0E5E reports that the processor of the on-board charger's control unit fails its self-tests. Mitsubishi spells this out for the 2023 Outlander PHEV: P0E5E-00 means a ROM checksum (CRC) error or a RAM read/write error in the charger control; the code lights both the PHEV warning and the MIL.
Control electronics of the on-board charger defective (unit replacement)
Unstable 12 V supply or ground of the charger during start-up
MIL and hybrid/PHEV warning, sometimes right after charging
P0E5F: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature A Too High

P0E5F is not a sensor fault: the coupler temperature sensor A works, but the charging inlet really got too hot. Three makers document it. Ford links it on the 2021–2023 Mustang Mach-E (stored in the SOBDM) to a red flashing charge indicator and no charging from a 48 A level 2 station, while 32 A or less may still work; SSM 51866 calls for a new charge port.
Excessive contact resistance in the vehicle charge port (Ford replaces the port)
Worn or damaged plug of the charging cable or station
High ambient temperature or direct sun while charging (Mercedes)
Charging stops or runs at reduced power
Charge indicator red or flashing red, warning in app or cluster
Charging restarts only after unplugging and replugging
P0E60: Battery Charge Mode Control Circuit Range/Performance

P0E60 concerns a wired control line that tells the on-board charger which mode to run in, set by the module that coordinates charging. Range/Performance means the line shows a valid level, but its state or response disagrees with the command. No manufacturer documents P0E60 or the modes it selects publicly.
High resistance or damage on the mode control line
Input stage of the on-board charger faulty
Output stage or software of the commanding module faulty
Plug-in charging does not start or stops
Charging runs at an unexpected rate
P0E61: P0E61 means the 12 V enable line that wakes or permits the on-board charger has a circuit fault, most often an open. GM documents it codegenau. In the 2016 Volt the VICM watches this charger enable circuit; in the 2019 hybrid tables the HPC2 module does so.
Enable wire open or connector at charger/module not seated
Output driver in the controlling module (VICM/HPC2) faulty
Enable input of the on-board charger defective
Battery heating in cold weather may be unavailable
P0E62: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit Low

P0E62 reports that the enable line of on-board charger A is held at a lower level than its commanded state allows, typically by a short to ground. If the module drives the line high to permit charging, the charger never sees the request.
Enable wire chafed and shorted to ground
Enable input of the charger shorted internally
Driver stage in the commanding module faulty
Charging does not start when plugged in
P0E63: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit High

P0E63 is the high-level counterpart: the enable signal to charger A sits above the level its commanded state allows, for instance because it touches a 12 V feed. In practice the charger may then be woken although no charging is requested, which can drain the 12 V battery while parked, or it may ignore a switch-off command.
Enable wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Enable input of the charger faulty
Driver stage in the commanding module stuck on
Charger active or charging not ending as expected
P0E64: Battery Charger A Enable Circuit Range/Performance
P0E64 covers an enable line that is electrically intact while the charger still does not respond as it should.
Charger and BECM do not complete start-up within 30 s (software or wake-up timing)
Battery energy control module not waking or not reporting ready
High resistance on the wake-up line producing a marginal level
Charging does not start although the cable is connected
Charging system warning or charge port light shows a fault
P0E65: P0E65 flags a fault on the wired command line through which the hybrid control unit operates the on-board charger, most often an interrupted line. GM uses it codegenau: in the 2016 Volt the VICM runs the test, in the 2019 hybrid tables (19OBDG01) the HPC2 module.
Broken or disconnected charger control wire
Corroded or pushed-out terminal at charger or control unit
Defective output driver in the commanding control unit
Vehicle does not charge when plugged in
MIL after the second trip with the fault (GM)
Charging fault message in the instrument cluster
P0E66: With P0E66 the controller finds the charger command line pulled lower than the state it is driving, which typically means the wire touches ground somewhere between the control unit and the on-board charger. If the command is active-high, the charger simply never receives it; a grounded line can also overload the output stage that drives it.
Control wire chafed through to body ground
Moisture in a connector bridging the signal to ground
Internal short in the charger's command input
Charging does not start after plugging in
Charge indicator shows a fault or goes out
P0E67: P0E67 is set when the charger command line reads higher than commanded, for instance close to battery voltage while the control unit is holding it off. A short to a live wire is the classic cause; with some driver designs an open line also floats high and lands here.
Control wire shorted to a battery feed or other supply
Open line read as high by the driver circuit
Output stage of the control unit stuck switched on
Charging aborted or not offered at all
Charger wakes up or runs without a charging request
P0E68: P0E68 is the plausibility code of the charger command line: no short or open is present, yet the charger does not react to the command in the expected way or in the expected time. Typical triggers are a charger that wakes too slowly, a voltage drop on the line that leaves the level ambiguous, or software in the two modules that disagrees.
Charger and control unit software not matching
Charger responding late or not at all to the command
Excess resistance in the line distorting the signal level
Charging starts late, stops or fails intermittently
Charge timer or scheduled charging not working
P0E69: Control Pilot Indicator Control Circuit Range/Performance

P0E69 belongs to the output that drives the small lamp or LED showing the state of the pilot connection to the charging station. Range/Performance means the driver circuit reports a state that does not fit what the module commanded, without a clear short or open. No manufacturer documents P0E69 publicly.
Indicator LED aged or partially failed, drawing the wrong current
Loose contact at the charge port lamp connector
Faulty feedback of the LED driver in the control unit
Charge port indicator flickers, stays dark or shows the wrong state
P0E6A: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit

P0E6A is the general code for the precharge contactor of the battery charging system. Before the main charging contactors close, this small contactor feeds the charger side through a resistor so the voltage can rise gently towards pack voltage; without it the main contacts would arc.
Precharge resistor burnt open or overheated
Worn or sluggish precharge contactor in the charging path
Charging session aborts right at the start
Charging not possible, driving usually still possible
P0E6B: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Closed

P0E6B means the precharge contactor of the charging system appears to stay closed although it has been told to open, usually because its contacts have welded. The battery management notices this when the charger side carries voltage before any precharge was requested, or when it does not drop after switch-off.
Coil kept energised by a control line fault
Residual voltage from another high-voltage unit misread as a closed contactor
Charging blocked and high-voltage warning displayed
Vehicle may refuse to switch to ready mode
P0E6C: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Circuit Stuck Open

P0E6C reports that the precharge contactor of the charging system does not close, or that no current flows through the precharge branch, even though the command was given. The charger side then cannot be brought up to pack voltage, the main charging contactors stay open and the session ends before any energy flows. No manufacturer documents P0E6C publicly.
Open precharge resistor interrupting the branch
Burnt or contaminated contactor contacts not conducting
Contactor coil not pulling in due to low supply
Charging stops a few seconds after plugging in
Repeated clicking from the battery area at charge start
P0E6D: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit/Open

P0E6D concerns the low-voltage side of the charging precharge contactor: the coil circuit through which the control unit switches it, typically interrupted. Unlike P0E6C, which judges what happens on the high-voltage side, this code comes from the driver output itself. No manufacturer documents P0E6D publicly.
Broken coil control wire or unplugged connector
Open winding in the contactor coil
Failed driver stage in the battery management unit
P0E6E: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit Range/Performance

P0E6E is stored when the coil circuit of the charging precharge contactor neither shows a clean short nor an open, but its electrical behaviour does not match the command: coil current outside the expected window, a slow pull-in, or feedback that lags behind the switching command.
Increased contact resistance in the coil connector
Contactor coil resistance out of specification
Low supply voltage at the contactor driver
Charging starts only on some attempts
Fault appears mostly in cold weather or with a weak 12 V battery
P0E6F: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit Low

P0E6F points to the coil control line of the charging precharge contactor sitting too low, most likely shorted to ground. With a high-side driver the coil then cannot be energised, so precharge never starts; the driver itself may shut down to protect itself. No manufacturer documents P0E6F publicly.
Coil control wire shorted to ground inside or near the battery
Shorted turns in the contactor coil
Driver stage switched off by its overcurrent protection
Charging does not start, contactor click missing
High-voltage fault message when plugging in
P0E70: Battery Charging System Precharge Contactor Control Circuit High

P0E70 is the high-side counterpart of P0E6F: the coil line of the charging precharge contactor carries voltage although the driver is off. A short to a 12 V feed can energise the coil without a command, which would let the precharge branch conduct unasked; the battery management therefore usually locks out charging. No manufacturer documents P0E70 publicly.
Coil control wire shorted to a 12 V supply
Driver stage in the battery management unit stuck on
Open ground return of the coil leaving the line at supply level
Charging locked out with a high-voltage fault message
Contactor clicks without a charging request
P0E71: P0E71 compares the torque that the hybrid generator or motor-generator actually provides with the value requested by the hybrid control. If the two drift apart beyond a calibrated margin, the code is set.
Fault in the inverter stage feeding the generator
Rotor position sensor (resolver) delivering a wrong angle
Damaged generator winding or internal contamination
MIL and service wrench lamp on (Ford)
Reduced power or emergency running mode
Engine runs more often, hybrid assistance missing
P0E72: P0E72 refers to the pulse train that an AC charging station places onto the pilot wire. Under SAE J1772, matched by IEC 61851-1, this is a rectangular ±12 V signal at 1 kHz, and its duty cycle tells the car how much current it may draw.
Charging station or portable charger generating an off-spec pilot
Faulty charging adapter or extension in the cable path
Pilot measuring circuit in the vehicle charger misreading
AC charging does not start or stops at one station
Charging works normally at other stations
P0E73: P0E73 is set when the control pilot pulses from the charging station arrive faster than the nominal 1 kHz. Above the permitted band the vehicle can no longer be sure that it decodes the duty cycle, and with it the allowed charging current, correctly; in practice it refuses or ends the session.
Electrical interference or ringing on the pilot line
Charging station with a faulty pilot oscillator
Damaged charging cable or corroded charge port pin
Faulty pilot input in the on-board charger
AC charging refused or stopped shortly after start
Fault tied to a specific station or cable
P0E74: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Internal Isolation Fault

P0E74 reports that the insulation between the cells or internal high-voltage parts of the traction battery and its housing has become too weak, as measured inside the pack. P0AA6, by contrast, covers isolation of the whole high-voltage system.
Coolant leak or water ingress inside the battery pack
Chafed or damaged insulation of internal high-voltage wiring
Faulty isolation measurement in the battery management
Battery or high-voltage warning lamp on
Vehicle may not enter ready mode or blocks charging
P0E75: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit/Open

P0E75 is the basic electrical code for coolant bypass valve A: the control unit finds that the output switching the valve, or the wire leading to it, does not form a closed circuit, in most cases because of an open.
Broken wire or loose connector on the valve A control circuit
Burnt or internally open coil/motor in valve A
Coolant or water ingress corroding the valve connector pins
Faulty output driver in the engine or hybrid control module
Little or no cabin heat, especially in electric mode
Engine warms up more slowly or runs more often than usual
P0E76: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Low

With P0E76 the voltage on the control line of coolant bypass valve A stays lower than the driver expects for its current state, which points to a short to ground somewhere in the harness or inside the actuator.
Chafed control wire touching body or engine ground
Internal short in the valve A actuator
Moisture bridging pins in the valve connector
Valve stays in one position, heating behaves oddly
Possible blown fuse if the short is hard
P0E77: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit High

P0E77 is logged when valve A's drive line carries more voltage than the driver should allow, typically because the wire has rubbed through against a 12 V feed. A low-side driver then sees battery voltage while it is trying to pull the line down and usually reports overcurrent; with some designs an open line can float high and end up here too.
Control wire shorted to a battery or ignition feed
Open circuit that the driver interprets as high
P0E78: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Circuit Range/Performance

P0E78 is the plausibility code for the actuator circuit of bypass valve A. Neither an open nor a short is present, yet current, feedback or response time of the actuator do not fit what the module has commanded: a coil whose resistance has drifted, a motor that labours against a sticky shaft, or a supply that sags under load.
Deposits or wear making the valve A mechanism sluggish
High resistance at connector or ground of the valve circuit
Low supply voltage to the actuator under load
Heating output varies from trip to trip
P0E79: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Stuck/Open

P0E79 reports that bypass valve A apparently remains open although the module has asked it to close. The control unit cannot see the valve directly; it infers the position from temperatures, typically by comparing two coolant sensors that should drift apart when the loops are separated. No manufacturer documents P0E79 publicly.
Valve A jammed open by debris or a broken internal part
Actuator no longer moves the valve
Hoses swapped at the valve after a repair
Skewed coolant temperature sensor misleading the check
Weak cabin heat in electric mode
Engine starts more often to supply heat
P0E7A: Coolant Bypass Valve A Control Stuck Closed

P0E7A is the reverse of P0E79: valve A should open and let coolant pass, but the temperature picture says it has stayed shut. Depending on what the valve connects, the result is a loop that gets no flow from the engine side, so heater output or heat transfer drops, or a branch that heats up because it is cut off from circulation.
Debris or deposits blocking valve A
Actuator or gear stuck in the closed position
Air pocket after a coolant service blocking flow
Rising coolant temperature in the affected loop
P0E7B: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit/Open

P0E7B covers an interrupted control circuit of the second coolant bypass valve, B. The module sees no proper load on its output, so the valve cannot be positioned and stays wherever it last was or springs back to its rest position.
Broken wire or unplugged connector at valve B
Internal open in the valve B actuator
Missing supply or ground at a networked valve actuator
Heating or engine warm-up behaves differently
P0E7C: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Low
P0E7C says that the wiring which operates bypass valve B reads too low, typically because a wire or the actuator itself has a ground fault.
Engine control software needing the update from the manufacturer bulletin (Stellantis 3.0 Hurricane)
Valve B control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the valve B actuator
P0E7D: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit High
P0E7D is stored when the line driving valve B sits above its expected level, for instance with the wire chafed against a powered line or a driver that cannot pull the circuit down.
Valve B control wire shorted to a voltage source
Open circuit pulled high by the module input
Other stored codes after the same software issue
P0E7E: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Circuit Range/Performance

P0E7E marks a control circuit of coolant bypass valve B that is electrically intact but does not respond as calibrated: actuator current, feedback or timing lie outside the window the software expects. Stellantis lists P0E7E most often of the valve B codes.
Engine control calibration fixed by bulletin 18-106-25 or 18-071-26 (Stellantis)
Valve B actuator moving slowly or not reaching its target
Usually no change in driving behaviour
P0E7F: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Stuck/Open
P0E7F means coolant bypass valve B is judged to stay open while the module wants it closed.
Machining debris lodged in the three-way coolant valve (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Worn or broken internals in valve B
Calibration issue addressed by an engine control update (3.0 Hurricane)
Electric drive mode unavailable, engine runs instead
P0E80: Coolant Bypass Valve B Control Stuck Closed

P0E80 reports that bypass valve B has stayed shut although flow through it is requested. Stellantis gives the criterion for the Jeep Wrangler plug-in hybrid (2021 to 2023): the code sets once engine coolant and the inlet of the electric coolant heater differ by more than 40 °F, about 22 K.
Hoses at the three-way valve shifted by one port (Wrangler 4xe, bulletin 07-006-23)
Valve blocked by machining debris (Pacifica Hybrid, bulletin 07-008-23)
Valve B actuator seized in the closed position
P0E81: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit

P0E81 is the general circuit code for temperature sensor A in an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit separate from the main engine loop, such as a heater loop of a plug-in hybrid or a loop that cools electric drive parts. The module sees a signal it cannot use at all, without classing it as too low, too high or implausible.
Loose, corroded or unplugged sensor connector
Heater or auxiliary pump runs on default values
P0E82: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

P0E82 is set when temperature sensor A of the auxiliary cooling loop delivers a clean electrical signal whose value does not make sense against other temperatures. No manufacturer documents P0E82 publicly, but Ford's 2019 hybrid summary spells out such a plausibility test for its heater-loop sensor ECT2 under P2183.
Sensor A reading drifted out of tolerance
Stuck bypass valve keeping the loops from mixing
Low coolant or air around the sensor tip
P0E83: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low

P0E83 means the signal voltage of temperature sensor A in the auxiliary cooling loop has fallen below its valid floor. Coolant sensors are normally NTC thermistors whose resistance drops as they warm, so a low voltage reads as extremely hot coolant.
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Genuinely very hot coolant in the auxiliary loop
Coolant pump or fan running continuously
Implausibly high temperature shown on a scan tool
P0E84: Auxiliary Cooling System Coolant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P0E84 is the high-voltage case for sensor A of the auxiliary loop: the signal sits near the reference voltage, which an NTC thermistor would only produce at extreme cold. Far more often the circuit is open, from an unplugged connector, a broken wire or a sensor with an internal break, or the signal line is shorted to a voltage source.
Unplugged connector or broken sensor wire
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
Scan tool shows the loop at minimum temperature
P0E85: Battery Charger B Temperature Too High

P0E85 reports that the second charger stage or second on-board charger, labelled B, has become hotter than its own protection limit allows. Like the A counterpart P0D24, it is a heat verdict, not a sensor fault: the charger trusts its reading and cuts back power or stops to save its semiconductors.
Too little coolant or air flow through charger B (low coolant, pump, blocked fins)
Internal defect in the power stage of charger B
Long full-power charging in very hot surroundings
AC charging slows down noticeably or stops before the battery is full
Charging fault message or flashing charge-port indicator
P0E86: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Too Low

P0E86 means charger B sees less voltage at its input than it needs to work, although charging has been requested. It mirrors P0D27, which carries no letter and is used for the first charger. No manufacturer documents P0E86 publicly.
Weak supply at the socket or charging station, long or undersized house wiring
Faulty charging cable, adapter or extension lead
Worn or burnt contacts in the charge inlet or its wiring to the charger
Voltage measurement inside charger B reads too low
AC charging does not start or stops shortly after starting
Charging works at another socket or station
P0E87: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Too High

P0E87 flags an input voltage for charger B above what the charger accepts. Ford uses the code in its plug-in hybrid OBD summary (OBDSM1901) in an unusual way: it is part of a plausibility test run on the battery controller (BECM) and judges the charging voltage request that reaches the charger.
Implausible charging voltage request from the battery control module (Ford logic)
Software fault in the charger or battery control module
Real overvoltage from the supply or charging station
Charging is refused or ends early
Amber wrench lamp in the instrument cluster (Ford)
P0E88: Battery Charger B Input Current Too Low

P0E88 is set when charger B takes in less current than it should for the charging power it is asked to deliver, with voltage present. Its counterpart without a letter is P0D29. No manufacturer documents P0E88 in public sources.
Charger B power stage does not reach the requested power
High resistance at inlet contacts or in the charging cable
Charging station or cable signals a lower current limit than expected
AC charging takes much longer than usual
Charging stops or a charging fault is shown
P0E89: Battery Charger B Input Current Too High

P0E89 reports more input current into charger B than permitted, and it is the best documented code of this series. Toyota lists P0E8919 on 2021 to 2023 RAV4 Prime XSE models with the 6.6 kW charger, together with P0D2A19 and PFC boost faults; the MIL is on, plug-in charging fails and the charger assembly is replaced (T-SB-0067-22).
Defective power factor correction or power stage in the charger (Toyota RAV4 Prime)
Calibration or software of the vehicle or charging control unit (Isuzu VCU, Mercedes DC charging unit, Ford request logic)
Current ripple or overcurrent from the charging station (Mercedes)
MIL or EV system warning lamp on
Plug-in charging stops or does not work at all
Vehicle does not start after DC fast charging (Mercedes)
P0E8A: Battery Charger B Input Current Sensor Circuit

P0E8A concerns the measurement, not the current itself: the sensor that tells charger B how much current enters at its input delivers no usable signal. It is the general circuit code; range, low and high faults of the same sensor sit at P2D85, P2D83 and P2D84, and the sensor of charger A uses P0D38. No manufacturer documents P0E8A publicly.
Current sensor or its evaluation inside charger B defective
Open or shorted sensor wiring where the sensor is external
Charger software misjudges the sensor signal
AC charging does not start or is aborted
Charging fault indication; driving remains possible
P0E8B: Battery Charger B Input Voltage Sensor Circuit

P0E8B covers an electrical fault in the voltage measurement at the input of charger B: the controller gets no valid reading of the supply voltage. Range, low and high faults of this sensor have their own codes, P2E84, P2E85 and P2E86; charger A uses P0D3D for its first input voltage sensor. Some code lists call it input voltage sensor A of charger B.
Voltage sensing circuit inside charger B defective
Loose or corroded connector, damaged sensing lead
Charging fault message or charge-port indicator signals a fault
P0E8C: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit

The inverter of drive motor A may measure its high-voltage DC level at more than one point; sensor B is the second of those channels. P0E8C is the general circuit code for it, used when the signal is missing or electrically invalid without a clear low, high or plausibility verdict.
Sensing circuit for voltage channel B inside the power electronics defective
Low-voltage connector or harness of the inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor control unit
Hybrid or EV system warning together with the MIL
Reduced electric drive power or vehicle not ready to drive
P0E8D: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0E8D says that voltage sensor B of the drive motor A inverter delivers a value that is electrically fine but disagrees with other readings of the same bus.
Fault in the power electronics or its voltage measurement (Mitsubishi, Audi)
Drift of voltage channel B so that it no longer matches the other channels
Wrong reference value from another high-voltage unit (rear motor unit, battery management)
Red high-voltage system warning at start, stop safely (Audi)
MIL and hybrid warning, reduced or no electric drive
P0E8E: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0E8E means the output of inverter voltage sensor B for drive motor A has fallen to the bottom end of its scale.
Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
No high voltage on the bus because of a blown fuse or open contactor path
Vehicle not ready to drive or only engine power available
P0E8F: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit High

P0E8F is the upper-limit fault of inverter voltage sensor B on drive motor A. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV sets it when the main channel at capacitor 2 (V2M) reports at least 4.75 V for 0.16 s, again with the unit supplied at 8 V or above, and lists it as a range check maximum.
Measuring circuit for capacitor 2 inside the power drive unit defective
Signal shorted to sensor supply or lost sensor ground
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus
Electric drive switched off or strongly reduced
P0E90: Drive Motor A Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0E90 is meant for a voltage sensor B signal of the drive motor A inverter that flickers, jumps or drops out for moments without staying wrong long enough for the low or high code. No manufacturer documents P0E90 publicly.
Loose or corroded low-voltage connector on the inverter
Chafed or partly broken signal lead
Measuring circuit in the power electronics failing intermittently with heat or vibration
Hybrid warning that comes and goes
Short power interruptions or jerky electric drive
P0E91: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit

P0E91 is the circuit code for the second DC voltage channel, sensor B, in the inverter of drive motor B, usually the second electric machine or the rear axle motor. It applies when this signal is absent or electrically unusable without a more precise verdict; its partner channel A is coded P0DA3, and the matching code for drive motor A is P0E8C.
Voltage channel B measuring circuit in the motor B inverter defective
Connector or harness of the motor B inverter loose or damaged
Software fault in the motor B control unit
Hybrid or EV warning with MIL
Loss of the second drive motor (for example no all-wheel drive), reduced power
P0E92: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P0E92 is stored when voltage sensor B of the drive motor B inverter gives a reading inside its electrical range that does not fit the other voltage values of the high-voltage system. No manufacturer documents P0E92 publicly.
Voltage channel B of the motor B inverter drifts
Internal fault of the motor B inverter or motor unit
Wrong comparison value from battery management or the front power electronics
MIL and hybrid or EV system warning
Second drive motor switched off, reduced acceleration
P0E93: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low

With P0E93 the controller sees the B voltage channel in the motor B inverter stuck near the bottom of its signal range, as happens with a short to ground, an open signal path or a failed measuring circuit. No manufacturer documents P0E93 publicly.
Measuring circuit for channel B in the motor B inverter failed
Signal line shorted to ground or open
High-voltage cable or connection to motor B open, no voltage at the inverter
Rear or second motor without power, front-drive only
P0E94: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit High

P0E94 records that voltage sensor B in the drive motor B inverter reports a value at the top of its signal range. A short from the signal to a supply, an interrupted sensor ground or a defective measuring stage are the usual explanations; a genuine overvoltage would normally show on the other channels too. No manufacturer documents P0E94 publicly.
Measuring stage for channel B in the motor B inverter defective
Signal shorted to a supply or lost sensor ground
Real overvoltage on the high-voltage bus
Second drive motor deactivated, less traction and power
P0E95: Drive Motor B Inverter Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E95 closes the sensor B series for drive motor B: the signal is unstable, with brief dropouts or spikes, rather than permanently low, high or implausible. No manufacturer documents P0E95 publicly.
Corroded or loose connector on the motor B inverter
Harness damaged where it moves with the axle or suspension
Measuring circuit in the motor B inverter failing intermittently
EV or hybrid warning that appears and clears again
Second motor drops out briefly, uneven traction
P0E96: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit

P0E96 opens the series for a third voltage measurement in a DC/DC converter, sensor C. It is the general circuit code, meant for a missing or electrically invalid signal; range, low, high and erratic faults of the same sensor follow from P0E97 to P0E9A.
Measuring circuit for channel C inside the converter defective
Loose connector or damaged sensing lead
Software fault in the converter or its controller
12 V or converter warning, possibly with MIL
P0E97: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P0E97 is the plausibility code for the third voltage channel of a DC/DC converter: sensor C delivers an electrically valid value that does not agree with what the controller expects. Two makers document it.
Converter or power electronics software with too tight plausibility limits
Converter stuck in an error state after an incorrect wake-up
Drifting voltage measurement inside the converter
MIL on, often without a noticeable driving fault
12 V battery or high-voltage warning messages in the cluster
Fault entry appears sporadically and returns after clearing
P0E98: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Low

P0E98 is set when the C voltage channel of a DC/DC converter is stuck at the lowest end of its range, typically because the measuring line is grounded or the sensing stage has lost its supply. No manufacturer documents P0E98 publicly.
Sensor C signal line shorted to ground
Measuring stage without supply or with an open signal path
Internal defect in the converter's measuring circuit
MIL on, depending on the manufacturer's rating
Converter output reduced or switched to a fallback value
Start-stop or 12 V support may be disabled
P0E99: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit High

With P0E99 the controller finds the voltage sensor C reading of a DC/DC converter pinned near its upper limit. That points to the signal touching a battery feed or reference supply, or to a broken sensor ground that lets the input float up, rather than to a real converter overvoltage. No manufacturer documents P0E99 publicly.
Sensor C signal shorted to battery voltage or reference supply
Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Actual overvoltage from a faulty converter regulation
MIL and charging or 12 V warning possible
Converter limits or stops its output
P0E9A: DC/DC Converter Voltage Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0E9A completes the sensor C voltage series of a DC/DC converter. It is meant for a signal that jumps, flickers or drops out for brief moments, which the low and high tests miss because they need a fault to persist. No manufacturer documents P0E9A publicly.
Loose or corroded terminal in the sensor C path
Harness chafing intermittently at a moving point
Cracked solder joint in the converter's measuring circuit
Warning lamp that appears and disappears
Short interruptions of start-stop or 12 V support
Code often stored as history only
P0E9B: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit

P0E9B opens the series for the second current measurement of a DC/DC converter, sensor B. It covers a signal that is absent or unusable on the electrical level and that the controller cannot classify as low, high or implausible; those cases follow as P0E9C to P0E9F. No manufacturer documents P0E9B itself.
Fault in the converter's internal current sensing
Connector or wiring fault on the sensor B path
Converter output reduced, 12 V battery charged less
P0E9C: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P0E9C means current sensor B of a DC/DC converter gives a value within its electrical window that does not match the operating state, for example a current that stays put while the load changes, or that differs from the figure the controller derives from voltages and switching. No manufacturer documents P0E9C publicly.
Current sensor B drifting or with a shifted zero point
Fault in the converter power stage causing unexpected currents
Software with an unsuitable plausibility window
MIL, sometimes after a single trip
Reduced converter output and weak 12 V charging
P0E9D: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Low

P0E9D reports that the signal of DC/DC converter current sensor B has dropped below its valid range. Porsche documents it for the Taycan of model years 2020 to 2024 as P0E9D00, current sensor 2 of the converter with a short to ground, logged by the HV power electronics on the front axle (A49), the rear axle (A50) or both.
Current monitoring threshold set too low in the software
Sensor B signal shorted to ground
Sensor supply missing inside the power electronics
Red warning to stop the vehicle safely
Fault no longer active after an ignition cycle
Drive power reduced or vehicle not ready to drive
P0E9E: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit High

P0E9E flags the B current channel of a DC/DC converter reading above its ceiling: the raw signal lies above anything the sensor should output. With a Hall sensor whose zero lies mid-scale, this usually means the signal line touches the supply or the reference ground has opened. No manufacturer documents P0E9E publicly.
Sensor B signal shorted to supply voltage
Open reference ground of the current sensor
Converter in an error state after wake-up, cleared by reset
Red 12 V battery or HV warning
Converter stops supplying the 12 V network
P0E9F: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0E9F is reserved for a current sensor B signal of a DC/DC converter that is unsteady: it spikes, drops out or shows noise yet never stays out of bounds for long. Publicly, no maker describes P0E9F.
Loose terminal or connector on the sensor B path
Solder joint that opens under heat or vibration
Electrical interference on the measuring line
Code stored without a current fault
P0EA0: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit

P0EA0 covers circuit faults of a third current channel inside a DC/DC converter, sensor C. Converters with several phases or with separate input and output sensing can carry more than two current channels; the letter C simply names the third.
Defect in the converter's third current sensing channel
Damaged connector or wiring on the sensor C path
Software fault in the signal evaluation
Warning for the high-voltage or 12 V system
Converter limited to a reduced output
P0EA1: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance

P0EA1 stands for a sensor C current reading that is electrically plausible yet disagrees with the converter's operating point or with its sister channels. If a converter measures several phase currents, those values should track each other, and one channel that deviates is a typical trigger. No manufacturer documents P0EA1 publicly.
Sensor C channel drifting away from the other channels
Fault in the converter phase measured by sensor C
Plausibility software in need of an update
P0EA2: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Low

P0EA2 is stored when current sensor C of a DC/DC converter reports a raw value under its lower limit. Because current sensors in these units normally place their zero-current output at mid-supply, a value near zero volts rarely means low current; it points to a ground short, a lost sensor supply or a broken signal path.
Sensor C signal shorted to ground
Missing supply voltage of the current sensor
Monitoring threshold in the software set too tight
Warning lamp and possibly a stop request
P0EA3: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit High

P0EA3 marks a current sensor C signal above the top of its accepted window. Electrically this means the signal line touching a voltage source, an open sensor ground or a failed output stage of the sensor; a genuine overcurrent of the converter is a different matter and has its own code, P0D33. No manufacturer documents P0EA3 publicly.
Sensor C signal shorted to supply
Open ground of the current sensor
12 V or high-voltage warning in the cluster
P0EA4: DC/DC Converter Current Sensor C Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EA4 ends the current sensor C series and describes a signal that wavers or breaks off momentarily instead of failing steadily. No manufacturer documents P0EA4 publicly.
Outdated control software evaluating the signal too strictly
Loose plug or damaged pin on the sensor C path
Connection that opens with temperature changes
Sporadic warnings without a lasting fault
12 V battery not kept fully charged
P0EA5: P0EA5 says that a second DC/DC converter, B, does not deliver what it is asked to, for example the commanded output voltage or current, although its sensors give no circuit fault. FCA documents it as DC/DC Converter 2 Performance for the 2019 Jeep Cherokee (KL) with the 3.2 litre V6 and engine start/stop: PCM flash bulletins 18-023-19 REV.
Engine or powertrain control software needing an update
Poor supply or ground connection of converter B
Engine does not restart after an auto-stop, start-stop disabled
Voltage dips in the 12 V network, for example audio dropouts
P0EA6: P0EA6 means the second DC/DC converter, B, has reached a temperature beyond its permitted limit. Unlike a temperature sensor code, the reading itself is accepted as true; the unit is simply too hot and will normally reduce or stop its output to protect itself.
Cooling air or heat sink of converter B obstructed
Sustained high load on the 12 V network
Control software misjudging the temperature condition
Weak internal power stage of converter B
Start-stop unavailable while the converter is hot
Electrical consumers affected during engine restart
P0EA7: P0EA7 reports that an auxiliary cooling loop, a coolant circuit kept apart from the main engine circuit, does not achieve the cooling effect the controller expects.
Thermostat in the auxiliary loop sticking closed (Volvo T8, earlier part design)
Low coolant level or trapped air in the auxiliary loop
Weak or failed auxiliary coolant pump
Module software reporting the fault wrongly (Ford Mustang GTD)
Often no noticeable change in driving behaviour
Possible power limits on electric drive parts that run too warm
P0EA8: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit

P0EA8 is the general circuit code for the second high-voltage measurement of an electric A/C compressor, labelled sensor B. Such compressors draw their power from the traction battery and convert it in a built-in inverter; the module reads the supply voltage to control the motor and protect its power stage.
Interrupted voltage sense path inside or at the compressor
Fault on the compressor's inverter or control board
Poorly seated high-voltage or signal connector at the compressor
Fault message for the climate system
Battery cooling via refrigerant may be unavailable during charging
P0EA9: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Performance

P0EA9 means the B voltage reading reported by the electric A/C compressor looks electrically valid but does not fit other information, usually the high voltage reported by the battery system that feeds the compressor directly. No manufacturer documents P0EA9 publicly.
Drifting voltage measurement inside the compressor module
Faulty data exchange between compressor and hybrid controller
Wrong battery voltage reference from the hybrid or battery controller
Air conditioning switches off or works only now and then
Fault often recorded without any other symptom
P0EAA: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit High

P0EAA flags a B voltage reading at the top of, or beyond, the plausible range of the compressor supply. Since the battery cannot really deliver that much, the cause usually lies in the measurement itself: an open or shorted sense path, a failed voltage divider inside the compressor or a wrong reference. No manufacturer documents P0EAA publicly.
Failed voltage divider or reference in the compressor module
Sense line shorted to a higher potential
Actual overvoltage on the high-voltage bus
Compressor stops, cabin is not cooled
Warning in the climate control display
P0EAB: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EAB is set when the B voltage channel of the electric A/C compressor reports far less than the high-voltage battery actually supplies while the contactors are closed.
Voltage sense line shorted to ground
High-voltage supply to the compressor interrupted (fuse, connector)
Measuring stage in the compressor module without supply
No cooling from the air conditioning
Charging power may be reduced if the battery cannot be cooled
P0EAC: A/C Compressor Motor Voltage Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic
P0EAC points to a B voltage signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of staying wrong. The module sees sudden changes no real battery voltage can make, or values that come and go.
Loose or corroded connector at the compressor
Harness chafed or cracked by engine and road vibration
Cracked solder joint on the compressor control board
Air conditioning cuts out briefly and then resumes
P0EAD: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit

P0EAD covers the current sensor of an electric A/C compressor, which measures how much current the motor drive takes from the high-voltage link. The controller needs this value to limit power and to shield the power stage and the high-voltage pack from overload.
Failed current sensing element in the compressor power module
Open internal connection between sensor and control board
Compressor or climate module software error
Compressor does not start, no cooling
Fault stored in the climate or compressor module
P0EAE: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Range/Performance
P0EAE says the compressor current reading is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state, for example a value that does not match motor speed or load.
Calculation error in the climate module software (Audi A3 e-tron, update available)
Drifting current measurement in the compressor
Internal compressor fault confirmed by the guided test
MIL on without an engine module fault code
Air conditioning may or may not be restricted
Entry stored as passive or sporadic
P0EAF: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit Low

P0EAF reports that the compressor current signal sits at the bottom of its measuring range. In a running compressor this cannot be true, so the module suspects the measuring chain: a grounded signal path, a sensing chip without supply or an offset error inside the power module. No manufacturer documents P0EAF publicly.
Current signal path shorted to ground
Offset error of the measurement in the power module
Compressor shut down, warm air from the vents
P0EB0: A/C Compressor Motor Current Sensor Circuit High

P0EB0 flags a current sensor signal at the top end of its range, beyond what the compressor drive could ever draw. It differs from a genuine overcurrent such as P0D6F, where the measurement is trusted and the motor is overloaded: here the signal itself is suspect, for example after a short to a supply voltage or a failed sensing element.
Current signal shorted to a supply voltage
Failed sensing element in the compressor inverter
Real overload from a stiff compressor or excessive refrigerant charge
Compressor switches off right after starting
No cooling, fault message in the climate display
P0EB1: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit

Electric A/C compressors run a three-phase permanent-magnet motor whose inverter measures the phase currents in order to commutate it and limit torque. P0EB1 is the general circuit fault of the phase U current sensor: the controller gets no usable signal and gives no finer verdict on it. P0EB1 is not described in any public maker document.
Failed phase U current sensor in the compressor inverter
Open signal path between sensor and inverter controller
Fault on the inverter control board
Compressor does not run, cabin stays warm
P0EB2: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit High

P0EB2 is set when the phase U current sensor of the electric A/C compressor sends a signal above its valid window. Current sensors in such inverters often output a voltage centred on zero current, so a stuck-high output reads like a large current in one direction even with the motor at rest. No manufacturer documents P0EB2 publicly.
Phase U signal shorted to the sensor supply
Damaged Hall element of the phase U sensor
Defect on the inverter board affecting the U channel
Compressor will not start or stops at once
P0EB3: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Circuit Low

P0EB3 means the phase U current signal has fallen below its permitted range. Depending on the sensor design this looks like a large negative current or like no signal at all; either way the controller can no longer trust the U-phase value it needs to drive the motor smoothly. No maker documents P0EB3 publicly.
Phase U sensing path shorted to ground
Supply to the phase U sensor missing
Internal fault in the compressor inverter
Fault message after switching the A/C on
P0EB4: A/C Compressor Motor Phase U Current Sensor Range/Performance

P0EB4 concerns the plausibility of the phase U current reading of an electric A/C compressor. The value is in range but disagrees with what the controller can work out for itself: in a motor fed by three wires the phase currents must add up to roughly zero, and each phase should follow the commanded current pattern.
Offset or gain drift of the phase U sensor
Ageing measurement circuit on the inverter board
Winding fault in the compressor motor distorting the currents
Compressor runs roughly or noisily before switching off
P0EB5: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit High

P0EB5 is the high-range fault of the phase V current sensor in the compressor inverter. The reading lies above the window the sensor can produce in normal service, which points to a short towards supply voltage, a defective sensing element or an internal fault in the power module rather than to real overcurrent.
