Phase V signal shorted towards supply voltage
Internal fault in the compressor power module
Battery may warm up more during fast charging
P0EB6: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit Low

P0EB6 reports that the phase V current signal reads below its permissible minimum. The compressor's power module cannot regulate phase V without it and stops the motor. Candidates are a sensing path pulled to ground, a sensor that has lost its supply or a defect on the inverter board; a problem in the refrigerant circuit cannot produce this code.
Phase V sensing path pulled to ground
Phase V sensor has lost its supply
Defect in the V channel of the inverter board
Fault stored in the compressor control module
P0EB7: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Range/Performance

With P0EB7 the compressor's phase V current value passes the electrical limits but is not credible. The controller compares it with the other two phases and with the current it is commanding; a persistent offset, a reading that lags or is scaled wrongly, or a three-phase sum far from zero all point at the V sensor. No manufacturer documents P0EB7 publicly.
Persistent offset or scaling error of the phase V sensor
Slow or filtered V-phase measurement on the inverter board
Fault in the V winding or its internal lead
Uneven compressor running or humming noise
P0EB8: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit High

P0EB8 indicates that the phase W current sensor of the compressor inverter delivers a value above its usable range. Since the motor is not actually drawing such a current, a short to a positive supply in the sensing circuit or a failed sensor element is the most probable explanation.
W-phase sensing circuit shorted to a positive supply
Fault in the W input of the inverter controller
Compressor will not restart until the fault is cleared
P0EB9: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit Low

P0EB9 is stored when the phase W current signal drops beneath its lower limit, for instance after the signal wire has made contact with ground or after the sensor has lost its feed. The value is then useless for motor control, and the compressor module shuts the drive down rather than run it on two phases of information.
Phase W measuring line shorted to ground
Defect of the W measurement inside the compressor module
P0EBA: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Range/Performance

P0EBA covers an implausible phase W current reading in an electric A/C compressor: the signal stays in range, yet it does not agree with the commanded current, the rotor position or the two other phases. No manufacturer documents P0EBA publicly.
Fault in the W measurement on the inverter board
Rotor position estimate disturbed, making the W current look wrong
P0EBB: A/C Compressor Motor Phase V Current Sensor Circuit

P0EBB is the general circuit code for the compressor's phase V current sensor, numbered after the W-phase codes instead of at the start of the V series. The module receives no usable V-phase value at all and does not classify it further as high, low or implausible.
Loose internal plug between sensor and board
Failed phase V sensor or inverter board
Air conditioning and possibly battery cooling unavailable
P0EBC: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit

P0EBC is the general circuit fault of the first refrigerant temperature sensor in the air conditioning loop: the control module gets no usable reading from it and does not narrow the fault down to high or low. Volkswagen lists P0EBC00 for the 2021 ID.4 as an electrical fault of refrigerant temperature sensor 1 in the A/C module (address 0008).
Internal electrical fault of the refrigerant pressure/temperature sender (VW G395)
Corroded connector or damaged wiring to the sensor
Faulty sensor input in the climate control module
Air conditioning inoperative or not cooling
Fault entry stored in the climate control module
P0EBD: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

P0EBD means the signal voltage of refrigerant temperature sensor A sits at the top of its range. With the usual NTC thermistor that equals an extremely cold reading, and in practice it points to an open signal path, a disconnected plug or a short to the reference voltage. No manufacturer documents P0EBD publicly.
Open signal or ground wire, or unplugged connector
Signal wire shorted to the reference or supply voltage
Compressor stays off or A/C output is reduced
Implausibly low refrigerant temperature in live data
P0EBE: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low

P0EBE is logged when the voltage from refrigerant temperature sensor A falls close to zero. For an NTC element a low voltage stands for high temperature, so the controller sees refrigerant that seems far too hot. Real heat at that level is unlikely; a signal wire chafed through to ground or a thermistor shorted internally is the usual finding.
Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
A/C compressor switched off as a precaution
Live data shows an unrealistically hot refrigerant
P0EBF: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor A Range/Performance

P0EBF reports that sensor A gives an electrically valid but implausible refrigerant temperature. Three makers name it. Audi stores P0EBF00 as passive or sporadic in the Climatronic module of the 2016 A3 e-tron; bulletin 2047037 blames a miscalculation in the refrigerant self-check and points to TSB 2046942.
Software misjudgement after preconditioning or self-check (Volvo, Audi; update available)
Wrong refrigerant charge distorting the comparison values
Check engine lamp on (Volvo) or MIL requested by the climate module (Audi)
Fault stored as intermittent or sporadic
A/C may cool poorly or not at all
P0EC0: A/C Compressor Motor Phase W Current Sensor Circuit

P0EC0 is the umbrella circuit code for the phase W current sensor in the inverter of an electric A/C compressor. It applies when no valid W-phase value arrives at all, without a split into high, low or implausible; those cases have their own codes P0EB8 to P0EBA. Like the phase V circuit code P0EBB it is numbered out of sequence.
Interrupted W-phase sensing path inside the inverter
Failed W-phase current sensor or inverter board
Missing supply voltage for the current sensors
Electric A/C compressor does not start
No cabin cooling, battery cooling via refrigerant may be limited
P0EC1: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit

P0EC1 covers a circuit fault of a second refrigerant temperature sensor, found mainly on electrified cars whose heat pump or battery chiller measures the refrigerant at several points. The module receives no usable value from sensor B. No manufacturer publishes P0EC1 or says which of its sensors counts as B.
Failed sensor B or combined pressure/temperature sender
Wiring, connector or shared LIN line fault
Mixed part versions on one LIN line after a repair
Heat pump or A/C switched off or limited
Fault stored in the climate control module
P0EC2: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

With P0EC2 the signal of refrigerant temperature sensor B is stuck near the reference voltage. An NTC thermistor would only get there at extreme cold, so an open circuit somewhere in the loop is far more likely. No manufacturer documents P0EC2 publicly.
Open signal or ground line between sensor B and module
Connector not fully seated after A/C work
Very low refrigerant temperature shown for sensor B
Heating via heat pump or cooling unavailable
P0EC3: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P0EC3 stands for a sensor B signal pulled down toward ground. Because a thermistor of the NTC type lowers its resistance as it warms, the module reads a refrigerant temperature far above anything the system could reach. Typical culprits are a harness pinched against the body, water inside the plug or a sensor that has failed shorted.
Harness pinched against the body, signal shorted to ground
Water ingress in the sensor plug
A/C compressor held off, cabin not cooled
Charging or driving power possibly limited if battery cooling depends on the loop
P0EC4: A/C Refrigerant Temperature Sensor B Range/Performance
P0EC4 is a plausibility fault: sensor B delivers a voltage inside its normal window, yet the temperature it reports does not agree with other information. No manufacturer documents P0EC4 publicly.
Sensor B drifting out of tolerance
Sensor not seated properly on the pipe, poor thermal contact
Incorrect refrigerant charge shifting the comparison values
Uneven or weak cooling, compressor cycling oddly
Fault often appears only after a long standstill
P0EC5: A/C Compressor Motor Speed Sensor Range/Performance

P0EC5 means the speed information of the electrically driven compressor motor is implausible: the motor does not turn at the speed the controller expects, or the reported value contradicts other data. Mazda uses the code on the 2024 to 2026 CX-90 PHEV and 2025 to 2026 CX-70 PHEV, describing P0EC5:00 in the PCM as an error signal coming from the compressor.
Internal short in the electric compressor after overcurrent (Mazda PHEV)
Blown high-voltage A/C fuse cutting compressor power
Mechanical drag or lack of oil keeping the motor below target speed
Accompanying compressor voltage, communication or insulation codes
P0EC6: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit/Open

P0EC6 concerns the control side of the relay that switches power to air conditioning components, typically the compressor or climate electronics. The module driving the relay coil notices that its output does not behave as commanded, most often because the coil circuit is open. No manufacturer documents P0EC6 publicly, and the exact wiring differs by maker.
Relay coil burnt open or relay missing
Open control wire or loose relay socket terminal
Failed output driver in the controlling module
A/C or electric compressor completely without function
No relay click when A/C is requested
P0EC7: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit Low

P0EC7 is set when the control line of the relay feeding the A/C reads too low a voltage, usually because it is shorted to ground. What the driver feels depends on how the coil is switched: with a low-side driver a grounded line can keep the relay energised even with the A/C off, while with a high-side driver the relay simply cannot be switched on.
Relay control line chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted turns in the relay coil
Output stage of the module stuck low
A/C power stays on with A/C switched off, or never switches on
Possible battery drain while parked if the relay stays energised
P0EC8: A/C Power Supply Relay Control Circuit High
P0EC8 indicates that the relay control circuit for the A/C power supply carries too high a voltage, typically a short to a battery-fed wire.
Control line shorted to a battery-fed wire
Relay coil with too low resistance overloading the driver
A/C has no power and stays off
Relay may stay energised permanently on high-side switched designs
P0EC9: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve A Stuck/Open

P0EC9 reports that refrigerant distribution valve A, a solenoid valve that splits refrigerant between branches of the A/C circuit, stays open or does not close on command. Such a fault is usually detected indirectly, because pressure or temperature behind the valve fails to react when it should be shut.
Faulty self-test calculation in the climate control software (Audi A3 e-tron, fixed by update)
Valve held open by dirt, debris or a sticking armature
Weak solenoid coil that no longer pulls the valve fully shut
MIL on without a code in the engine control module
Code stored passive/sporadic in the climate control module
Reduced or uneven cooling in one branch, or no noticeable change at all
P0ECA: Hybrid/EV Battery Temperature Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation

P0ECA treats the temperature sensors of the hybrid or traction battery as one system: the battery controller compares the readings with each other and flags the group when one of them strays from the rest or shows an impossible value. Ford documents it for its 2019 hybrid and plug-in models.
One battery thermistor drifting away from the others
Battery controller software misjudging the comparison (Bentley super capacitor, update 114)
Loose or corroded connector on the temperature sense harness inside the pack
Genuine local hot spot, e.g. a blocked cooling channel at one module
Hybrid or battery warning, MIL depending on manufacturer
Reduced electric power or charging rate
On the Bentayga, Dynamic Ride fault message and no roll compensation
P0ECB: Hybrid/EV Battery Voltage Sensor System - Multiple Sensor Correlation

P0ECB indicates that the voltage measurements of the hybrid/EV battery contradict each other. Battery controllers usually capture the same voltage along more than one path, for example the whole pack directly and as the sum of all cell readings, or each half of the pack against its own cells; once these paths drift apart, at least one sensor must be wrong.
Drifting pack or half-pack voltage sensor in the battery controller
Loose or corroded cell sense lead falsifying the cell sum
Internal fault of the cell monitoring electronics
Measurement taken on the wrong side of a contactor that is not fully closed
Limited electric power, unstable state of charge display
Contactors may stay open, vehicle may not reach ready mode
P0ECC: P0ECC is the general voltage code for hybrid/EV battery E. The letters A to F mark separately monitored sub-batteries, modules or energy stores of one system; E is the fifth, so the code can only occur where a manufacturer divides its storage into at least five such units.
Aged or damaged cells in unit E
Fault in the voltage sense leads or connectors of unit E
Battery controller measuring or software fault
P0ECD: P0ECD flags an unstable voltage in hybrid/EV battery E: the value moves faster or further than the controller tolerates, whereas a lasting offset would set P0ECE or P0ECF. No manufacturer documents P0ECD publicly.
Cell with high internal resistance whose voltage collapses under load
Loose busbar screw or cell connector in unit E
Corroded or intermittent voltage sense terminal
Battery controller software, curable by update
Intermittent battery warning, often only under load
P0ECE: P0ECE sets when the voltage of hybrid/EV battery E remains below the window the controller expects for the present load and charge. Its counterparts are P0ECF for too high and P0ECD for unstable readings. No manufacturer documents P0ECE publicly.
Unit E deeply discharged after long standstill or a high self-discharge cell
Internal short or capacity loss in a module of unit E
Balancing switch stuck on and draining one cell group
Engine starts more often, EV mode unavailable
P0ECF: P0ECF is stored when unit E of the hybrid/EV battery exceeds its upper voltage limit. It mirrors P0ECE, while unstable readings belong to P0ECD. No manufacturer documents P0ECF publicly.
Cell balancing of unit E no longer works, group overcharged
Voltage sense channel reading too high
Vehicle may switch off the high-voltage system
P0ED0: P0ED0 is the general voltage code of hybrid/EV battery F, the sixth and last unit in this letter series. It reports an implausible voltage of the unit without separating unstable (P0ED1), low (P0ED2) and high (P0ED3) readings.
Aged or damaged cells in unit F
Open or high-resistance voltage sense lead of unit F
Cell monitoring electronics or software fault
P0ED1: P0ED1 reports that the voltage of hybrid/EV battery F fluctuates beyond the permitted band instead of staying steadily off, which would be P0ED2 or P0ED3. No manufacturer documents P0ED1 publicly.
Cell group of unit F drifting because balancing cannot keep up
Sense lead or connector with intermittent contact
Warning that comes and goes, often over bumps or under load
P0ED2: P0ED2 means hybrid/EV battery F delivers less voltage than the controller predicts from current draw and state of charge. No manufacturer documents P0ED2 publicly.
Aged module in unit F with lost capacity
Cell with internal leakage drained during standstill
High-resistance connection inside unit F dropping voltage under load
P0ED3: P0ED3 is logged once battery F of the hybrid/EV system climbs above its permitted maximum voltage. It is the high member of the F series, next to P0ED2 (low) and P0ED1 (unstable). No manufacturer documents P0ED3 publicly. GM's hybrid tables show how strictly overvoltage is treated at pack level: above 479 V the P0ABD monitor fails within one trip.
Balancing circuit of unit F failed, cells overcharged
Measuring channel of unit F reading too high
Charging refused or regenerative braking weak
P0ED4: P0ED4 is the general current fault for phase X of the hybrid generator. J2012 names the generator phases U, V and W and adds a separate X, Y, Z series, which presumably serves machines with a second three-phase winding set fed by its own inverter bridge; which vehicles use it is not published, and no manufacturer documents P0ED4.
Fault in the inverter bridge or current regulation for phase X
Phase X current sensor out of tolerance
Loose or damaged high-voltage connection of phase X
Reduced charging, engine may start less smoothly
P0ED5: P0ED5 means that phase X of the hybrid generator carries, or appears to carry, too little current while the generator is supposed to deliver torque. No manufacturer documents P0ED5 publicly.
Open or loose phase X cable or terminal
Inverter power switch for phase X not conducting
Burnt or broken winding connection in the generator
Weak or no battery charging by the generator
Rough engine start or vibration from the generator
P0ED6: P0ED6 is stored when the current in phase X of the hybrid generator exceeds its permitted limit. No manufacturer documents P0ED6 publicly.
Turn-to-turn or ground short in the phase X winding
Current sensor reading too high (false overcurrent)
Sudden hybrid system shutdown or loss of ready mode
P0ED7: P0ED7 is the general current code for phase Y, the middle phase of the generator's X-Y-Z set. Without being narrowed to low (P0ED8) or high (P0ED9), it says that the Y current no longer behaves as the inverter controller expects. No manufacturer documents P0ED7 publicly, and it is not known which production machines label their phases X, Y and Z.
Inverter fault affecting the phase Y bridge
Phase cables mixed up or poorly seated after repair work
P0ED8: P0ED8 reports too little current in phase Y of the hybrid generator. No manufacturer documents P0ED8 publicly. Ford's 2019 hybrid summary describes a phase circuit test at power-up for the U-V-W phases: the motor/generator control unit declares a phase circuit fault if less than 5 A is seen over the 100 ms test window.
Open or corroded phase Y cable or terminal
Inverter switch for phase Y not turning on
Phase Y current sensor reading too low
Uneven running or noise from the transaxle
P0ED9: P0ED9 is set when phase Y of the hybrid generator draws more current than allowed. No manufacturer documents P0ED9 publicly. Overcurrent in a generator phase is a protection event: the inverter must switch off within fractions of a millisecond, before its power semiconductors are destroyed.
Short in the phase Y winding or to the housing
Chafed phase cable shorting to ground
Hybrid system shuts down, vehicle may lose ready mode
P0EDA: P0EDA is the general current fault of phase Z, the last of the three X-Y-Z generator phases, without the detail of P0EDB (low) or P0EDC (high). No manufacturer documents P0EDA publicly.
Phase Z current sensor offset or failure
Inverter fault on the phase Z bridge
Poor contact at the phase Z high-voltage terminal
Hybrid warning, often with further phase or sum codes
P0EDB: P0EDB means phase Z of the hybrid generator shows less current than the commanded operating point calls for. No manufacturer documents P0EDB publicly.
Loose or corroded phase Z high-voltage terminal
Broken conductor in the phase Z winding
Power switch for phase Z no longer conducting
Humming or vibration from the hybrid transaxle
P0EDC: P0EDC is the overcurrent code for phase Z of the hybrid generator and ends the X-Y-Z series. No manufacturer documents P0EDC publicly; the closest published logic is Ford's for its U-V-W generator phases (P0A71, P0A74, P0A77), which also flags any current above 15 A in the first 200 ms after power-up, a moment when the machine should be idle.
Damaged or leaking power module for phase Z
Insulation fault or turn short in the phase Z winding
Hybrid system shutdown, engine may not start
MIL and hybrid warning, possibly with sum check codes
P0EDD: P0EDD is the state-of-health verdict for the second section of a traction battery: section B has lost so much capacity or gained so much internal resistance that it falls below the maker's limit. P0A7F covers section A, P0EDE to P0EE1 sections C to F.
Battery module or cell group in section B aged beyond its limit
Battery controller software misjudging state of health (FCA reflash cases)
Pack defect covered by a warranty extension (Pacifica Hybrid)
MIL or hybrid system warning on
Engine runs more often, less electric assist
P0EDE: P0EDE flags the third battery section, C, as worn out. The controller estimates each section's usable capacity and resistance from voltage behaviour under load and at rest; if section C drifts too far from its new-state values, it is judged deteriorated.
Cells in battery group 3 aged (capacity loss, higher resistance)
Strong voltage spread inside the section
Controller estimate wrong, module still healthy
Electric driving mode cannot be selected or ends early
P0EDF: P0EDF belongs to the fourth section of the traction battery. It is not a sensor or wiring code but a capacity and power judgement: the battery controller has concluded that section D can no longer deliver what the maker expects of a healthy unit. Audi maps P0EDF00 on the Q5 PHEV to battery group 4 in the battery management unit 008C.
High-voltage module of group 4 worn out
Single weak cell pulling the section down
Evaluation logic of the battery controller
P0EE0: With P0EE0 the controller reports ageing of section E, the fifth part of the traction battery. A section is usually a module or a group of cell blocks with its own monitoring; once its share of the pack has lost too much capacity or become too resistive, the whole battery can no longer reach its rated energy, which shows up first as shorter electric range.
Cell voltages in the section spread too far (often with P0BBD)
P0EE1: P0EE1 is the last code of the P0E range for section ageing and covers section F. The series runs A (P0A7F) and B to F (P0EDD to P0EE1); for further sections J2012 continues in the P2 block, with G and H as P2CCC and P2CCD.
Section aged faster due to heat or poor cooling
Evaluation error of the battery controller
P0EE2: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Stuck/Open

P0EE2 says the second refrigerant distribution valve, B, stays open or fails to close. In plug-in hybrids and EVs such shut-off valves route refrigerant either to the cabin evaporator or to a chiller that cools the battery; Egelhof sells solenoid versions with 12 V or 24 V coils for exactly this use.
Thermal management software misjudging the valve (Audi J1024)
Valve seat contaminated or armature stuck open
Weak coil that no longer moves the armature
Often no noticeable effect beyond the warning
P0EE3: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit/Open

P0EE3 concerns the wiring between the controlling module and refrigerant valve B, most often an interrupted path. With the output switched off, the driver normally sees a defined voltage through the coil; with it switched on, current flows.
Loose, corroded or pushed-back pin at the valve connector
Broken coil winding in valve B
Broken wire in the harness to the valve
Valve B no longer switches, affected refrigerant branch stays as it is
P0EE4: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit Low

P0EE4 is stored when the control line of refrigerant valve B is pulled to a lower voltage than the driver commands, usually by a short to ground. With a high-side driver the valve would then stay energised or the output would be overloaded; with a low-side driver the coil may be switched on permanently. No manufacturer documents P0EE4 publicly.
Control wire chafed through to ground
Coil winding shorted to the valve body
Valve B behaves as if permanently energised or not at all
P0EE5: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit High

P0EE5 means the control line of refrigerant valve B carries more voltage than its commanded state allows. If the driver switches the coil to ground, a short to a 12 V feed is the classic reason; with some driver types an open coil can also float the line high.
Control wire shorted to a 12 V feed
Open coil letting the line float high
Faulty output stage in the controlling module
Cabin or battery cooling not working as requested
P0EE6: A/C Refrigerant Distribution Valve B Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High
P0EE6 is reported by the output stage itself: the switch that powers refrigerant valve B has measured too much current or got too hot and has protected itself.
Shorted turns in the valve B coil raising the current
Partial short in the valve wiring
Valve B switched off, cooling branch not served
P0EE7: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit

P0EE7 is the general circuit code for the second temperature sensor of the charging inlet. High-current inlets carry several sensors; the supplier Sailtran fits one PT1000 at the L1 pin and two independent PT1000 at DC+ and DC- of its CCS2 inlet, so A and B often stand for two different contacts.
Loose low-voltage connector between inlet and charger
Damaged sensor wire in the inlet harness
Failed sensor element B (usually means a new inlet)
P0EE8: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

P0EE8 is set when sensor B in the charging inlet delivers an electrically valid value that does not fit the situation. A plausibility test may compare it with sensor A on the neighbouring pin, with the outside temperature after a long rest, or with the heating expected for the charge current.
Worn station plug heating one contact unevenly
Sensor B lost thermal contact to its pin
P0EE9: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit Low

P0EE9 reports that the voltage of coupler temperature sensor B lies under its valid window. What that means thermally depends on the element. An NTC thermistor loses resistance when heated, so a low signal reads as an extremely hot pin.
Sensor B signal wire shorted to ground
Moisture or water in the charging inlet
P0EEA: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit High

P0EEA is the opposite case: the sensor B signal of the charging inlet sits above the valid window. In a pull-up design that is what an unplugged connector, a broken sensor wire or a short to a supply voltage looks like.
Unplugged connector or broken sensor B wire
Signal wire shorted to a supply voltage
Open sensor element B inside the inlet
Charging aborted at once or refused
P0EEB: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature Sensor B Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0EEB catches a sensor B signal from the charging inlet that jumps or drops out for moments. A metal contact and its plastic housing have real thermal mass, so a change of many degrees within milliseconds cannot be a true temperature and points to the circuit. No manufacturer documents P0EEB publicly.
Loose contact in the sensor B circuit or at the charger plug
Moisture that comes and goes in the inlet connector
Cracked sensor element with temperature-dependent contact
Fault cannot be reproduced at once
P0EEC: Battery Energy Control Module B Performance

P0EEC says a second battery energy control module, B, has failed its own internal checks. Large or split packs can carry more than one such controller, each watching cell voltages, temperatures and current of its part. No manufacturer documents P0EEC publicly.
Software fault or watchdog reset in module B
Low or unstable 12 V supply to the module
Internal hardware fault of module B
P0EED: Hybrid/EV Battery System Discharge Circuit Performance

P0EED concerns the active discharge path on the high-voltage side, the circuit that drains the DC link capacitors once the contactors have opened so that no dangerous voltage lingers. The code says this path does not perform as intended, whereas P0C76 only judges how long the voltage takes to fall.
Loose or arcing high-voltage cable terminal at the inverter module (FCA 08-107-17)
Discharge resistor or its switching transistor open or degraded
Internal fault in the inverter or its voltage measurement
Main contactor sticking closed so the bus stays charged
MIL or hybrid system warning on
Loss of propulsion or vehicle will not enter ready mode
Further high-voltage codes such as P0C76 or P0C77 stored at the same time
P0EEE: Battery Charger Coupler Temperature B Too High

P0EEE is the overheating verdict for the second measuring point of the charging inlet: sensor B works electrically, but the contact it watches has become too hot, so charging is throttled or stopped. Electrical faults of sensor B have their own codes P0EE7 to P0EEB; overheating at point A is P0E5F, at points C and D P2E4E and P2E53.
Software of the charging diagnostic module misjudging the temperature (Ford SSM 55080)
Worn, dirty or corroded pins in the charging inlet
Loose crimp or screw connection behind the inlet pin raising contact resistance
Worn plug of the charging station heating the contact
DC fast charging stops or does not start
Charging power reduced while AC charging still works
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
P0EEF: Drive Motor A Control Module Overtemperature

P0EEF reports that the control module of drive motor A, the inverter electronics that switch the motor phases, has run too hot. The temperature reading itself is considered valid; faults of the inverter temperature sensors, such as P0AEF, are separate codes. No manufacturer documents P0EEF publicly.
Low coolant level or air in the power electronics cooling loop
Electronics coolant pump weak or failed
Long full-load operation such as towing or climbing in high ambient heat
Degraded power semiconductors or thermal interface inside the module
Reduced drive power or hybrid system warning
Electric drive switched off until the module cools
P0EF0: Battery Charger Coupler Unlock Disabled - High Voltage Present
P0EF0 describes a safety lockout rather than a broken actuator: the vehicle keeps the charging connector locked because it still measures hazardous voltage at the inlet.
DC charging contactor stuck closed, inlet stays connected to the battery
Charging station does not switch off or discharge its output
Faulty inlet voltage measurement reporting voltage that is not there
Charging control software ending the session in the wrong order
Charging cable cannot be unplugged after charging
Charging fault message, sometimes only at certain stations
Emergency release of the connector needed
P0EF1: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit

P0EF1 is the general circuit code for the temperature sensor of drive motor C, the third traction motor on vehicles with three or more electric machines. It must not be confused with P2DB1, which means sensor C inside drive motor A.
Loose, corroded or damaged connector of the motor C temperature sensor
Temperature sensor in the winding failed
Controller configuration not matching the installed motor (Volvo RD21-022)
Warning lamp for the electric drive
Motor temperature shown as invalid in the scan tool
P0EF2: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Range/Performance

P0EF2 flags a plausibility error of the drive motor C temperature sensor: its signal is electrically fine, yet the value does not fit what the controller expects. No manufacturer documents P0EF2 publicly.
Sensor no longer in thermal contact with the winding
Corroded pin adding resistance and shifting the reading
Comparison sensor such as coolant or oil temperature reading wrong
Warning lamp after a long standstill, often at the first start of the day
Usually no noticeable drivability change at first
Power limitation of motor C in some cases
P0EF3: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit Low

P0EF3 is stored when the signal voltage of the drive motor C temperature sensor drops below its valid range. With the usual NTC thermistor on a pull-up resistor, a low voltage stands for an extremely hot winding, so electrically the suspects are a short to ground, a pinched harness or a sensor with an internal short.
Signal wire shorted to ground or motor housing
Water or coolant in the connector bridging the pins
Drive power of motor C reduced immediately
Implausibly high motor temperature in the live data
P0EF4: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit High

P0EF4 reports a drive motor C temperature signal above the plausible window. For an NTC sensor on a pull-up this equals an impossibly cold winding, the picture produced by an open sensor, a broken wire, an unplugged connector or a short to the reference voltage. No manufacturer documents P0EF4 publicly.
Sensor connector unplugged, loose or with pushed-back pin
Broken signal or ground wire of the sensor
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Motor temperature stuck at the lowest value in the live data
P0EF5: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

P0EF5 covers a drive motor C temperature signal that jumps or drops out for short moments instead of staying wrong. Because of the thermal mass of a traction motor, the winding temperature can only change slowly; a step of many degrees within milliseconds therefore points to the wiring and not to the motor.
Loose or corroded pins in the motor connector
Harness chafing at brackets or moving parts
Cracked sensor lead inside the motor that opens with vibration or heat
Warning lamp that comes and goes
Short power interruptions of motor C, often on rough roads
Jumping motor temperature in the live data
P0EF6: Drive Motor C Temperature Sensor Over Temperature
P0EF6 is not an electrical fault: the drive motor C temperature sensor delivers a believable value, but that value has passed the motor's protection limit. No manufacturer documents P0EF6 publicly.
Low coolant or oil level, or air in the motor cooling circuit
Failed coolant or oil pump, or clogged cooler
Long full-load phases such as towing, track use or steep climbs
Shorted turns in the stator winding generating extra heat
Clearly reduced power until the motor has cooled down
P0EF7: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit

P0EF7 stands for an electrical fault in the second input voltage sensor of on-board charger A, the measuring channel that reads the AC supply voltage coming from a wallbox, station or household outlet. Chargers designed for several phases or split-phase supply may carry more than one such channel; the first one, sensor A, uses P0D3D to P0D41.
Fault in the voltage sensing stage inside the charger
Open or high-resistance signal line between sensor and controller
Corroded low-voltage connector at the charger
AC charging does not start or stops shortly after start
Charging fault message in the cluster or app
P0EF8: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance
P0EF8 is set when input voltage sensor B of charger A delivers a value that is electrically valid but wrong for the situation. No manufacturer documents P0EF8 publicly.
Offset drift of the voltage sensing electronics in the charger
Partial internal fault of the charger input stage
Charger software misjudging the plausibility window
AC charging interrupted or slower than expected
Code may set while driving without any charging attempt
P0EF9: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit Low
P0EF9 means the signal of input voltage sensor B in charger A has fallen below its valid range. No manufacturer documents P0EF9 publicly.
Missing supply voltage of the sensing circuit
Internal fault of the charger measuring stage
Charging fault message right after plugging in
DC fast charging usually still possible
P0EFA: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor B Circuit High

With P0EFA, the signal from the second input voltage sensor of charger A, sensor B, lies above the plausible window. No manufacturer documents P0EFA publicly. GM's comparable check for sensor A, P0D40 in its 2019 plug-in hybrid tables, trips at a duty cycle of 92 % or more but below 100 %, or at exactly 0 %, in 30 of 40 samples, and is rated Type B.
Defective measuring stage on the charger board
Open signal line pulled high by the input circuit
Signal shorted to a supply voltage
AC charging refused or ends after a few seconds
P0EFB: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit

P0EFB flags an electrical fault on the third AC input voltage channel of on-board charger A, sensor C. Channel A reports through P0D3D to P0D41, channel B through P0EF7 to P0EFA; a third channel fits chargers that read each phase of a three-phase supply separately.
Failed measuring channel C on the charger board (divider, amplifier or converter input)
Open or loose sense connection for this phase inside the charger or at the AC inlet harness
Charger software marking a valid channel as faulty
AC charging does not start or is limited
Possible reduced charging power on three-phase stations
Charging fault shown in the cluster or app
P0EFC: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit Range/Performance
With P0EFC, sensor C of charger A delivers an electrically sound signal whose value conflicts with the charger's other readings. No manufacturer documents P0EFC publicly.
Voltage dips, brown-out or power cut at the outlet or station during charging (GM PIC5803 for the sensor A code)
Faulty or poorly calibrated charging cord set or wallbox
Gain or offset drift of measuring channel C in the charger
Charging stops part-way or does not reach full charge
Fault appears only at certain outlets or stations
Charging fault message, sometimes with a warning lamp
P0EFD: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit Low

P0EFD reports that the reading of input voltage sensor C in charger A sits below its plausible band. No manufacturer documents P0EFD publicly. GM's 2011 Volt charger module gives a reference for sensor A: once AC is detected at the inlet, a peak value under 90 V for 1500 ms within a 1875 ms window sets P0D3F, Type A with the warning lamp after one trip.
One phase missing at the supply (tripped breaker or fault in the station or cable)
Sense path of channel C shorted to ground
Defective divider or converter input for channel C in the charger
AC charging refused right after plugging in
Charging works on a different station or outlet
P0EFE: Battery Charger A Input Voltage Sensor C Circuit High
P0EFE is stored when channel C of charger A reports more input voltage than a household or station supply can deliver. No manufacturer documents P0EFE publicly.
Open lower resistor in the voltage divider of channel C
Sense signal shorted to the converter reference or a supply rail
Actual overvoltage or surge from the supply
AC charging stops within seconds of starting
P0FFF: P0FFF has no documented meaning. CARB requires the SAE J2012-defined codes such as P0xxx and P2xxx wherever possible and allows manufacturer-defined codes only in the ranges J2012 sets aside for them, such as P1xxx.
